News.title: Woman ‘seriously sexually assaulted’ while walking her dog in ‘terrifying’ attack – as cops launch manhunt
News.content:
HORROR 'ASSAULT' Woman ‘seriously sexually assaulted’ while walking her dog in ‘terrifying’ attack – as cops launch manhunt

COPS have launched a manhunt after a woman was allegedly seriously sexually assaulted near a popular park.

The victim had been walking her dog when she was said to have been targeted during the “terrifying” attack.

She was reportedly targeted near a playpark at around 10pm on September 8.

The attacker approached her, before seriously sexually assaulting her and then fleeing the area, cops said.





He is described as being white and around 5ft 9in tall and is believed to have been wearing a black beanie during the horror.

Police Scotland has urged anyone with more information on the attack, which occurred in Blantyre, South Lanarkshire, to come forward.

Det Sgt Raymond Giulianotti said: “This was a terrifying experience for the woman and extensive enquiries are ongoing to trace the individual responsible.

“This attack happened very close to a busy residential area, and we are appealing for help from the local community.



“If you heard or saw anything at all suspicious, or noticed a man matching the above description, please get in touch.

“We’d be particularly keen to hear from anyone with private CCTV or dashcam footage which could be of significance to our investigation.

“Incidents of this nature can understandably cause concern.

“We’ll have additional patrols in the area to provide reassurance as we continue our enquiries.”



Anyone with information has been asked to contact Police Scotland quoting incident 1402.

Crimestoppers can also be contacted anonymously on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Brit tourist, 54, dies while swimming at popular Bali beach – just after holidaymaker plunged down cliff on same island
News.content:
ISLAND TRAGEDY Brit tourist, 54, dies while swimming at popular Bali beach – just after holidaymaker plunged down cliff on same island

A BRIT tourist has died while swimming at a popular beach near Bali – just one day after another holidaymaker plunged to death on the same island.

The man, 54, drowned on Sunday afternoon at Crystal Bay Beach while on a trip with his family, according to local police.



Indonesian cops said: “The victim was a British citizen who was on vacation with his family.”

The tragic man and his loved ones were reportedly on a sightseeing tour of Nusa Penida island.



They had decided to stop at Crystal Bay beach for a swim at around 2:30pm, according to local media.

Their driver left the group and agreed to come back about an hour later.

But when the man failed to return to the meeting point, the driver went to find them before being told what had happened.

Emergency services rushed to the scene and took the Brit holidaymaker to Griya Penida Medical Clinic.

He was pronounced dead despite efforts to resuscitate him.

Police added: “According to the medical team, the victim was pronounced dead after fluid entered his lungs, causing cardiac arrest as a result of drowning.”



It is currently unclear what caused the man to drown in the sea.

His death came just one day after an Australian tourist died after plunging from a cliff on the same holiday hotspot island near Bali.

Brianna Cronin, 29, was found at the bottom of a steep drop at Kelingking Beach on Saturday morning.

The woman, an ecologist from Queensland, was initially found stuck on the side of the cliff, police said.

But as emergency services rushed to the scene, she tragically fell down and plummeted to her death.



Local authorities believe she dropped down onto the beach, which is also known as T-Rex Bay, at around 9am local time.

They said: “At the time, she was seeking an independent path toward the edge of the cliff before slipping and falling into the ravine.

“When found, the victim had sustained several fractures; we secured her onto a stretcher to facilitate the evacuation process.”

Kelingking beach is one of the most popular destinations for Bali tourists.

The shoreline offers panoramic views from the 180-metre-high coastal cliff.

News.title: M3 closed after lorry ploughs into central reservation & spills 300 litres of diesel – as road to remain shut for hours
News.content:
A MAJOR motorway has been forced to close after a lorry ploughed into the central reservation and spilled 300 litres of diesel on the road.

Commuters have been warned the M3 will remain shut throughout the “morning peak period” after the crash near Winchester, Hampshire.

Recovery crews have been scrambled to repair the damage after the eastbound smash in the early hours of this morning.

The HGV struck the central barrier between Junction 9, for the Winnall Interchange, and Junction 8, for the Popham Junction, at around 1am.





Some 300 litres of diesel then spilled across the busy route as the lorry’s fuel tank ruptured during the smash.

Teams managed to recover the HGV two hours later, but drivers have been warned a “full resurfacing” is required on the road.

Commuters are currently being diverted and have been urged to follow solid diamond symbol.

National Highways said: “The M3 eastbound in Hampshire is closed between J9 Winnall Interchange and the Popham Junction with the A303.



Eastbound diversion Road users are advised to exit at J9 and follow the route marked with a solid diamond symbol on local road signs From the M3 eastbound, leave at junction 9.

At the roundabout, use the 2nd exit and join the A34 towards Newbury.

Follow the A34 for approximately 8 miles to the A303 Bullington Cross Interchange.

Leave the A34 using the second slip road and continue to the roundabout.

At the roundabout use the first exit and join the A303 eastbound towards Basingstoke.

Follow the A303 for approximately 7.5 miles to the M3 junction 8 interchange, at which point the A303/M3 merges with the M3 eastbound.

“A Heavy Goods Vehicle struck the central reservation at approximately 01:00 resulting in its fuel tank becoming ruptured.

“As a result, there is a large amount (300 litres approximately) of diesel now spilt across the carriageway.

“The Heavy Goods Vehicle was recovered at 03:00.

“A full resurfacing of the road is required and therefore the M3 is likely to remain closed through the morning peak period whilst this is carried out.



“If this closure impacts on your planned route, please allow extra journey time.

“Plan ahead, you may wish to re-route or even delay your journey.”

News.title: Boy who survived 62 hours lost at sea desperately tried to hang onto bodies of his brother & cousin in harrowing ordeal
News.content:
A BOY lost at sea for 62 hours fought desperately to hold onto the bodies of his brother and cousin, his family has revealed.

Derek Parker Aghnaanga, 15, was the sole survivor after his fishing boat capsized in freezing waters off an Alaskan island on September 4.



Derek had been fishing for halibut with his older brother and cousin when their small skiff overturned near St. Lawrence Island and drifted into the Bering Sea.

His brother and cousin both died in the horror ordeal, leaving him alone on the overturned skiff for three days until rescuers finally spotted him.



His aunt, Colleen Walker, said her young nephew tried to hang on to his family for “as long as he could after they drowned,” in a recent GoFundMe appeal.

The alarm was first raised when the group didn’t return on schedule.

Read more in US news LOST AT SEA Boy, 15, is only survivor after fishing boat capsizes, killing brother & cousin

The Coast Guard eventually spotted the freezing, starving, exhausted teen sitting on the capsized boat around 10.30am on September 7.

Dramatic footage showed Derek still kneeling on the overturned boat before the Northwest Explorer blasted its horn to let him know help had arrived.

The teenager was unable to reach life rafts that had been dropped nearby and the crew had to throw him a line.

Rescue boat captain Adam White said: “We were lucky enough, because the kid was so tough, so strong that that he was able to grab a hold of a heaving line that we threw to him.



“And he was able to hold on while we sort of reeled him in. And I just, like, can’t believe how tough this kid is.”

Recounting the horror, the boy’s mom, Vina Kulowiyi, wrote on Facebook: “4 days and 3 nights. He lived on prayer with no food and water. … He said he sat like this praying the whole time.”

She said her son is now catching up on his sleep after the harrowing ordeal that claimed the lives of his brother, Sidney Kulowiyi, 35, and cousin, Barton Rookok, 34.



His mum revealed in an emotional post that a new grandchild in the family has been named after her son Sidney.

Sidney was the skiff’s captain and drowned after getting stuck under the capsized vessel.

Barton survived with Derek for a day before becoming distressed, entering the water and dying.

Rescue boat captain Adam told KTUU: “Through the teeth chattering, [Derek] had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff.”

The surviving teen was suffering hypothermia symptoms when Northwest Explorer crew members wrapped him in blankets and kept him talking as they headed toward home to reunite him with his family.



A week on, the family believe that one of the fishing lines which became tangled in the motor caused the boat to overturn.

The teen’s aunt said the entire village is mourning the tragic loss of the two lives.

She said: “Please donate what you can or share to help his family and my sister.

“All funds will go straight to my other nephew.”

News.title: Digital ID set to replace physical proof of age for buying booze at pubs and shops
News.content:
PUBS and shops will soon be able to accept digital ID as proof of age when buying alcohol.

Punters will be able to use their phone to prove their age instead of showing physical ID at boozers, festivals and concerts.



The new system will be available through apps such as Yoti which is used by young people for age-restricted cinema tickets.

The public will need to scan their face or enter a code on the app which then generates a token such as a QR code which last around 30 seconds to allow verification.



Ministers expect it will take some time for the age ID to be adopted before its scope is extended to tobacco and vape sales.

PM Andy Burnham scrapped a wider digital ID programme that was planned under Sir Keir Starmer.

Digital Government Minister Stephanie Peacock said: “It will remain an individual or business’ choice whether to use or adopt it, and physical ID will remain a valid way for customers to prove their age.

“This groundbreaking change in the law will mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information such as your name or address just to prove your age – allowing everyone to feel safer on a night out.”

Allen Simpson, boss of UKHospitality, said: “The roll-out of the voluntary digital proof of age will provide an easier experience for customers, allowing them to verify their age securely from their phones.”

News.title: Britain’s gas supply at risk this winter as Labour warned over North Sea drilling delay
News.content:
LABOUR has been urged to speed up its decision on North Sea drilling to avoid affecting gas supplies this winter.

Ministers have been warned by the sector the Jackdaw gas field is an “important component” for the UK but urgently needs to be given the green light.



More than 100 projects could be kick-started if ministers change the tax regime and licensing rules, which could unlock £50billion in investment.

But the Jackdaw decision is now likely to come after the October 8 by-election with Labour battling the Green Party for Sir Keir Starmer’s old seat.



Offshore Energies UK boss David Whitehouse said: “The truth is that Jackdaw is an important component of our gas delivery for the winter period 2026-27.

“It can produce up to 6% of the gas we will need and we are now at a point in the coming weeks where without regulatory approval we are going to delay the production of that field.



“We’re now at a point where further delays are going to push back bringing that production on line.”

He added: “I do think we are now at a point where we are looking for those decisions to come – and more broadly that signal that actually the UK wants to produce more of its own energy; wants to produce more oil and gas.”

The organisation also says more than 100 new oil and gas projects could be given the go-ahead if the government changes the tax regime for the sector and makes changes to licensing.



The sector is demanding reform of the Energy Profits Levy early next year, along with Ministers adopting new regulations that boost domestic supplies.

Mr Whitehouse said without the changes the “consequences are clear”.

He added: “We will continue to see the loss of jobs in the UK; we will continue to see significant, increasing imports of our energy; the country will become less resilient.”

The OEUK also warned that Europe’s gas storage levels “are now at a five-year low”.

Experts warn this could lead to sustained high European and UK’s gas prices throughout the winter.

News.title: Donald Trump blasts calls to slow AI development as ‘sick conspiracy’ that would hand China advantage
News.content:
DONALD Trump rejected calls to slow artificial intelligence development — branding opposition a “sick conspiracy” that would benefit China.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 1.2 per cent in early trading, while the broader S&P 500 slipped 0.5 per cent as fears of tighter controls swept through markets.



Nvidia, the chipmaking giant at the centre of the AI boom, sank 3.6 per cent, while robotics specialist Teradyne plunged 9.2 per cent.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which sells AI systems to businesses, was also among the biggest fallers.



The sell-off followed a warning from Anthropic boss Dario Amodei, who urged the industry to “slow the pace” of development to prevent powerful systems escaping human control.

He warned an AI swarm could potentially take over the internet within a year.



Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed the call, intensifying concerns that major companies could curb investment and delay new products.

Analysts warned that any retreat could hit economic growth, given the huge sums being poured into chips, data centres and other AI infrastructure.



Trump responded with a furious Truth Social post, claiming America needed no new AI “guardrails” beyond a “strong and smart” president.

He accused critics of helping China and insisted his administration already had sweeping criminal and regulatory powers over technology companies.

“Whoever wins AI, wins,” he declared, warning “conspiracy theorists, treasonists, traitors and leakers” to beware.

Despite the market rout, Nvidia remained the world’s most valuable company, with a market value of about $5trillion, underlining how heavily investors are betting on AI’s future.

News.title: By ignoring the people of Piddington, Labour is turning a deaf ear to all communities blighted by illegal migration
News.content:
Taking the Pidd

TODAY residents of the sleepy Oxfordshire village of Piddington will vote on securing independence from Great Britain.

The referendum result won’t be legally binding. But it will show the sheer force of their opposition to having more than 1,200 illegal migrant men being dumped on their doorstep.



Piddington is tiny. It has no shop, no pub and no school.

Yet Labour wants to convert a former MoD garrison into accommodation for undocumented asylum seekers who WON’T be locked up.



Potentially dangerous young men will be allowed to wander freely in and out.

When 1,000 migrants go missing every year and Essex County Council sends private security guards on to the streets, how does the Government expect to keep Piddington villagers safe?

For every female resident, including elderly grandmothers, mothers and daughters, ten young, unvetted men will be roaming the village.

Many widows and single mums living within a stone’s throw of the camp must face this alone.

Piddington women are now so scared they have even felt forced to take self-defence lessons.

The referendum is a response to their protests being met by a shaming wall of silence from the Government.



Many locals are asking: Where are the voices of female Labour MPs — usually so quick to rightly defend women and girls from male violence?

By ignoring the people of Piddington, Labour is cocking a deaf ear to all our communities blighted by illegal migration.

Unjust giving

LABOUR’S hypocrisy over donations to political parties is breath-taking.

It is up to Reform to prove that the £72million handed over by two crypto-currency billionaires is legal and within the rules.

But for ministers to start bleating that “democracy is not for sale” overlooks Labour’s own record.



Over the past 25 years, the party has taken £52million from Unite, £44million from Unison and £39million from the GMB.

Last year it took £5million from the unions and in 2024 accepted £4million from an offshore hedge fund.

Union leaders have repeatedly demanded extensions to workers’ rights and minimum wage increases. Labour has duly delivered both.

That’s one hell of a coincidence.

Driller killers

FOR every day that the Government fails to approve drilling in the North Sea, Britain’s bill for importing foreign energy soars.



Imports of liquefied natural gas from the US rose by nearly 40 per cent last year.

But a decision on the crucial Jackdaw gas field is not expected until after the Holborn and St Pancras by-election.

News.title: Virgin Media customers hit by major September change some call a 'real headache'
News.content:
Virgin Media customers hit by major September change some call a 'real headache'

People told their email accounts will be deleted unless they take action

View Image People with Virgin Media email accounts have been warned they will close down (Image: Getty)

Virgin Media customers have been told of a major change to their accounts - their email addresses are being axed. The service which has 5.5 million customers has said that its existing email customers will be moved to a new provider called Junara.

‌



This means that people will either have to go to a paid service - or find a new provider. The new was described as a ‘real headache’ as many people who have relatives who have used the service for decades will be forced to make the change.

‌



Virgin said for 99p people can have the first 12 months on Junara - but after that reports are that users will be charged £65 - for a service most get for free. On Reddit one user said: “People who have been with the same ISP for many years. If my MIL (in her 90s) loses her btinternet address she has had over 25 years it will be a real headache.”

‌



One added: “My brother still has an email address from when Virgin Media was called Blueyonder lol. I don’t know if it’s in active use or if he’s been told about this, but I think he still has some accounts that aren’t migrated to it. Others are just there because they just never bothered to change what accounts they set up with that email address.”

A user added: “Junara charges £65 per year per mailbox. Aliases feeding the same mailbox are just charged as a single mailbox, but if you have six separate mailboxes, you’re looking at nearly £400 a year to keep them after the first year.”

A Reddit user said: “VM will charge you 99p when they transfer you, and the service with Junara is free for one year. After that, Junara is going to be charging you £65 per mailbox per year (unless something strange happens - but if it was going to, they’d be saying it right now).

‌



“Remember that VM has around 5.5 million fixed broadband users, so the 99p ‘transfer fee’ will net them £5.5 million just for turning something off. It also has over 40 million mobile users, so that could net them up to £40 million for those.”

Virgin Media 02 said it had stopped offering accounts to users in 2022. Alan Stott, Chief Operating Officer, Virgin Media O2 said: “Email is something most of us use to manage everyday life, keep in contact with friends and family and store important information or personal memories. While most people use an email platform not provided by their broadband provider, we know this isn’t the case for everyone, and we understand the importance of these email accounts to those that still use them.

“That’s why we want to clearly explain some upcoming changes being made to the Virgin Media email service. We know changes like this can cause concern, so we want to give impacted customers clear information, enough time to decide on the best next steps for them and provide extra support where required.“

‌



Virgin said it is transferring the ongoing management of these email services to Junara, a specialist and dedicated email provider owned by Atmail. This means customers who want to continue using their existing Virgin Media email address, as they do today, will have to move their service to Junara, who will provide a dedicated email platform .

It added: “Alternatively, customers who do not want to move to Junara will have the option to download their emails and documents and move to another provider of their choice, including free email services, or simply close their email account if they wish.“

This change will impact anyone with a Virgin Media email account, including ntlworld.com, blueyonder.co.uk, virgin.net and virginmedia.com email addresses.

‌



What options do customers have?

Customers have three clear options and time to decide what they want to do:

Option 1: Sign up and move their existing email service to Junara

Option 2: Download their emails and data and move to another provider of their choice

Option 3: Close their existing Virgin Media email account

Customers will have at least 45 days from receiving their first communication to decide what action to take. Virgin said it will contact customers in phases, starting in September, with clear instructions and details of the support available.

‌



Virgin said it is also providing an additional 120-day window to support customers who may miss initial communications or need additional help throughout the migration process.

During this period, email accounts can be recovered if necessary, helping ensure important emails, documents or photos are not permanently lost or deleted.

If no action is taken after the 165-day window, the email account will be permanently deleted.

‌



Current customers of Virgin Media’s broadband, landline or TV services will be offered the first 12 months of the new email service free of charge, subject to a 99p transfer fee paid to Junara. Customers who have told us they need additional support will be offered the first 18 months free of charge.

“Former Virgin Media customers who no longer have broadband, landline or TV services will need to sign up to a standard plan with Junara if they want to continue using their existing email service. Customers who do not want to transfer to Junara can download their data and easily move to another provider of their choice, including where there is no cost involved. “

Virgin Media did not give any pricing details about Junara accounts - but last year a standard Junara email account cost £65 per year or £6.50 per month per mailbox.

News.title: Workers warned real terms pay cuts 'extremely likely' in coming months
News.content:
Workers warned real terms pay cuts 'extremely likely' in coming months

Latest data from the ONS shows more evidence of cracks in the jobs market, along with only a slight increase in pay rises

View 2 Images It is getting harder to find work amid a fall vacancies (Image: GETTY)

Millions of workers have been warned real terms pay cuts are “extremely likely” over the coming months.

‌



Latest data from the Office for National Statistics revealed average pay in the private sector rose 2.9% in the three months to July, largely in line with inflation.

‌



However, all eyes will be on separate figures from the ONS on Wednesday which will show if inflation has picked-up more recently on the back of an oil price hike as a result of escalating tensions in the Middle East.

‌



Thomas Pugh, chief economist at audit, tax and consulting firm RSM UK said: “With inflation also at 2.9% in July and set to rise higher over the rest of the year, a real terms pay cut for private sector workers looks extremely likely.”

View 2 Images Families face a new squeeze on incomes in the coming months if inflation picks up again (Image: GETTY)

Exact amount state pension set to rise by next April under triple lock READ MORE :

Pay rises in the public sector average 6.3%, although this is impacted by timings of awards, the ONS explained. TUC General Secretary Paul Nowak said: “The labour market picture remains finely balanced. Jobs and pay remain under pressure."

‌



The ONS data also showed the UK's jobless rate remained at 4.9% in July - but the number of vacancies continues to fall. The estimated number of workers in payrolled jobs fell by 101,000 in the year to July, and was down 19,000 between June and July, the ONS reported. Vacancies also continued to fall, down another 8,000 to 702,000.

ONS Director of Economic Statistics Liz McKeown said: “The labour market remains broadly stable, with employment and unemployment rates largely unchanged in the latest period. However, payrolled employee numbers continue to edge down, with falls over the past year particularly evident in the retail and hospitality sectors.

“Vacancies remain at their lowest level outside the pandemic period for more than a decade, with smaller businesses continuing to report that increased labour costs are affecting hiring decisions.

‌



“Regular wage growth has remained relatively stable in recent months, while total pay growth, which includes bonuses, has eased and was last lower nearly six years ago. There remains a notable difference between public and private sector pay growth, with public sector figures continuing to be affected by the timing of NHS pay awards this year.”

The ONS data also revealed a slump of 62,000 retail jobs in the past year. Trade body the British Retail Consortium said the number was down 122,000 on two years ago, and 410,000 fewer than a decade ago.

Helen Dickinson, BRC chief executive, said: “Entry-level retail jobs are vanishing at the very moment they are needed most. With one in seven young people now not in education, employment or training, the loss of 122,000 jobs in the last two years means tens of thousands fewer opportunities for young people to get their first step on the career ladder, build skills and earn a living."

Article continues below

Alex Hall-Chen, Principal Policy Advisor for Employment at the Institute of Directors, said: “Today's figures show that the labour market is continuing to soften. The IoD's own data paints a similar picture, showing that more business leaders expect to reduce headcount over the coming year than increase it.

"While a subdued economic outlook and weak business confidence are important factors, employers are also grappling with a series of policy changes that have increased the cost and risk of hiring."

News.title: Prince Harry given special birthday message by wife Meghan Markle with unseen photos of kids
News.content:
Prince Harry given special birthday message by wife Meghan Markle with unseen photos of kids

Meghan Markle has shared a sweet photo reel in tribute to Prince Harry who turns 42 today - just weeks after moving back to the UK from California

View 9 Images Meghan Markle has shared a sweet photo reel in tribute to Prince Harry (Image: Meghan/Instagram )

Prince Harry celebrates his 42nd birthday today with wife Meghan sharing a sweet tribute to "my love".

‌



The Duchess of Sussex took to her Instagram account to share a series of unseen photos. It included the message: "He's simply the best. Happy birthday, my love."

‌



The photos included Harry holding Lilibet's hand while they were both skiing, Harry driving the kids on an ATV, and a sweet photo of him kissing Meghan in an orchard.

‌



Harry celebrates his birthday today - just weeks after he, Meghan and their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet made the shock return to the UK after six years of living in California.

It is shaping up to be a big week for the Duke of Sussex, as he is understood to begin his first public engagements in Britain later this week since coming back to his homeland.

News.title: Ukraine defies Trump with Russian oil refinery strike that risks President's fury
News.content:
Ukraine defies Trump with Russian oil refinery strike that risks President's fury

The diesel-producing Syzran Oil Refinery in the Samara region of Russia was attacked by Ukraine despite Donald Trump's call to stop strikes on fuel facilities

View 2 Images Ukraine has risked Trump's anger with an attack on a Ukrainian oil refinery (Image: Getty)

A major Russian oil refinery has been hit despite Donald Trump's call for Ukraine to stop attacks on fuel facilities due to worldwide shortages.

‌



The diesel-producing Syzran Oil Refinery in the Samara region was struck another tense night of fighting where NATO was also forced to scramble military aircraft for the second time in less than four hours.

‌



The US president had claimed on Truth Social: "Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy Targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”

‌



He alleged the world diesel price rise was mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran."

But Volodymyr Zelensky went ahead with the attack on Syzran insisting "no one has seen any genuine desire on Russia's part" to halt energy strikes.

‌



Meanwhile, Russian jet-powered drones attacked western Ukraine prompting emergency Alliance action in Poland over the security of its border following a Putin strike on a train on Sunday “targeting Boris Johnson and other Western backers of Kyiv”.

“Due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory, military aviation operations have commenced in Polish airspace,” said a statement from Warsaw’s operational command.

Three hours 40 minutes earlier, Italian duty NATO fighters had been scrambled in Lithuania from Šiauliai Air Base to blast out of the sky an unidentified incoming drone from Russian-ally Belarus. It was the first time a drone had been shot down over Lithuania.

‌



The wreckage was later found and a military spokesman said: “We will not rush to conclusions. An investigation will be carried out and all the circumstances assessed. The fact is that incidents like this are not going to become less frequent.”

Ukraine's attack on the Syzran Oil Refinery came hours after Donald Trump prematurely claimed there was an energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow.

View 2 Images Zelensky was told to halt attacks on fuel facilities due to worldwide shortages (Image: Ukrinform/Shutterstock)

‌



The US president had said on Truth Social: “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy Targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!” He alleged the world diesel price rise was “mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran.”

But Volodymyr Zelensky went ahead with the attack on Syzran insisting “no one has seen any genuine desire on Russia’s part” to halt energy strikes. He called the move by the US to seek “a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure” a “strong” proposal, but made clear Putin had not agreed to this yet.

The hit on Syzran will deepen Russia’s fuel crisis which is already causing major damage to Putin’s economy. The total Russian oil refineries strikes this summer stands at 42, said Kyiv’s Centre for Strategic Communications.

‌



Russia also defied Trump hitting at least two fuel filling stations in Ukrainian capital Kyiv. “Four people have been injured, two of them are in serious condition,” said Mayor Vitali Klitschko.

Ukraine also struck workshops producing Russian Molniya and Orion drones in Taganrog, and the nearby Beriev Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex where Putin’s warplanes and his Doomsday Il‑80 airborne command post, for use in nuclear war, are repaired.

In the same city, an Ozon online marketplace logistics hub was also hit. In Volgograd, a key cement plant - vital to repairs of military sites - was hit in a Ukrainian strike. Russian drones also hit two ships in two ships being loaded with grain in Ukraine’s port of Chernomorsk.

Article continues below

Meanwhile, Germany is mobilising several hundred soldiers to serve with its new 4,800-strong armoured brigade in Lithuania after failing to fill every specialist post with volunteers.

News.title: Exact amount state pension set to rise by next April under triple lock
News.content:
Exact amount state pension set to rise by next April under triple lock

But this will also take the state pension above the £12,570 tax-free allowance, which is the amount you can earn every tax year before you start to pay tax

View Image The state pension is likely to rise by just under £500 a year (Image: Getty)

The state pension looks set to rise by just under £500 a year from next April - but it means millions of retirees will be pushed over the tax-free threshold.

‌



The state pension rises every year in line with the triple lock promise, which guarantees that it goes up by whichever is higher out of inflation (using the previous September inflation figure), wages (average growth between May and July) or 2.5%.

‌



New figures published today shows average wage growth, including bonuses, was 3.9% in the three months to July. In comparison, inflation is currently at 2.9% - this means unless inflation rises sharply, it is wage growth which is likely to be used to determine the state pension next April.

‌



We will not know the final inflation figure until it is published in October and the Government will not officially announce the state pension for next year until the Budget.

The new state pension is currently worth £241.30 a week. An increase of 3.9% would add £9.40 a week to this figure, taking it to £250.70 a week - an increase of around £489 a year.

‌



But this will also take the state pension above the £12,570 tax-free allowance, which is the amount you can earn each year before you start to pay tax.

The new state pension is currently worth £12,547.60 a year but would rise to £13,036.40 if an increase of 3.9% is applied. The Treasury has announced that people whose sole income is the state pension "without any increments" will not have to pay income tax - though it has not spelled out how this will work.

We also treat our community members to special offers, promotions, and adverts from us and our partners. If you don’t like our community, you can check out any time you like. If you’re curious, you can read our Privacy Notice. NEWSLETTER: Or sign up to the Mirror's Money newsletter here for all the best advice and shopping deals straight to your inbox.

‌



Former pensions minister Sir Steve Webb has warned that this could mean people who receive a higher state pension amount may have to pay tax. This could affect those who deferred their state pension, or receive additional top-ups.

Sir Steve, now a partner LCP, said: “The sting in the tail is that this will take the standard rate of the new state pension above the tax threshold.

"The Government’s plans to address this point are a mess, and likely to benefit only a small fraction of pensioners. They will also create unfairness between different groups of pensioners and between pensioners and low-paid workers, who do not qualify for any exemption.”

Article continues below

Jenny Holt, Customer Savings and Investment Director at Standard Life, said: "Those with no other income, meaning people with even a relatively small amount of additional taxable income - for example from a workplace or private pension - could still find themselves with a tax liability.

"With the personal allowance remaining frozen at £12,570, that brings the interaction between a rising state pension, private retirement income and tax thresholds into even sharper focus."

For pensioners on the old state pension system, the full basic pension is worth £184.90 a week and this could rise to £192.10 - an increase of around £374 a year.

News.title: Oasis 2027 tour live: How to register for tickets as full tour dates and prices revealed
News.content:
Oasis have finally confirmed their upcoming Live '27 tour, with a string of dates across the UK and Ireland next year and shared details on how to get hold of tickets

The news you've all been waiting for – the 'period of reflection' is over and Oasis are back. Following months of speculation, the Manchester legends have confirmed they're hitting the road again.

And fans don't have to wait long. They'll kick off with their first show on May 21 at Glasgow's Celtic Park, before concluding their five Scotland shows on May 29. After a few days off, they'll be returning to their hometown for 11 dates at the Etihad Stadium, with their first show taking place on June 4, before wrapping up on June 26.

After touring around Europe and America, they'll be back to perform four shows at Knebworth on September 11, 12, 18 and 19. Noel has also confirmed that this tour announcement has been a year in the making. But fans hoping to get their hands on tickets need to be quick. A registration system has been implemented to reduce wait times in virtual queues and prevent ticket touting.

Fans must register by 4pm BST on September 17. Those who are successful will receive a non-transferable code to access their allocated on-sale window. Ticket sales will take place in the UK on September 25, 26 and 27, with three windows each day.

Speaking on TalkSport tonight, he said the decision to tour again was made after their second Wembley show last year. He said: "Nobody knew what was going to happen and how it was going to go. We did Cardiff and Manchester, and by the time we got to Wembley, someone said 'Well y'know...' And yeah, it was decided we were gonna do it. And it was all set in motion then."

But, unfortunately, there won't be any new music from the band. "There won't be any new music, no," he revealed. And could the band continue after 2027? "I dunno," Noel said.

News.title: Man suffers serious injuries in Australia spear attack involving 100 people 'armed with compound bows'
News.content:
Man suffers serious injuries in Australia spear attack involving 100 people 'armed with compound bows'

The 22-year-old man suffered the horrific injuries during the disturbance which emergency services attended at around 11.45pm on Monday. The fight involved two family groups with some armed with weapons

View 2 Images Police believe many of the people involved were armed (Image: ABC News)

A man has been rushed to hospital after being stabbed with a three-pronged spear during a large disturbance involving up to 100 people overnight.

‌



The 22-year-old man, who has not been identified, suffered the horrific injuries during the disturbance which emergency services attended at around 11.45pm on Monday. The fight, involving two family groups, soon got out of control as many people were armed with weapons, including compound bows, spears and metal objects.

‌



Police are investigating the armed "disturbance" in the remote Northern Territory community of Wadeye, 250 kilometres south-west of Darwin, overnight. So far no arrrests have been made.

‌



View 2 Images Wadeye is a community of about 2,000 people on the Northern Territory's south-west coast (Image: ABC News)

A Northern Territory Police spokesperson said: "Northern Territory Police are investigating a large disturbance involving approximately 100 people in Wadeye overnight.

‌



"At around 11:45pm, police responded to reports of a disturbance involving two family groups. A number of people were allegedly armed with weapons, including compound bows, spears and metal objects.

"During the disturbance, a 22-year-old man suffered serious injuries after allegedly being struck in the back with a three-pronged spear. Police entered a residence and safely extracted the injured man before escorting him to the Wadeye Health Clinic for treatment.

"A vehicle located near the rear of a residential property was also set alight after allegedly being surrounded by members of one of the groups. Police have not yet identified the vehicle’s owner.

Article continues below

"Additional officers were recalled to duty to assist with the response and restore order. Investigations remain ongoing.

"Anyone with information or relevant footage is urged to contact police on 131 444 and quote reference number NTP2600089258. Anonymous reports can be made through Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000."

News.title: State pension likely to rise by £488 a year in April
News.content:
The state pension is likely to rise by Â£488 next April to Â£13,036.40 a year, new official figures suggest.

Under the triple lock pension guarantee, the annual increase is based on either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.

Average wage growth, including bonuses, eased to 3.9% between May and July, according to the Office for National Statistics. However, it remains above the inflation at 2.9%.

Labour made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock - something Prime Minister Andy Burnham has committed to although the cost of the policy has come under scrutiny as the number of pensioners is expected to rise in the coming years.

The triple lock is creating a "ratchet effect" where "pensioners' living standards grow even faster than just a typical worker," said Ruth Curtice, chief executive of the Resolution Foundation think tank.

The policy was introduced under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government.

Curtice told the BBC's Today programme: "It's not affordable in any situation to simply have pensions rising faster than earnings because earnings are a big part of the tax base.

"Pensioners have seen living standards grow three times more than typical workers over the last 20 years."

Almost 13 million people receive the state pension in the UK. If it does rise by 3.9%, it would take the flat-rate state pension above the personal allowance of Â£12,570 and therefore be liable for income tax.

The Labour government has previously promised that pensioners who rely solely on the state pension would not be required to complete a tax return, nor be chased to pay.

The increase to next year's state pension will not be confirmed until September inflation is released next month. Inflation is currently 2.9% and not expected to be higher than the wages figure.

This means:

the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 â will likely be Â£250.70 a week, or Â£13,036.40 a year. That would be an increase of Â£488

the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 â will likely be Â£192.10 a week, or Â£9,989.20 a year, an increase of Â£374.40

Liam McLaughlin, an associate economist at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr) think tank, said the increase in the state pension added "fiscal pressure at a time when the triple lock is already under scrutiny".

The ONS also published figures on the UK labour force. While the unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.9%, the number of vacancies and employees on payrolls fell in recent months.

News.title: Lucy Letby public inquiry findings set to be published
News.content:
The findings from a public inquiry into how Lucy Letby was able to repeatedly murder and harm babies will be published later on Tuesday.

The Thirlwall Inquiry was set up to look into what happened at the Countess of Chester Hospital between 2015 and 2016, while Letby was working as a nurse in the neonatal unit.

Letby, now 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, including one baby whom she tried to murder twice.

The inquiry was not tasked with examining Letby's guilt. Instead, it investigated how concerns about the neonatal nurse were handled by the hospital and whether action could have been taken sooner to stop her.

Among the key questions the report may answer is whether any babies might have lived or avoided injury if action had been taken earlier.

Letby was moved from the neonatal unit to administrative duties in July 2016 after consultants expressed concerns about her to the hospital's executive team. But the inquiry has been examining whether alarm bells should have started ringing earlier, for example in June 2015 after three babies died in quick succession.

The inquiry, led by one of the country's most senior judges Lady Justice Thirlwall, involved six months of evidence and thousands of documents at a cost of more than Â£18.5m.

It is expected that the report will find there were significant safeguarding failures, and will recommend changes across the NHS.

The chairwoman of the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) - the only organisation with the power to send Letby's case back to the Court of Appeal - has told the BBC the CCRC would be paying close attention to the report.

Letby has previously been denied permission to appeal against her convictions on two occasions.

Her defence lawyer Mark McDonald told BBC Newsnight on Monday he had submitted "nearly 30 expert reports to the CCRC really undermining the whole safety of the convictions" - and that it was "more evidence" than "any other case" in the CCRC's history.

He added: "If she is innocent, as I believe, as 30-odd experts believe, then everything that has gone before the inquiry and every recommendation has operated on the wrong premise."

News.title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet
News.content:
The Â£72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers from two British billionaires is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.

In short, how should political parties be paid for, and by who?

And, what is a legitimate donation and what isn't?

The government is planning to tighten residency rules for people giving money to political parties, to ensure that those making significant donations live in the UK.

But it is worth setting out the law, in broad terms, now and how the government hopes to change it.

Right now, there is no limit on how much anyone, living in the UK or abroad, can give to a British political party as long as the individual is registered to vote in the UK.

But the government has been planning a change in the law for months, which would limit donations from Brits abroad to Â£100,000 each per year, backdated to 25 March this year.

But, crucially, the law hasn't changed yet and some of the key details in that proposed new law - such as what residency requirements would need to be passed to be classified as no longer being abroad - haven't been decided yet.

The reason for that date, 25 March, ministers argue, is that is the day a review by the retired civil servant Philip Rycroft was published,, external the first recommendation of which was that there should be "an annual cap on political donations from British voters living abroad".

On that same day, the then-cabinet minister Steve Reed told the Commons, external that cap would be Â£100,000 per year. He also added that it would "apply retrospectively" from that date onwards, even though the law at the time, and indeed now, has not yet changed.

Two big questions arise from this plan: is it proportionate to limit what British folk abroad can donate to UK political parties, given they are arguably less invested in the country than people living here?

And is it unfair, even morally questionable, to pass a law, but then backdate when its impact begins?

Fast forward to the last few days and along come these colossal donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, two cryptocurrency billionaires who until recently lived in Hong Kong and Thailand respectively.

They have both now returned to the UK.

In his first interview since these donations became public, Nigel Farage told me unequivocally that the money from both men was legal under the law as it stands now.

But he was equivocal when I asked him if they would be legal under the law the government hopes to pass shortly.

"Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever," Farage told me.

Ah, today, I pointed out.

"Retrospectively declaring donations illegal - that simply cannot be," he pressed on, adding "you cannot confiscate money that has been given legally within the law as it stands."

That is a political, perhaps moral argument, but not a legal one - if the government changes the law, the law of the land will have changed, possibly with consequences for whether those donations are legal.

News.title: Harry and Meghan to have security review and children change school
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are going to be given a review of their publicly-funded security, following their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

It has also emerged that the Sussexes have changed their children's school, only days after they first started, over security concerns about the school run.

The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.

A source close to the couple said: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

News.title: UK set to turn cooler as unsettled weather continues
News.content:
Much of the UK is set to feel cooler from Tuesday, as more changeable weather moves in.

Parts of the UK are also likely to see some spells of rain, especially to northern and western parts of the UK.

The rest of the week stays a little unsettled with further spells of rain.

It could turn more settled into next week with temperatures rising above average for some, though heatwave conditions are looking increasingly unlikely.

Tuesday will start off relatively warm and muggy across central and south-eastern areas of England but further north and west it will start to feel a little cooler.

That cooler air will be moving south-east behind a cold front that will also bring a spell of rain across England and Wales for a time.

Fresher north-westerly winds will develop across all areas bringing showers - some heavy - to Scotland, Northern Ireland and more north-western parts of England and Wales.

Maximum temperatures will be around five degrees lower than Monday's values with 17 to 22C across the UK.

This is closer to the average for the time of year.

News.title: Man admits drugging and raping wife over 20 years
News.content:
A man accused of drugging and raping his wife without her knowledge over a 20-year period has admitted 60 offences against her.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's legal right to anonymity, had already admitted some counts at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court, including rape.

The wife watched proceedings from the public gallery supported by members of her family.

The husband, in his sixties, became visibly emotional as he repeated the word guilty to dozens of charges - including multiple counts of rape, assault by penetration and administering a substance with intent - and at one point was invited to sit down in the dock by the judge.

Twelve other men deny multiple serious sexual offences against the same woman.

The husband, from the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, will be sentenced for the counts he has admitted at the conclusion of the trial.

A 13th man previously admitted sexual offences against the woman.

The husband's offending against his wife, who he was married to for decades, took place over a period going back to 2004, while the accusations involving the other men range from September 2018 to November 2025.

The other defendants are:

Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport

Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester

Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester

Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport

Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport

News.title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
News.content:
Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way.

His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb.

But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta.

And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present.

"If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can."

Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. And it delivers vital food and medicine to people on the margins of society.

As such, it offers a lifeline to millions of poor and elderly Ukrainians living in remote villages where shops are rare and trips to the city are expensive and dangerous. In a vast rural nation wracked by war, Ukrposhta is part of the glue that holds the country together.

News.title: We must heed warnings of AI tech developers, says UK minister
News.content:
The UK government must "heed the warnings" of "those who are at the forefront" of developing artificial intelligence (AI) technology, a senior minister will say later.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh will address the growing anxiety over AI safety when she speaks at the TUC congress on Tuesday.

She is expected to say the government is "ready to work with international partners" to prioritise public safety and national security.

Fears about the potential dangers of AI have ramped up in recent days after executives and current and former staff in the field warned the tech could endanger humanity.

On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed the recent discussion of the risks, with his spokesperson saying: "It's a good thing that the companies developing the most advanced AI systems are now talking openly about the risks as well as the opportunities."

Speaking at the TUC congress later on Tuesday, Haigh is also expected to acknowledge the benefits, saying: "AI has enormous potential to transform our public services, make our businesses stronger and deliver new scientific breakthroughs."

News.title: Balaclava ban comes into force in Nottingham city centre
News.content:
A ban on face coverings in Nottingham city centre has officially come into force.

From today, police and community protection officers will be able to ask people to remove coverings if they "reasonably believe" they are being used to conceal their identity to commit crime or anti-social behaviour.

Anyone who refuses to comply could face a Â£70 fixed penalty notice or be prosecuted, with courts able to impose a maximum fine of Â£1,000.

The leader of Nottingham City Council, Neghat Khan, said residents had felt intimidated when they saw people wearing balaclavas, skeleton masks or other face coverings without a legitimate reason.

"Our residents should be able to live, work and spend time in Nottingham without feeling frightened or unsafe," Khan previously told the BBC.

"That is why we are taking decisive action and becoming one of the first cities in the country to introduce a restriction of this kind."

The enforcement will not apply to face coverings worn for legitimate reasons, including religious, cultural, health, work, weather or personal safety reasons.

It will be up to officers to determine whether or not coverings are being worn legitimately.

Confirmation of a start date for the action in Nottingham comes after Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called for full face coverings, including those worn for religious reasons, to be banned in public, following masked protesters gathering in Dover.

Elsewhere in the country, Stafford Borough Council approved plans to prohibit balaclavas as part of its updated public spaces protection order (PSPO) earlier this year.

More recently, community leaders in the West Midlands said they would like to see their region follow suit following the ban in Nottingham and bring the action to their area.

News.title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age
News.content:
Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.

Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff.

Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list.

The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would.

The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work.

It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document.

The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it.

Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app.

The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age.

This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult.

Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'".

Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step".

He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector.

This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said.

News.title: UK could 'unlock' 100 more oil and gas projects, say North Sea bosses
News.content:
The UK could supply half of its oil and gas needs without imports if the government showed more support for the sector, an industry report claims.

Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) said changes to the windfall tax on energy firms and approval of the controversial Rosebank and Jackdaw fields could unlock 111 projects, attracting investment worth Â£50bn.

North Sea output has been falling and projections suggest that the UK's domestic supplies will meet only about a third of demand until 2050.

Environmental group Uplift branded the report a "fantasy" and said that the Prime Minister should not listen to "self-interested demands" of oil companies.

The OEUK report sets out the industry's case for supporting domestic production of oil and gas and displacing imports, which have increased.

It calls for the current Energy Profits Levy (EPL), a windfall tax on oil and gas producers which is due to be replaced in 2030, to be scrapped by next January.

The replacement Oil and Gas Revenue Levy would be triggered only when prices spike.

The sector has long said the EPL has significantly stifled investment because it remains in place even when wholesale oil and gas prices fall.

Last year, for the first time since the North Sea began producing oil and gas, not a single exploration well was drilled.

News.title: Giant jellyfish with '40ft tentacles' captured on camera
News.content:
Morgan said he was swimming near Trefin Beach in Pembrokeshire when he spotted the tentacles in the water.

"Three turned to 10, and then to 20. They just kept on coming," he added.

The jellyfish was so big the tentacles went "beyond the range of visibility".

He initially thought it was a compass jellyfish, which are native to UK waters, before realising it was too big.

"It must have been the length of a bus or small train. I couldn't believe how big it was."

The Wildlife Trusts, external said the lion's mane jellyfish gets its name from its long tentacles, and has "all the beauty and bite of a lion".

They can grow up to 3m (9ft 8in) in length, but the tentacles - which are used to catch their prey - can exceed 30 to 36.5 metres (98ft 4in to 119ft 8in) making it one of the longest animals on Earth.

Marine biologist Dr Cathy Lucas, from the University of Southampton, said Morgan's video showed the animal's incredible length.

"The tentacles are so long and so fine you might not even see them," she said, recalling how during field work in Scotland divers would get bits of tentacles on them when there were no jellyfish around.

"They still sting after they break off," she said, adding that while the sting was "nasty" and "the worst in the UK", it was not dangerous.

News.title: Speedboat killer jailed for attack on girlfriend
News.content:
Speedboat killer Jack Shepherd has been jailed for 20 months with a further four years on extended licence for violently assaulting his girlfriend, including hitting her chest with a set of hot barbecue tongs.

The 38-year-old had pleaded guilty to two counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and damaging property at Isleworth Crown Court in July.

The attacks happened in February and June last year and sparked Shepherd's recall to prison.

He was originally jailed in 2018 for six years and six months for manslaughter over the death of 24-year-old Charlotte Brown when his speedboat crashed during a first date.

Shepherd was jailed for a further four years at Exeter Crown Court in 2019 for a drink-fuelled attack on a barman in March 2018 at a Devon hotel.

He was released on licence in January 2024, but faced recall to prison in September last year after he was accused of violence towards the woman.

According to a prosecution summary of the case, Shepherd started dating his former partner in August 2024, but towards the end of the year she accused him of being abusive and threatening.

In February 2025, he admitted pinning down the woman and "punching her several times, causing bruising to her arm and top of leg" during an argument.

In the second incident, in June 2025, Shepherd got angry with her after she said that he had burned a pizza on the barbecue, and "proceeded to hit her with the barbecue tongs on her left breast which caused a permanent scar".

News.title: No police collusion in sectarian murder but multiple RUC failings included tip-off to suspect
News.content:
An inquiry into the sectarian murder of Robert Hamill has found police officers who were in a vehicle near the attack did not condone or collude with the attackers.

However, the inquiry said there were multiple police failings in the investigation, including a tip-off to a suspect to destroy the clothing he wore that night.

The report, published on Monday, external, highlighted multiple wrongful omissions in the subsequent murder investigation including a failure to properly search the home of a key suspect.

Robert Hamill was 25 when he died after he was beaten by loyalists in Portadown, County Armagh, in 1997.

The inquiry concluded in 2009 and its report was completed in 2011 but the findings could not be published until three prosecutions in connection with the case concluded.

The inquiry concluded: "We find that Robert Hamill had been assaulted before the Land Rover officers got out of their vehicle.

"However, they were not aware of the assault and after they had got out of their vehicle, they attempted to restore order.

"They did not in any way condone or collude with attackers."

Although the inquiry found that the four officers in the police Land Rover could not have prevented the murder, the police investigation was flawed â both at the scene and in the days that followed.

"The inquiry found that serving RUC [Royal Ulster Constabulary] officers were guilty of wrongful omissions and that those omissions arose both at the scene and during the initial investigation," it said.

The inquiry concluded that some of the mistakes in the investigation were negligent, while others were deliberate.

The 290-page report followed an inquiry which cost approximately Â£33m.

The actions of the officers in the Land Rover have been the subject of many claims and counter-claims in the past three decades.

Given how close they were to the scene, questions have been asked about why they did not intervene sooner.

The inquiry found that they were "distracted talking to two members of the public".

On whether they could have done more, the three-person inquiry panel did not have a unanimous view.

Two members concluded that the officers in the police vehicle were not guilty "of any wrongful act or omission in relation to the death of Robert Hamill".

However, on this issue the chairperson Sir Edwin Jowitt "expressed a dissenting view".

News.title: Burnham cancels engagements after death of father
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has cancelled official engagements on Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's.

He had been due to host a meeting of business leaders in Downing Street on Monday, and was expected to speak at the annual trade union TUC Congress in Brighton on Tuesday.

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

He had also said his father's illness was so advanced that he did not know his son had become prime minister.

Burnham told the BBC that while his father could not be there when he entered No 10 to take up the role, he and his mother had "exchanged a few words about my dad and how proud he would be".

"That's a little hard, but then again I've said, it's their achievement", he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg in July.

"The emotion of that moment was, well, bittersweet - it was painful in one way but beautiful in another."

The prime minister later said care home staff had shown his father footage of him entering Downing Street, calling it a "wonderful" thing.

Burnham said he wanted to help "my dad and the millions like him" when setting out plans to reform adult social care.

He said he had been "overwhelmed" by the skills and professionalism of care workers supporting his father.

Burnham has described how his father, a former telephone engineer, had raised him with "laughter, love and support" alongside his mother Eileen in Culcheth, Cheshire.

In his 2024 book Look North, he wrote that neither of his parents had attended university, but could have done had they "grown up in a different time and different place".

"Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go."

Opposition politicians have offered their condolences to Burnham and his family.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.

"A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won't ever be the same again."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "My heart goes out to the prime minister on the loss of his dad.

"From our conversations he sounded like a wonderful man."

Green party leader Zack Polanski said: "There are moments in life such as this sad time that transcend politics and I join the whole country in sending condolences."

Taylor Swift returned to Arrowhead Stadium on Monday night, joining Tom Cruise in the stands to watch her new husband Travis Kelce and his Kansas City Chiefs kick off the NFL season against the Denver Broncos.

This marked the first match Swift has attended to watch Kelce play since their summer wedding ceremony.

The 14-time Grammy Award winner chose not to attend the Emmy Awards in Los Angeles, a move that was largely expected. Although The Eras Tour: The Final Show received a nomination for outstanding variety special (pre-recorded), the award had already been presented at the Creative Arts Emmys earlier this month, where The Muppet Show claimed top honours.

Organisers of the Emmys played on the speculation surrounding Swift’s potential appearance, broadcasting a pre-recorded segment in which the Law & Order: Special Victims Unit cast, featuring host Mariska Hargitay, attempts to determine if she will show up. Swift makes a closing cameo, albeit playing a fictional character.

open image in gallery Taylor Swift and Tom Cruise watch the Kansas City Chiefs take on the Denver Broncos on Sunday ( AP )

"Maybe she’ll do one those cool, pre-taped sketch things to support the host," her character remarks.

Instead of attending the ceremony at the Peacock Theatre, Swift was present at the stadium where her relationship with Kelce began.

The couple's romance originated when Swift performed a concert at Arrowhead Stadium, where Kelce unsuccessfully attempted to give her a friendship bracelet as a fan. Kelce then took to social media to invite her to see him play, an offer Swift accepted for a 2023 fixture against the Bears, initiating a relationship that ultimately led to their very high-profile wedding held on July 3 inside Madison Square Garden.

Adam Sandler was the unexpected officiant for the event, with Stevie Nicks singing before a guest list packed with prominent figures across entertainment and sport, such as actors Bradley Cooper, Zoë Kravitz, Hugh Grant and Ethan Hawke, models Gigi Hadid and Karlie Kloss, comedian Chris Rock, film director Steven Spielberg, alongside retired quarterback Tom Brady and several of Kelce’s teammates.

open image in gallery Taylor Swift, right, appeared alongside host Mariska Hargitay in a pre-taped Emmys skit ( AP )

"The ceremony was gorgeous," stated Jason Kelce, Kelce’s brother and retired Eagles center, during ESPN's pregame show. "They did such an incredible job, Adam Sandler officiated it in a very Adam Sandler, beautiful way. From then on, it was a party."

The newly married couple have had a busy summer period, even with Swift currently off tour. Kelce has been expanding his business portfolio, which featured his decision to purchase a small share of David Blitzer’s stake in the hometown Cleveland Guardians.

There was some speculation that Kelce might retire following last season, when the Chiefs struggled to a 6-11 finish and his close friend and quarterback Patrick Mahomes tore ligaments in his left knee. Instead, he chose to return for a 14th season, and Mahomes rehabbed in time to face the Broncos as the Chiefs attempt to rebound from their very first losing season since 2012.

Tom Pelphrey made sure to thank his “very pregnant” fiancée, Kaley Cuoco, during his acceptance speech for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Drama Series at the 2026 Emmy Awards.

Pelphrey, 43, won the award Monday night for his role as Robbie Prendergrast in HBO’s critically acclaimed crime drama, Task.

Getting up on stage, the actor began by saying: “I thank god for my life and my sobriety. I thank my family and my friends for all your love and support all these years, from Emmys to black box theaters and everything in between.”

He went on to thank HBO executives and his co-stars, including “the beautiful Mark Ruffalo,” adding, “Thank you for this incredible role and this opportunity and your friendship. I’m so proud to be your friend.”

Finally, Pelphrey paid tribute to “my favorite actor in this room — my love, my best friend, my partner, the very pregnant Kaley Cuoco.”

open image in gallery Kaley Cuoco was in floods of tears at her fiancé Tom Pelphrey’s emotional Emmy acceptance speech ( Getty/The Television Academy/NBC )

open image in gallery Cuoco and Pelphrey have been dating since 2022 and got engaged in 2024 after welcoming their first daughter together ( AP )

“I love you more than anything, and our family is the crown jewel of my life,” Pelphrey told the Big Bang Theory star, who was shown weeping in the audience.

Referencing their three-year-old daughter, Matilda, and the baby girl he and Cuoco, 40, are expecting, Pelphrey concluded: “Matilda, daddy loves you. Baby girl, daddy loves you. Thank you. God bless.”

Cuoco was again shown saying “I love you” while in floods of tears.

The couple announced their engagement on Instagram in August 2024, a year after Matilda was born. They have been dating since 2022.

Announcing her second pregnancy in June, Cuoco shared on Instagram: “Completing our little family , what a dream come true ! This second time around journey has been a little windier in many ways , but wow we are so grateful for this moment!! Little sissy on the way!!! @tommypelphrey girl dad for life.”

Cuoco revealed back in 2022 that they were set up by their mutual manager, Andrea Pett-Joseph, who thought they would be “perfect for each other.”

When they later met in person at the Ozark premiere (in which Pelphrey starred as Ben Davis), Cuoco said it was “love at first sight.”

“I heard his voice, and I turned around, and it was like my life was over, or just starting,” she recalled USA Today. “We were immediately connected. I do feel like I’ve known him my whole life, but I wasn't ready for him.”

“We’re ready to build a life together,” she added.

Cuoco has previously been married twice, to tennis player Ryan Sweeting from 2013 to 2016 and equestrian show jumper Karl Cook from 2018 to 2022.

Reform UK’s crypto-billionaire donors could face enhanced checks to prove their ongoing presence in the UK as the government considers tightening proposed laws after the party received £72 million over the weekend.

Ministers have already moved to introduce a £100,000 cap on the amount of money that can be given to political parties by British citizens based overseas, which would also apply for the first 12 months after any expats return to the UK.

The changes would be backdated to this March, raising questions about whether Reform can keep the twin £36 million donations from Ben Delo, who was based in Hong Kong, and Christopher Harborne, who was based in Thailand.

But amid reports both men have already returned to the country, ministers are looking at how to toughen residency requirements governing political donations.

Reform UK’s billionaire donors could be subject to new checks (Will Colebourne/PA) ( PA Wire )

In a parliamentary debate as part of the second reading of the Government’s Representation of the People Bill in the Lords on Monday, minister Baroness Taylor said: “In addition to introducing a robust regime that ensures donors contributing above the £100,000 annual cap must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection to the United Kingdom, we are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements including ensuring the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy.”

Government sources said an enhanced test would mean donors also have to demonstrate an ongoing presence in the UK, details of which will be set out shortly.

Areas that have existing residency requirements include immigration law, welfare and tax. For example, HMRC declares people resident if they have lived in the UK for 183 days a year.

Earlier on Monday, Nigel Farage acknowledged Reform UK’s record-breaking windfall may fall foul of government efforts to clamp down on foreign donors, and hit out against the move to apply the new law retrospectively.

He told the BBC on Monday he believed the two donations were “compliant” with the law as it stands, but suggested they would not be acceptable as a result of a law change in the Representation of the People Bill, which has now entered committee stage.

Asked whether Mr Delo and Mr Harborne were UK residents as of March 25, as this would have an impact on their donations, Mr Farage said: “I’m not going to go into their particular details.

“All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.

“Now, there is talk, and Angela Rayner was talking about this yesterday, there is talk of them retrospectively declaring donations illegally. Well, that simply cannot be.”

He later vowed to retaliate by cutting off union funding if Reform wins the next election.

“If anyone is giving money to do political bidding, it’s the trade unions,” Mr Farage told the Telegraph. “So I would just warn the Labour Party here and now: If you try and ban our donors, we in government would certainly ban funding from the trade unions.

“I don’t want to go down that route. But it is something we would be prepared to do.”

Justifying the government’s decision to clamp down on donations, business secretary Jonathan Reynolds told Sky News: “This is not about Reform or Labour or Tories or Lib Dems. This is about: if you want to have an influence to british politics, shouldn’t you have a connection to the UK?

“I'm not talking about if any of these people do or don’t. I'm not talking about individual circumstances. To me, it is entirely reasonable that to involve yourself in the British political system, you should be involved in it, you should care about it."

Reform UK has started using the funding to expand its staff, including doubling its policy team from 10 to 20 and 400 new field agents, with a new online channel also expected to be broadcast over YouTube, The Times reported.

The government has said it will set up a taskforce to tackle the issue of “mega-donors” after MPs pressed ministers to go further by imposing a general limit that would also cover domestic donations in its draft legislation.

On Sunday, communities secretary Angela Rayner suggested a wider cap was still on the table, saying she wanted to stop people “being able to overpower and buy their way into democracy”.

The cabinet minister on Monday told the TUC Congress: “Nigel Farage’s sugar daddies made their money in crypto, but there’s nothing cryptic about their motives. They know full well that a Reform government will act in their interest, not the public interest.”
