World.title: 10 years after taking a knee, Colin Kaepernick is still waging a 'Perilous Fight'
World.content:
10 years after taking a knee, Colin Kaepernick is still waging a 'Perilous Fight'

toggle caption Ezra Shaw/Getty Images

Former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick was adopted as a baby into a white family, in a town that was almost entirely white. He was 8 when a group of older boys called him the n-word and tried to tie him to a tree — an incident he never mentioned to his parents.

"Instinctively, as a Black boy, I didn't think they would believe me," Kaepernick says. "I went [home] and got cleaned up, came downstairs, and went about the day like nothing had happened. But it was a moment that also shaped and defined me."

For Kaepernick, football became a space for him to understand his Blackness. He found support in his fellow teammates and their mothers, who shared their own experiences with racism and advised him on how to navigate situations involving the police. He went on to play college football for the University of Nevada, Reno.

Sponsor Message

"One of the things that I always appreciated about sports is it became much more difficult for people to approach things from a subjective lens. Sports is very — you won or you lost, you did your job or you didn't, you scored a touchdown or you did it, you completed the pass or you didn't," he says.

The San Francisco 49ers drafted Kaepernick as quarterback in 2011. He played in the NFC championship games in 2013 and 2014 and in the 2013 Super Bowl. But he also became increasingly concerned by incidents of police violence against Black people, including the fatal shootings of Mario Woods in San Francisco, Alton Sterling in Baton Rouge and Philando Castile in a suburb of Saint Paul, Minn. At the beginning of the 2016 season, he took a knee during the national anthem in protest.

Hachette Book Group

"The treatment of Black people and the systems that have been built to continue to oppress Black people and people of color more broadly — that's not something I was OK with," he says. "And I wasn't gonna show pride in those systems that are continuing to kill us, continuing to target us and hold us back and discriminate against us."

Kaepernick's protest sparked a firestorm of criticism and commentary. After the 2016 season, he never played another NFL game. Kaepernick would go on to file a grievance accusing NFL owners of colluding to keep him out of the league; they reached a settlement in 2019. In his new memoir, The Perilous Fight, retraces his journey to joining the NFL — and explains why he's still hoping to make it back to the league.

Sponsor Message

"The NFL tried to send a very clear message that if you protest police killing Black folks, if you fight for a better society and better community, we're going to try to take your career from you," he says. "I ... don't accept that that is going to be the end outcome of this, and will do everything I can to make sure that I change that narrative."

Interview highlights

On one player saying: "I want to protest, but I need to ask my owner."

I did not think in my lifetime I would hear a Black man say, "I need to ask my owner for permission."

It was mind-blowing candidly. I did not think in my lifetime I would hear a Black man say, "I need to ask my owner for permission." I think it speaks to the mentality that the NFL tries to breed though, which is be obedient and we'll give you opportunity. Do as we say and you'll be rewarded for it. If not, we'll try to take away what you have built your lifetime towards earning. And again, I understand players trying to navigate this and say, "I'm supportive of it in theory, but in practice, I'm afraid to lose what I have." And I think the dynamic of players being afraid to lose what they have, that is an environment that the NFL has created.

On the media coverage of his protest

The coverage overall, I think, was used to detract from the actual issue of addressing police killing Black people. ... We are talking about police brutality. We're talking about the issues directly in our community, and a lot of the narrative is, "Well, are you disrespecting the flag? Are you disrespecting the military? Is this the right form of protest? Should you be doing it a different way? Should there be a different approach?"

Oftentimes, a missing piece of this was actually the intention behind the protest and the thing that we had repeated over and over again as to why we were protesting. I think that was a part that was frustrating to have to navigate. I will say there were some phenomenal journalists and phenomenal people within the media that were steadfast in covering this true to form in relation to our goals and objectives, and also calling out some of the broader manipulation within the media.

Sponsor Message

On the NFL's response to his protest

The response from the NFL and the positioning of a lot of the conversation is also a little bit mind blowing to me. Just looking at it from a fundamental level of, "Hey, we want to stop police killing Black people." And the NFL had an issue with that being said. I want people to just pause and take a moment and think about that. Why would that be an issue for anybody to say we want police to stop killing Black people? ... The NFL revealed who they were and their intentions and also where they sit politically in that moment.

On that false narrative, following the 2016 season, that he didn't want to play football

Really what that became is a way to try to manipulate people to say, "Oh, you shouldn't care about this because he doesn't care about it." And that's just demonstrably false. I love playing football. I am passionate about it. I was actively seeking and pursuing my career, but I also didn't see the need to sit down in an interview and explain that I wanted to play football when I had been saying it and showing it in all of the other ways.

On whether or not he'd let his kid play football

We would avoid our kids playing football at at all costs. ... If we had a son that was adamant on playing, I don't think we would let him play contact football until he was much older ... not until high school. ... The studies that exist today show significant impact on their brain, in particular because their brain is still developing.

Anna Bauman and Susan Nyakundi produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

World.title: Trump's latest round of 50% tariffs on Canadian goods take effect
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A new round of U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods took effect just after midnight on Tuesday, adding 50 per cent levies to 110 products ranging from specific cheeses to motorboats, all-terrain vehicles (ATVs) and furniture.

The fresh tariffs are part of a series of additions and removals announced by the Trump administration last week. Categories added to the tariff list include aluminum products, paper and wood products, iron or steel beams, electric lamps and mattresses.

The White House said it would simultaneously remove tariffs on 10 items including salt, sugar, cement, switchboards and toilet paper in an effort to "offset the burden to U.S. commerce while better serving the public interest."

In 2024, Canada exported approximately $328 million US worth of toilet paper to the U.S., making it the country's largest international provider.

Canada is also one of the biggest salt providers south of the border, with the U.S. importing roughly $159.2 million US worth of salt from Canada in 2025, according to UN Comtrade and World Bank trade data.

WATCH | How much toilet paper does the U.S. get from Canada?: Is toilet paper an unlikely pressure point in the Canada–U.S. trade war? | Duration 2:28 U.S. President Donald Trump dropped tariffs on certain Canadian products, including toilet paper, cement and salt. In 2024, Canada exported approximately $328 million worth of the product, making it the largest international provider of toilet paper to the U.S.

The removals and additions amount to nearly the same economic value, effectively cancelling each other out, experts say.

"In dollar terms they are basically the same," Wolfgang Alschner, the Hyman Soloway chair in business and trade law at the University of Ottawa, told CBC News.

The categories that had tariffs removed represent roughly $2.41 billion, while the added tariffs cover roughly $2.56 billion of 2025 trade, according to an analysis by Alschner. This amounts to only a slight increase in tariff coverage, representing a fraction of trade between the two countries.

The biggest dollar value is in the category of switchgear assemblies and switchboards — the U.S. imported roughly $750 million US of these from Canada in 2025, which have applications ranging from cars to airplanes, Alschner said.

'You need to salt your roads'

The decision to remove some tariffs shows that the U.S. is paying attention to which costs get passed down to the American consumer, and are willing to recalibrate to ease their own economic pain, Alschner said.

"You need salt to salt your roads in winter. So this is not something that's easily substituted away," he said. "Similarly for cement."

The new measures come after the U.S. and Canada failed to reach a trade agreement in August, ramping up an ongoing trade war.

On Aug. 22, the U.S. followed through with its threat of crushing 50 per cent tariffs on a wide swath of Canadian goods. Canada retaliated with its own tariffs on nearly 700 categories of U.S. goods, which came into effect on Sept. 8.

WATCH | How will U.S. retaliatory tariffs impact Canadians?: How will the new U.S. retaliatory tariffs impact Canadians? | Duration 5:22 U.S. President Donald Trump has hit Canada with a new round of trade measures, escalating the trade war. CBC's Peter Armstrong says the scope of the trade war has grown, and as a result, regional disruptions could lead to job losses and the closure of small businesses.

In addition to new tariffs on Sept. 15, U.S. President Donald Trump announced a pending import ban on Canadian booze, motorcycles and a handful of other goods. The import ban doesn't take effect until Sept. 29.

Experts say the scope of the trade war has grown, and as a result, regional disruptions could lead to job losses and the closure of small businesses.

Alschner says the latest tariffs will limit some Canadian companies from pivoting. For instance, an aluminum company might have been able to shift more production to types of aluminum that weren't tariffed before.

But with the addition of more hyper-specific tariffs, "some of these loopholes have been closed."

WATCH | Carney on upcoming import ban: 'We're looking closely' at Trump's import bans and tariffs, Carney says | Duration 1:03 Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday that the government is looking at U.S. President Donald Trump's recent measures which include bans on Canadian imports including most alcohol products and new 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products. 'We fully recognize that for individual companies and in individual sectors these are significant, and there's a response there,' Carney said.

Economist Andrew Dicapua told CBC News the muted response from the U.S. to Canada's counter-tariffs, coupled with the longer timeline before the import bans come into effect, could be a sign that we're closer to a deal.

Trump recently commented that a trade deal with Canada could come "fairly soon," while meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin over the weekend, Dicapua noted.

"The fact that those bans were put later than the tariffs themselves should give us an indication that the U.S. is leaving room for negotiation," Dicapua said.

"The bottom line is that we've got to get to an agreement with the United States as quickly as possible. This tit-for-tat strategy, although well-intentioned, is not a sustainable route."

World.title: 2026 Emmys: Widow's Bay upsets, The Pitt triumphs at Canada-preoccupied ceremony
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Despite a raft of surprises that included Canada call-outs, numerous Law & Order gags and Taylor Swift, the biggest surprise of the night was in who took home the gold.

Because even as the Emmys tends to honour the series and stars with more seasons under their belts, it was Apple TV's smash success Widow's Bay that earned top honours. Winning lead actor, supporting actress, supporting actor and director — as well as the night's biggest award, best comedy series — the horror-comedy pulled in a record 14 wins off an impressive 19 nominations.

That beat the single-season record of 13 wins The Studio earned last year, making Widow's Bay the comedy series with the most ever trophies in a single year.

But the star heading into the night was The Pitt, which led the pack with 25 nominations, including for best drama series — which it won — and supporting actress (Taylor Dearden, Fiona Dourif, Katherine LaNasa and Sepideh Moafi).

Its lead Noah Wylie was awarded with outstanding lead actor in a drama series about midway through the ceremony — his second win in the category after triumphing last year as well. However The Pitt lost best supporting actor to Tasks' Tom Pelphrey: that show's first of the night off of its six nominations.

And despite The Pitt's dominance in the best supporting actress in a comedy category, it was The Diplomat's Allison Janney who took home the award. It is her eighth career Emmy, following her last win in 2021 for Mom. That relatively huge upset set the stage for what would be a night of them — splitting honours between established entertainment juggernauts, and surprise new finds.

Interspersed with all the wins, though, was the comedy. One of the big moments of the night was a scene-specific recreation of Law & Order by host Mariska Hargitay, in which the show's actual stars — including Ice-T — tried to predict whether or not Taylor Swift would show up at the Emmys.

Swift herself appeared in disguise as one of the SVU detectives, theorizing along with the rest of them.

Mariska Hargitay, Taylor Swift and her cat Olivia Benson appear on screen during the 78th Emmy Awards on Monday. (Patrick T. Fallon/Getty Images)

"Maybe she's going to do one of those cool pre-taped sketch things to support the host," Swift said in the pre-taped sketch.

"Do you think she'll sing?" asked one of the other detectives.

"No."

Canadian comments

A speech with a bit more heft came from Sally Field, who won outstanding lead actress in a limited or anthology series or movie for Remarkably Bright Creatures. The actress, who received her first nomination in 17 years for this role, barrelled off the thanks for different people in her life — before arriving at a familiar one.

“And Canada! Blessed Canada!" she said, smiling. Remarkably Bright Creatures was filmed in Deep Cove, B.C. "Our neighbours, our friends!”

Later on was an emotional tribute to the late Catherine O'Hara by Home Alone co-star Macaulay Culkin, and Schitt's Creek co-stars Annie Murphy and Dan Levy.

"The greatest lesson I learned from Catherine, both professionally and personally, was to always say yes. Say yes to her instincts; all of them," Levy said of the comedy legend who died in January. "Always say yes to any opportunity to revel in the presence of greatness."

Also honoured was Michael J. Fox for the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award. Fox, who retired from acting in 2020 due to the physical toll of Parkinson's disease, was introduced as a "proud son of Canada" and received a standing ovation.

"Eventually I understood that accepting Parkinson's didn't mean I had to surrender to it," he said in his acceptance speech. "It just meant doing what I could for everyone living with this disease."

Actors Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy speak onstage during an homage to late actress Catherine O'Hara. (Patrick T. Fallon/Getty Images)

Slightly behind The Pitt in nominations was Hacks, another strong performer at the seminal TV awards show. Its nominations for its fifth and final season put it ahead of all comedies with a record-breaking 24.

Lead Jean Smart was, in many bettors' cards, perhaps the biggest lock of the night for best actress in a comedy — an award she won early on, becoming the first woman to win an Emmy for every season of their show.

Hannah Einbinder , who had a breakthrough win last year as best supporting actress in a comedy after four nominations , was up against Kate O'Flynn, who wowed with a breakout performance in the debut season of Widow's Bay — and who ended up taking home the prize.

WATCH | The Pitt, Hacks lead Emmy nominations: The Pitt, Hacks lead 2026 Emmy nominations | Duration 4:19 The nominees for the 2026 Primetime Emmy Awards have been unveiled, with HBO's The Pitt leading all programs with 25 nominations, followed by Hacks with 24. Apple TV's freshman dark comedy Widow's Bay secured 19 nods and its post-apocalyptic Pluribus pulled in 16.

Her win was followed shortly after by a best supporting actor in a comedy award for Widow's Bay star Stephen Root — a category for which Hacks' Paul W. Downs was nominated.

The Emmys' track record had suggested they would shower Hacks in awards for its final, send-off season. But with 19 nominations for a show with a real campaign and surprise upset win for best comedy series, the trajectory of Widow's Bay was far more successful than previously expected.

Fellow newcomer Pluribus, from Breaking Bad phenom Vince Gilligan, was just behind with 18 off the back of its first season. A stunningly bizarre dramedy about an alien invasion and mind control, it was similarly positioned in opposition to The Pitt. With four early wins already, the narrative had long been circling around star Rhea Seehorn.

Rhea Seehorn accepts the Emmy for outstanding lead actress in a drama series for Pluribus. (Patrick T. Fallon/Getty Images)

Given the entire show's focus on her singular performance, voters rewarded the Better Call Saul star with her first Emmy after four nominations.

A laughing, tearful Seehorn briefly thanked her co-nominees, cast and crew, her family and Gilligan. She was eventually played off in the longest speech thus far of the night — where all other winners barely took a minute before rushing off the stage.

Elsewhere, the limited series categories had a diminished role at the main Emmys show after four of them were demoted to the early Emmys weekend.

HBO Max's DTF St. Louis was the big winner of those awards, taking best supporting actor and actress for David Harbour and Linda Cardellini.

Beef brought star power to the lead acting categories, with Carey Mulligan, the consensus favourite for best actress in a limited series, however losing to Field. The show's Oscar Isaac was favoured for best actor, but was similarly upset by Matthew Rhys for The Beast in Me. Rhys also won best lead actor in a comedy series for his role in Widows Bay, making him the first man to win two lead actor awards in the same night.

And after another year of antagonizing U.S. President Donald Trump, the late night shows of Jimmy Kimmel and the now-cancelled Stephen Colbert were both up for outstanding variety series, the latter of whom won.

That show received nine nominations for this Emmys ceremony, following the news that CBS announced its end earlier this year. In his acceptance speech, Colbert joked that if the audience enjoyed the comedy they should thank his old writers — as they wrote it all.

"I got some great news, they are all 'tech avail,'" he said, before speaking earnestly. "We hope you enjoyed the show, we had a great time doing it for you ... we'll catch you all on the flip."

World.title: Over 1,000 protesters demonstrate against Carney's investment summit in Toronto
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There was a heavy police presence around the Art Gallery of Ontario on Monday night as hundreds of activists gathered to protest against an investment summit organized by Prime Minister Mark Carney.

More than 1,000 demonstrators gathered in downtown Toronto on Monday to protest against an investment summit organized by Prime Minister Mark Carney.

The Canada Investment Summit, set for Monday and Tuesday in Toronto, is being hosted by Carney, who has invited over 100 of the world's largest investors from around the world in the hopes of securing $1 trillion in investments in some 167 projects across the country over the next five years.

The prime minister is pitching Canada as a safe and reliable place for investment at a time of economic uncertainty, but some aren't sold on outside investment yielding positive results for everyday Canadians.

Rachel Small, an organizer with World Beyond War, a non-profit that campaigns against conflict, said Canadians are struggling to afford rent and the cost of living, and need more investment in education, transit and health care.

"Carney is doing the opposite of that," she said.

"He is selling our public resources without any guaranteed returns and at the same time growing industries that will push the world towards greater war and climate catastrophe."

"These billionaires make decisions behind closed doors in our city to decide our futures. Our future is not for sale," Small said.

The protesters, a diverse group that includes representatives of labour unions, Indigenous leaders and climate and housing advocates, say they reject the idea of leaving Canada's economic future in the hands of CEOs and worry about the future of public services, pipelines and arms manufacturing.

On Monday evening, protesters gathered first in Nathan Phillips Square, then marched to a police barrier near the Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO), where the summit's opening gala that was closed to the public and the media was being held. The crowd grew in size as it made its way to the AGO.

Between 200 and 300 Toronto police officers were estimated to be in the area of the AGO to prevent protesters from breaking through the barricade.

Protesters, including representatives of labour unions, Indigenous leaders and climate and housing advocates, say they reject the idea of leaving Canada's economic future in the hands of CEOs and worry about the future of public services, pipelines and arms manufacturing. (Michael Cole/CBC)

Monday's assembly of speakers gathered under the banner "The Many vs. The Money," arguing the summit is designed to "auction off" Canadian public resources, according to its website.

The crowd chanted, drummed and waved signs that urged investments in people, health care and the environment.

AI spending, environmental impact, sovereignty among concerns

"We're here today because we represent young workers who want good jobs and a livable future," said Hailey Asquin of the group Common Horizon.

Asquin said her peers are not against investments but are concerned about spending on artificial intelligence, the military and fossil fuels.

"We want to be part of building a Canada that we can be proud of, one that is a superpower in things like renewable energy and health care," she said.

Tom Deadman, a teacher from Ottawa, said he takes issue with Carney inviting executives from American companies in the midst of a trade war with the United States.

"Our concern is that he is basically giving away massive parts of our public services to American CEOs," he said.

Between 200 and 300 Toronto police officers were estimated to be in the area of the AGO to prevent protesters from breaking through the barricade. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Kakeka ThunderSky, a member of Poplar River First Nation, travelled from Winnipeg to join the protest out of concern about fast-tracked environmental assessments and government policies that affect First Nations' land.

"I came here … to confront Carney's CEO summit to let them know that our lands and our resources are not on the chopping block for their profit and their benefit," ThunderSky said.

National sovereignty and the impact of various projects on the environment was also a prominent concern throughout the speeches.

"Everybody worries about their own backyard. Our front yard is this entire planet and we must stand together to protect it." said Wet’suwet’en Nation Hereditary Chief Na'Moks.

"They're taking everything we survive on and are willing to sell it to foreign investors."

'We would never compromise our national security': Joly

Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, asked if the Canadian government is selling off Canada to foreign interests through the summit, said: "We would never do that. Why? Because, fundamentally, we always would work for Canadians and be able also to deliver for Canadians.

"My job as minister of industry is to protect Canada's interests through the Investment Canada Act," Joly added.

"Of course, we would never compromise our national security but fundamentally we are 42 million people and we don't have enough capital to develop all of our companies and also to develop all of the infrastructure projects we need to develop the potential of this country.

"So that's why, like many other countries on Earth, we need to attract more foreign capital."

Joly said a successful summit would result in "good deals" and memorandums of understanding to show intent to do more deals. She said the government will see the impacts of the summit in three months to a year.

WATCH | Carney invites investors to Toronto to discuss future partnerships: What is the Canada Investment Summit? Inside Carney's investment summit in Toronto | Duration 3:33 Hundreds of deep-pocketed investors have descended on Toronto for the first-of-its-kind summit. CBC’s Clara Pasieka breaks down Prime Minister Mark Carney’s pitch — and the pushback from critics.

Meanwhile, speaker Nik Barry-Shaw, trade and privatization campaigner for the Council of Canadians, which advocates for clean water, green energy and fair trade, referenced the prime minister's speech to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland in January when he said: "If we're not at the table, we're on the menu."

"I've been looking around the table that Carney has set for this summer and I don't see any of us at the table," he said. "Does that mean we're on the menu?"

Nik Barry-Shaw, trade and privatization campaigner for the Council of Canadians, speaks at a news conference at Toronto's city hall organized by a coalition of local leaders in opposition of the Canada Investment Summit on Sept. 14, 2026. (Claude Beaudoin/CBC)

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said in a statement Sunday that he welcomes foreign investment, noting 15 major projects in the province "worth tens of billions of dollars" are set to be discussed. They range from mining to energy production and AI.

"We are building an economy that can compete with anyone, anywhere," he said in the statement. "That’s going to be my message throughout the Canada Investment Summit."

"Ontario has what the world needs and we’re going to make sure the world knows it."

Concerns over foreign investment not new: expert

Jeff Mahon, director for geopolitical and international business at consulting firm StrategyCorp., told CBC Radio's Metro Morning earlier on Monday that concerns over foreign investment are not new, and pointed to Canada's Investment Canada Act, which reviews deals for their net benefit and impact on jobs and economic competitiveness.

"Foreign investment is really important for the Canadian economy, but there's always going to be some considerations on whether the owner or type of investment will lead to some challenges down the line," he said.

Mahon said Canada's trade war with the U.S. is "definitely" a catalyst for the initiative, and understands the push to drive more outside funding.

"When the U.S. shuts down market access or threatens market access, that undermines investment confidence in Canada," he said. "If we don't have investment coming in then that means future economic activity is inhibited, it's going to be undermined."

"Those investment dollars lead to productive investment … that means future economic growth could be higher."

World.title: Alberta NDP win in Calgary-Shaw byelection
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta NDP candidate Kyle Campbell has won the byelection in Calgary-Shaw, unofficial results from Elections Alberta show.

With all polls reporting, Campbell earned 7,461 of the 16,002 votes counted, about 47 per cent, 582 votes ahead of the UCP candidate Mike Derry.

Campbell's win represents the first time the NDP has won the riding since the party's "orange wave" when it formed government in 2015, with the UCP winning the seat in 2019 and 2023.

"I have always had running for political office on the bucket list, and it showed up really fast, but I'm glad that we get to focus on what truly matters. It's our family, it's our friends, it's our community," Campbell told supporters at a pub in southeast Calgary on Monday evening.

"This opportunity is a chance to live what I believe in my heart, which is that leadership is about service."

The seat has been vacant since its previous representative, UCP MLA and former cabinet minister Rebecca Schulz, resigned earlier this year, triggering the byelection and what one political scientist said could be seen as a test of the government's popularity just over a month before the Oct. 19 provincial referendum.

Kyle Joseph, who ran for the Progressive Tory Party of Alberta, came in third with 978 votes, Alberta Liberal Party Leader John Roggeveen received 602 votes, while Independent candidate Rolly Ashdown earned 82 votes.

UCP candidate Mike Derry speaks to reporters following the announcement of results in the Calgary-Shaw byelection. Derry came in second with 6,879 votes, or roughly 43 per cent of the vote. (Colleen Underwood/CBC)

Speaking at a UCP watch party in southeast Calgary, Derry congratulated Campbell and thanked his team for their work throughout the campaign.

"The team has been door-knocking for the last, I think 243 days," he said. "We were listening to their voice. I had a lot of support that came down and I'm very, very thankful for the team."

Preliminary voter turnout figures show 6,955 advance votes were cast, around 16 per cent of the eligible electors.

Official results will be confirmed on Sept. 24.

World.title: What we know about Carney's push for a 'unique alliance' with the EU
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that Canada plans to begin discussions on a "unique alliance" with the European Union.

Carney was responding to a Wall Street Journal article that said Canada was seeking to become an "associate member" of the 27-nation bloc.

That report included this quote from Finnish President Alexander Stubb: "Wouldn’t it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?"

In response to the article, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and other MPs in his party said on X on Sunday that Canadians should be concerned about becoming the "28th EU state."

Here is what we know about the Canada-EU partnership as Carney prepares to deliver a speech to the European Parliament on Thursday morning.

Is Canada planning to join the EU?

No, Carney says. The prime minister reiterated at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday that that is not the plan.

"We're not looking to become a member of the European Union," Carney said, adding that officials are instead looking to begin discussions on a "unique alliance."



"We share the same values, we have the same priorities, and we have very complementary strengths," he said.

WATCH | Carney travels to Europe this week to deepen relationship: 'Friends need to stick together': Canada pitches 'unique alliance' with EU | Duration 2:25 With both facing U.S. political aggression, Prime Minister Mark Carney is pitching a 'unique alliance' between Canada and the EU that falls short of membership in the 27-member bloc.

Has the idea of full EU membership been floated?

Not officially, but the idea has made the rounds among media and some people in power as Canada seeks to become less dependent on its relationship with the U.S.

One public instance was a comment by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, who said in March that "maybe Canada at some point" could 

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, shown in Helsinki on Monday, casually floated the idea of Canada joining the EU in March. (Mikko Stig/Lehtikuva/The Associated Press)

Barrot's comments at a European conference in Berlin generated laughs and applause at the time, though Carney has consistently said, as early as June 2025, that membership is not on the table.

He said then that he wants to "co-operate much more clearly and broadly to our mutual benefit."



"Not as a member, but along that continuum."

What is an 'associate' member?

Saturday's Wall Street Journal article said Carney is pushing his team to take Ottawa's relationship with the EU "to the next level" — including having Canada take on a new title: "Associate Member of the European Union."

"Associate member" is not a legal designation.

A senior Canadian official, who offered information to CBC News on a not-for-attribution basis, said the "associate member" label is one of a few that have been considered and that Canada did not propose it.

The official added that the government is still examining what the relationship could look like, and hopes to more clearly sketch it out at the EU-Canada summit at the end of October.

The official said they did a deep analysis of the EU's relationships with non-members Norway, Switzerland, the U.K. and Georgia and said none of those would work because the Canadian government does not want to give up independence in return for access.

What do we know about deepening ties between the EU and Canada?

Carney and the EU's ambassador to Canada, Geneviève Tuts, have both used the same word: "unique."

But there have been few on-the-record details beyond a willingness on both sides to work something out.



Carney said on Aug. 22 that the two sides would talk this fall about building a "much stronger and deeper" security and economic partnership. This is on top of their only partially applied free-trade deal (CETA) and the non-trade Strategic Partnership Agreement, as well as the Security and Defence Partnership they signed in June 2025.

Tuts said what that looks like is still being worked out.

WATCH | Canada should increase trade, Dion says: Canada will 'not become a member of the EU,' Stéphane Dion says | Duration 1:21 Former Liberal leader and Special Envoy to the European Union Stéphane Dion says the idea of Canada joining the EU 'will never happen,' but Canada must look to increase trade with the EU above eight per cent. Conservatives and Liberals 'should all agree it's the thing we need to do,' he added.

The Wall Street Journal report says Canada and the EU are "eyeing ways" for Canada to move closer on energy, AI, critical minerals and defence.

The Canadian official said they're aiming for more options on where Canadians study, travel, do business and retire.

What are the possibilities?

Tuts said she expects only discussions about any new partnership at this point, possibly with more detail from speeches by Carney on Thursday and by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday.

Achim Hurrelmann, co-director of the Centre for European Studies at Carleton University, says it seems the new agreement is being put together in a hurry.

He said the plan might include things like collaboration on a European stockpile of critical minerals, university student exchanges through the Erasmus program and a digital trade agreement.

Hurrelmann said this all might amount to a series of agreements instead of a major pact, or a grab bag of ideas assembled under the label of "co-operating on strategic capabilities."

"There are lots of initiatives, but they don’t at this point really amount, from what I can see, to this systematically new step in the relationship," he said. "I’m not really sure if the substance will actually justify the new label."

World.title: U.S. Supreme Court rejects Trump's bid to restrict mail-in ballots ahead of November midterms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Monday to let the U.S. Postal Service enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to U.S. President Donald Trump's effort to restrict voting by mail ahead ‌of November's midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.

The justices denied the Justice Department's request to lift a ruling by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston that blocked the U.S. Postal Service from enforcing the measure while legal challenges by states and voting-rights groups proceed. The agency adopted the measure after Trump issued a March executive order aimed at tightening rules governing mail voting.

"The government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to ​the District Court's preliminary injunction," the court said in its brief, one-paragraph order.

Justice Samuel Alito, ​joined by fellow conservative Justice Clarence Thomas, dissented from Monday's decision, comparing some of the challengers' claims to a "Hail Mary pass" that is "unlikely to be successfully completed," using a football analogy.

"The Postal Service has broad authority to regulate the mail," Alito added.

An election worker places a vote-by-mail ballot into a secure bin at the Miami-Dade County Supervisor of Elections Office during the Florida primary election, Aug. 18. (Lynne Sladky/The Associated Press)

Mail-in restrictions would likely benefit Republicans

No other justice dissented publicly. ​The court has a 6-3 conservative majority.

Trump's fellow Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the midterms. Restricting mail-in ballots would stand to benefit Republicans, given that Democratic voters disproportionately use mail-in ballots, according ​to various surveys.

Under ⁠the new rule, states must provide ⁠lists of mail ballot recipients to the Postal Service and use agency-approved outgoing and ‌return ballot envelopes outfitted with unique barcodes. The Postal Service could then refuse to send out ballots that do not comply with the new standards or are associated with voters who do not appear on the lists.

Critics have said the plan could disrupt the delivery of thousands of legitimate ballots as the November 3 midterm vote approaches and cause chaos, given imminent plans by many states to ⁠send out mail ballots to eligible voters.

Talwani imposed ​an injunction on Sept. 4 blocking the rule, finding that it likely violated the U.S. Constitution, under which states administer elections. Talwani also said it would be impossible for the states to comply given the ⁠rapidly approaching midterms.

Another federal judge, U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols in Washington, D.C., also ruled against the new rule on Sunday.

An individual demonstrates against proposed changes to the U. S. Postal Service and Trump's executive order regarding mail-in ballots July 28. (Marta Lavandier/The Associated Press)

'Testing the limits' of power

Sophia Lin Lakin, voting rights project director at the American Civil Liberties Union, which helped to represent some of the challengers to the USPS rule, welcomed Monday's decision.

"This administration keeps testing the limits of its power, as if the rules ‌governing our elections are merely suggestions to ignore when they don't suit the president's agenda. But the Constitution gives states and Congress the power to set the rules for federal elections — not the president, and not the Postal Service," she said.

"Today is a good day for democracy, the rule of law and the American people looking to exercise their constitutional right to vote," said California Gov. Gavin Newsom, whose state led one of the lawsuits against the rule.

"Trump's attacks on democracy these last 20 months ​have been nothing short of un-American."

Trump himself often votes by mail

Trump signed his executive order targeting mail-in ballots after years of casting doubt on their security, though he often votes by mail himself. Trump has made false claims of widespread fraud ‌in U.S. elections, including claims that fraud contributed to his 2020 loss to former Democratic president Joe Biden.

The administration, in a Sept. 6 emergency request, urged the Supreme Court to allow it to implement an "important federal policy to protect the mails from being used to commit voter fraud."

WATCH | What's behind Trump's bid to limit mail-in: The truth behind Trump’s push to ban mail-in voting | About That | Duration 11:16 President Donald Trump wants to do away with mail-in voting, claiming it's responsible for 'massive voter fraud' in the U.S. Andrew Chang explores what might really be behind Trump's contempt for mail-in ballots and what he can actually do about it. Images provided by Getty Images, The Canadian Press and Reuters.

The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston refused last Thursday to put Talwani's order on hold. The 1st Circuit said that the rule "will ⁠likely result in the disenfranchisement of millions of voters across the country while providing minimal — if any — gains in combating voter fraud."

Nichols granted ⁠a request ⁠from the Democratic Party and groups including the NAACP for ​a preliminary injunction blocking the rule. Nichols wrote that the rule could make it harder for some people to vote by mail and that it exceeded ​the Postal Service's authority.

"No statute grants the Postal ⁠Service the power to issue key parts of the rule," Nichols wrote.

All 50 states allow for some form of mail-in voting. Of those, 29 states allow voters to request mail ballots without providing a reason, and eight conduct their elections entirely by mail.

The battle over mail ballots is one in a series of efforts by the administration to boost federal involvement in voting ahead of the midterms. On Aug. 24, the Supreme Court lifted an earlier injunction imposed by Talwani in ⁠June blocking Trump's executive order, including the USPS ‌rule before it had been finalized.

World.title: Former Saskatoon private school admin, pictured with paddle in 1997, testifies at former principal's trial
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A photo of a former administrator for a Saskatoon private Christian school holding a wooden paddle, published in Maclean's magazine 30 years ago, is now evidence in the assault trial of a former principal at the school.

Duff Arthur Friesen faces five counts of assault with a weapon. He has pleaded not guilty to all of them.

Friesen is accused of hitting students with a wooden paddle. The charges stem from his time at Christian Centre Academy from 1997 to 2007.

The school was later renamed Legacy Christian Academy, then Valour Academy. It's closely associated with Mile Two Church, now called Encounter Church.

Duff Arthur Friesen makes his way into Saskatoon Court of King's Bench last week for the start of his jury trial. He faces five counts of assault with a weapon. (Travis Reddaway/CBC)

Lou Brunelle, the man in the magazine photo from 1997, was the first defence witness at the trial. He testified Monday that paddling was school policy and parents signed off.

Brunelle worked at the school from 1989 to 2001, first as a supervisor and then an administrative assistant, reporting to the director and senior to the teachers. He said the role can be compared to that of a vice-principal.

He said the paddle was one of multiple methods, alongside things like demerits and detentions, that the school used to enforce discipline for things like stealing, lying or cheating.

“We would chat with the child. If warranted — three swats,” he told the jury.

He said the student and the discipliner would then pray together.

Brunelle also testified that none of the staff at the school at the time were certified to work as teachers. He added that the curriculum was approved and that students received Ministry of Education transcripts that allowed them to go on to university.

Crown witnesses

The Crown closed its case Friday after calling five former students, each of whom testified about being struck with a wooden paddle.

Robbyne Randall said Friesen spanked her hard enough to leave bruises for days. She said it was extremely "humiliating, shameful and terrifying."

Coy Nolin, who testified on Wednesday, told the jury he was called to Friesen's office during a school day after Friesen sent a letter to his mother about his schoolwork, and was told he would be taken off the basketball team if he didn't catch up.

He said Friesen told him he’d be getting paddled and sent back to class. Nolin said he then put his hands on the seat of a chair and bent over.

“He struck me three times,” Nolin said.

The trial is set for two weeks, with Justice Daryl Labach presiding.
