World.title: Alarm in Denmark after Russian ship fires at military helicopter
World.content:
“It is part of the pattern we see throughout Europe,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen warned on Tuesday morning.

A Russian ship fired flares at a Danish military helicopter off the southern coast of Denmark on Monday, triggering alarm in Copenhagen as the Kremlin's belligerence against Europe ramps up.

"The Russian frigate fired two flares at the helicopter. One of the flares fired passed within a short distance of the helicopter," the Danish armed forces announced late Monday night.

European nations have accused Moscow of conducting a campaign of so-called hybrid warfare to destabilize the continent while it also persists in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine — but capitals and NATO have hesitated about an escalatory response to Russia.

World.title: Can less paperwork get EU workers moving?
World.content:
Why is it easier for a jar of peanut butter to cross EU borders than it is for a European worker?

According to the Commission, varying social security systems and professional qualifications make it hard for Europeans to work outside their home country in the bloc. The EU executive’s Fair Labour Mobility Package — unveiled today — aims to fix that. On today’s show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Nick Vinocur dissect the initiative.

Next, NATO allies are debating a tougher response as Russian sabotage and hybrid attacks creep closer to home.

And eight years after former Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker promised to stop Europe changing the clocks twice a year — why are we still doing it?

Our audience survey is still live, and we’d love to hear what you think about the pod.

Do you have something you want Ursula von der Leyen to mention in her State of the European Union speech? Let us know on our WhatsApp here or at +32 491 05 06 29.

World.title: Meet the most powerful woman in Sweden
World.content:
Those two dozen or so votes in the Riksdag would be invaluable to both rivals for the job of prime minister.

Center-right incumbent Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson is scrambling to try to keep his job and won’t concede until he has tried everything. He’s now widely expected to try to tempt Thand Ringqvist to join his bloc, perhaps offering sweeteners in keeping with her business-friendly agenda, and arguing that she doesn’t really want to work with socialists and the far left.

Until now, she has been aligned with the opposition side — a bloc of four parties led by center-left Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson. The most likely first step remains for the Center Party to work toward a deal with Andersson’s left-wing grouping.

But, like everything else in Sweden’s coalition-building process, it’s complicated — and there’s history.

Thand Ringqvist tends to make one overriding point above others when asked which parties she could team up with: She won’t let politicians on the extreme edges of the left or the far right force the mainstream parties to dance to their tune.

“We are ready to form a government with others,” she said as votes were being counted on election night. But she warned: “The fringes should not dominate a government.”

World.title: Carney puts exclamation point on Europe courtship with French archipelago visit
World.content:
While Carney has for months sought to move Ottawa closer to Brussels and Paris as part of his middle powers alliance against the U.S. under President Donald Trump, the pivot has taken on renewed urgency amid the Canada-U.S. trade war, which has seen each side slap reciprocal tariffs on billions of dollars worth of goods.

“Canada has understood that the U.S. has changed its paradigm and wants a way into the EU — the front door is Saint-Pierre and Miquelon,” said Stéphane Lenormand, an independent lawmaker who represents the archipelago in the French parliament.

Saint-Pierre and Miquelon was among the many territories and sovereign states of North America that Trump covered with the U.S. flag in a Truth Social post last week, eliciting widespread condemnation in Europe. Though the trip was planned before the post went live, it reinforced the need for new partnerships “based on sovereignty, open systems, and democratic control,” said a person close to Macron, who was granted anonymity to discuss the trip’s planning.

Carney said over the weekend he was looking to build a “unique alliance” with the EU after the publication of a Wall Street Journal report suggesting he had floated making Canada an “associate member” of the bloc — a novel status rather than an existing category of membership. The Canadian PM’s office similarly boasted of the “unique partnership” shared by France and Canada in its statement announcing the trip.

There are still wrinkles to iron out in that partnership, however — including one in Saint-Pierre and Miquelon itself.

Fishers on both sides of the France-Canada maritime border have squabbled for decades over access to lucrative Atlantic halibut in the overlapping waters between Newfoundland and Saint-Pierre and Miquelon. A 2024 agreement limits French fishers to catching 3% of the allowable halibut quota set by the Canadian government after complaints from industry representatives, who accused France of aggressively targeting halibut outside their territorial waters.

World.title: America’s democratic decline is becoming Europe’s problem, new report says
World.content:
Comparing 2025 with 2020, IDEA recorded seven statistically significant declines in U.S. democratic performance, including judicial independence, access to justice, the effectiveness of parliament, press freedom and freedom of expression. Nearly half of the 30 indicators it uses to measure American democracy have fallen to their lowest levels since 1975.

The erosion is unfolding against a deeply polarized backdrop. A July Lowy Institute analysis described U.S. politics as increasingly tribal, with rival camps that see each other as threatening and excuse anti-democratic behavior when it suits them.

The report says U.S. President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch in 2025 and that the consequences were “far-reaching, undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally and testing long-standing alliances and multilateral cooperation.”

That assessment also has a concrete policy backdrop. A February 2025 executive order directed officials carrying out U.S. foreign policy to act under the president’s authority and warned that failure to implement his policy could lead to professional discipline.

Casas-Zamora elaborated that the spillover was evident in the way governments justify attacks on democratic institutions and civil society. “What we are seeing is that all the countries take cues from what has happened in the U.S. in the recent past. We see it in very concrete cases,” he said.

“Many of the arguments used in the U.S. when USAID was shut down were later used in Serbia, for example, to clamp down on civil society organizations that were deemed undesirable by the government,” he said.

World.title: Von der Leyen U-turns, will attend landmark Carney speech
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen delivers a press statement before a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at EU headquarters on September 2, 2026, in Brussels. | Omar Havana/Getty Images

STRASBOURG — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will attend Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday, reversing an earlier decision to skip the speech.

The U-turn comes after Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho told POLITICO on Monday morning that von der Leyen would miss the address because of “prior commitments” in Brussels that day, including the presentation of a new child online safety law.

“The President will attend PM Carney speech at the EP in Strasbourg on Thursday. In view of that, we managed to move the press conference by President von der Leyen and [Executive Vice President] Virkkunen to Strasbourg, also on Thursday morning,” Pinho said in a text message on Monday evening.

World.title: NATO 'committed and ready' after shooting down drone over Lithuania
World.content:
NATO stands "vigilant, committed, and ready," Lithuania's foreign minister said Tuesday, after an allied fighter jet destroyed a drone that crossed into the country's airspace from Belarus — the latest in a string of aerial incursions testing the alliance's eastern border with Russia.

 

Kestutis Budrys credited the interception to the strength of collective defence, thanking the allies whose air presence, he said, protects Baltic skies and reinforces regional security.

But the message lands beyond Vilnius: as Russia's war on Ukraine grinds on, the alliance's eastern members are increasingly treating airspace violations — deliberate or not — as tests of NATO's resolve, and Tuesday's response was framed as proof the system works.

President Gitanas Nauseda confirmed the incident on social media, saying the drone had been destroyed.

"A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets," Gitanas Nauseda wrote in a post on X.

"With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region," he added.

Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre said the drone had crossed from Belarus, moved through the Lentvaris and Trakai areas heading west, and came down in a rural area near the village of Pratkūnai, in Kaunas county — the first time a drone has been shot down over Lithuanian territory.

Moscow has not commented on the incident.

The episode was not isolated. Hours later, Poland announced it had launched its own "aviation operations," citing Russian jet-powered drones striking Ukrainian territory near its borders.

Warsaw described the measures as preventive, intended to secure airspace in regions adjacent to the conflict — a sign that vigilance is spreading well beyond the Baltic states.

Testing fragile energy site truce

Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have reported repeated drone incursions since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, but interceptions by NATO aircraft remain rare enough to draw attention.

The alliance's air-policing mission shot down a Ukrainian drone that strayed into Estonian airspace in May — its first such interception since the war started.

European officials have also pointed to Russia diverting Ukrainian drones aimed at industrial and oil facilities near St Petersburg, on the Gulf of Finland.

The incursion comes at a delicate diplomatic moment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Kyiv is ready to take "de-escalatory steps" if Moscow reciprocates, after US President Donald Trump announced the two sides had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure.

Even so, fighting continued overnight: Ukrainian forces struck Russian military targets in Krasnodar Krai, while Russia launched 102 drones at Ukraine.

The incident also lands against a longer-running shift in Lithuanian policy. Since Nauseda said in July he wanted the country involved in Western nuclear deterrence against Moscow, Lithuania has begun the process of lifting its constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons — a move likely to draw fresh attention across European capitals as the debate over the continent's own deterrence intensifies.

World.title: Would you trust one app with all your digital identity?
World.content:
Brussels wants to streamline and simplify personal administrative tasks. By the end of the year, the EU will launch the EU Digital Identity Wallet (EUDI Wallet). It’s a private digital space where citizens, residents and businesses can store and share personal documents, access private and public services, and sign documents digitally.

 

The Digital Identity Wallet is a free app that users can download on their mobile devices. It reduces reliance on major tech companies' storage solutions, like Apple and Google Wallet, and on national systems, while giving users more control over their personal data.

There won't be a single digital wallet app for the entire EU. Instead, each member state has to create its own. These apps will share the same technical standards, allowing users to access their wallets and service providers to deliver services anywhere in the EU at any time.

What is the EUDI Wallet?

The EUDI Wallet is part of the eIDAS 2.0 Regulation, which aims to create a single digital market for electronic identification. It’s a digital identity app for citizens, residents, and businesses in the EU that simplifies document storage, streamlines digital identification, and makes it more secure and reliable.

Instead of carrying printed copies of personal documents or using multiple mobile storage apps, the Wallet lets users keep all their important documents in one private digital space. These can include official credentials such as national IDs or birth certificates. Medical prescriptions, university diplomas, mobile versions of driving licences, gym memberships and boarding passes can be included too.

Through the Wallet, users can share documents with private and public authorities, both online and offline, across the EU. For example, when applying for a job in Germany, users can show employers a Spanish university certificate without submitting paperwork from scratch. When renting a flat in Stockholm, users can show their rental history from Milan directly from the Wallet, without using a national app.

Users can access national or cross-border public services, including health insurance or social security portals, or apply for a passport or file taxes. They also have direct access to private services, including applying for a bank loan or opening an online bank account.

When applying for services, users must identify themselves, but remain in control of their digital identity throughout the process.

"People should have the right to say no, to not share any of your information or only selectively share information. For example, if someone asks for your student ID, you could give them your university name and maybe the subject you study, but not your student ID", said Thomas Lohninger, Executive Director of the digital rights NGO epicenter.

Built-in features, such as “selective disclosure” and “zero-knowledge proof”, will let users share only the required information, without revealing other identifying details. This ensures that service providers collect only the minimum data needed to provide a service. Through a privacy dashboard, users will track who has access to their data, while digital document issuers must not track or profile users.

Users can sign documents directly from the Wallet using a free e-signature that has the same legal validity as a handwritten one across member states.

Security and privacy

Since the Wallet consolidates a wide range of vital credentials into one digital system, centralising so much sensitive information creates a single point of failure.

“If you put all eggs in one basket, then that basket hopefully never fails,” said Lohninger. A hack, technical failure or outage could potentially affect access to everything from public transport and government services to digital accounts and identity documents.

If a user’s phone is compromised or stolen, the thief could gain immediate access to a citizen’s entire legal, medical, and professional information.

Second come the technical risks. Even though the legal framework forbids member states from tracking wallet usage, the application still has to communicate with government servers to check if a credential is valid. If a state implements a centralised verification system, it creates a digital trail. This would allow a government or collaborating private corporations to cross-reference timestamps and keys, tracking exactly where and when a citizen authenticates.

There is also growing concern about what privacy advocates call “over identification.” Lohninger argues that the Wallet could make verified identification so easy and inexpensive that organisations begin requesting it even where it was previously unnecessary. “Things that we can do pseudonymously or anonymously right now might soon become more and more under real name obligation,” he said.

The risks will vary depending on how each member state decides to store the data. The option that guarantees the most privacy is decentralised architecture, where all credentials live exclusively on the smartphone’s physical secure hardware chip. But if a country prefers cloud-based backups or central servers, it creates a massive target for cybercriminals and insider threats, significantly weakening data security.

Some of the privacy protections envisioned for the Wallet also depend on cryptographic technology that is still being developed. Lohninger pointed to zero knowledge proofs, which could, for example, allow someone to prove they are over 18 without revealing their date of birth.

But he cautioned that parts of the required technical framework remain unfinished and described some of the privacy preserving technology as “the frontier of cryptographic science.” In practice, he said, developers are balancing a difficult triangle of privacy, security and usability.

Who is behind EUDI?

Three actors work together to make the system work. Wallet providers are private companies that build the wallet apps, make them available for users to download, and provide technical support. Issuers are trusted public or private organisations that issue digital documents, such as education certificates, residence permits and driving licences. Service providers are private or public entities that use the information in the wallet and request user authentication before offering their service, such as pharmacies or universities.

Six large-scale pilots (LSPs) combine public and private-sector expertise to test and improve the Wallet’s functionality across a range of real-life scenarios, such as ticket purchase and travel check-in, ahead of its rollout. 550 private companies and public authorities across the EU, Norway, Iceland and Ukraine are involved in the current LSPs and test more than 11 everyday use cases.

Two LSPs are currently active, while four started in 2023 and have now completed their work. APTITUDE, is testing the Wallet for applications like the Digital Travel Credentials (DTC), a secure digital version of the passport for faster, smoother border checks. WE BUILD Consortium focuses on streamlining payment interactions between businesses, between businesses and governments, and between businesses and consumers.

Member states will have their own national wallet app. The Commission has set up a common EU-wide toolbox that wallet providers must implement. This includes technical specifications, such as agreed standards, protocols, and formats.

National situation

EU countries are racing against a deadline, as they need to provide citizens with a fully functional EUDI wallet by the end of 2026. But Lohninger expects the rollout to be uneven. “Very few member states will be able to hold this deadline,” he said, as some countries may launch systems that resemble the Wallet without being fully functional or interoperable from the start. The frontrunners are Italy, France, Finland, and Bulgaria.

Their strategy was to leverage pre-existing digital services and widely adopted apps, updating them to fit EUDI. They already have open testing environments where developers and third-party credential verifiers can integrate with the upcoming wallet infrastructure.

Italy’s government integrated the EUDI framework directly into its popular public services app, IO, via the IT-Wallet initiative. Italian citizens can already load digital health cards and driving licences into a live test environment.

Meanwhile, France launched the EUDIW Unfold Playground through its pre-existing France Identité ecosystem. It’s a specialised sandbox that allows external technology tools to issue and verify digital credentials within the French environment.

Another country racing ahead is Croatia, which is re-coding its pre-existing Certilia Wallet app to align with the EU’s strict Architecture Reference Framework. This allows it to turn an already-trusted domestic app into a legally compliant European wallet well ahead of the deadline, saving time and development resources.

Other member states struggle with technical delivery, government bottlenecks, commercial motivations, and security issues. Many countries lack the local cybersecurity framework to certify apps to this standard quickly.

Sweden and Germany haven’t yet figured out practical delivery, with Sweden publishing a roadmap that sets a 2028 or 2029 EUDI Wallet release date. Germany hasn’t moved from the prototype phase to a cohesive national rollout; It’s slowed by complex procurement and debate over whether the wallet should be fully public or a public-private hybrid.

All this while Greece, Slovakia, and others remain stuck in private testing phases. Unlike Italy or France, they do not have an open public sandbox or external APIs for developers to test against. Romania was in this group until a private partnership with Mastercard helped it fast-track a hybrid model.

World.title: US military says it is facing a shortfall in ammunition as a result of Iran war
World.content:
A report by the US Defence Department's inspector general has confirmed that the war with Iran has caused shortages of ammunition and advanced weapons in the US military.

 

Between the start of the war on 28 February and 30 June, "Operation Epic Fury" cost an estimated $33.4 billion (€29 billion). Of that, $22.3 billion was spent on munitions alone.

The report to Congress said the scale of weapons used during the conflict had resulted in “strategic inventory shortfalls” and exposed bottlenecks in the US defence industry’s ability to replenish supplies. Experts have estimated it could take around three years to restore stocks of advanced missiles and defensive interceptors to pre-war levels.

It also detailed losses of military equipment, including four F-15 fighter jets destroyed, one F-35 damaged and seven KC-135 tanker aircraft damaged or destroyed, five of them after being struck by Iranian munitions while on the ground in Saudi Arabia. Up to 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones, which cost around $30 million (€26 million) each, it says were also destroyed.

Responding to the report, President Trump has continued to insist that the military’s ammunition supplies are “virtually unlimited” and that weapons production is at record levels.

In a post on his Truth Social platform on Monday, Trump claimed the US was producing “more exquisite and elite weapons than at any time in our history”.

President Donald Trump posting on his own online platform, Truth Social via Truth Social

The Pentagon has maintained that the US military has the weapons it needs to fight any conflict.

The inspector general’s report also documented extensive damage to US bases from Iranian strikes. Hundreds of buildings and other structures were damaged or destroyed at bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.

U.S. embassy personnel inspect the damage caused by a bombing in Baghdad in March AP Photo/Hadi Mizban

The cost of repairing or rebuilding those facilities is not included in the $33.4 billion estimate. US authorities have not yet determined whether all of the damaged facilities will be rebuilt or who will foot the bill.

World.title: Leak: EU Commission to pitch social media restrictions for under-15s
World.content:
The European Commission is set to unveil an EU Kids Act proposal restricting minors' access to platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, alongside new safety requirements for online services including video games and AI chatbots.

 

Minors under 15 would be barred from creating accounts on social media and video-sharing platforms without parental approval, while tech companies would be required to make their digital services safe by design, according to a confidential document obtained by Euronews.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is expected to preview the legislative proposal during her State of the Union address to the European Parliament, meeting in plenary session. The bill itself is due to be published on Thursday.

France, Greece, Austria, Denmark, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Germany, Poland and the Netherlands are all considering or advancing national legislation on social media bans, piling pressure on Brussels to present an EU-wide measure and avoid fragmentation.

In July, a group of experts convened by the EU executive released a series of recommendations on improving child safety online, many of which are reflected in the upcoming draft law.

"Technology companies bear the primary responsibility for making their products safe. Parents, not algorithms, should raise Europe's children," the document reads.

Scope

The scope is broader than originally anticipated: the bill will also cover other online services deemed potentially harmful to minors, notably video games and AI companions – a move Spain and the Netherlands requested only last week.

The draft EU Kids Act covers social media, video-sharing platforms and online games, considered to pose "specific design risks for minors," as well as AI-powered chatbots and companions, described as "virtual tools that can give mental health and personal development advice to minors."

Services designed and operated for education or by public authorities, as well as AI systems intended for office or industrial use, are excluded from the scope.

Age limitations

The proposal combines safety-by-design requirements for all the digital services concerned with a minimum age requirement that applies only to social media platforms like TikTok and video-sharing platforms like YouTube.

The age restrictions apply to all minors under 15, following a graduated approach. Children under three are barred entirely from social media and other high-risk services.

From three to 13, children can access child-friendly services under adult supervision. Those aged 13 to 15 would get restricted access to social media and video-sharing platforms, with limited features and under parental control.

Safety-by-design rules remain in place for minors aged 15 to 18, even though teenagers in this age group could access the platforms without parental consent.

Companies like Meta and Google will have to verify users' age when they open a new account, using an EU-wide age-verification app or other national solutions that check only whether the user is above a certain age.

Proportionate verification is required for existing accounts, based for instance on how long the user has subscribed to the service.

Safety by design

The draft EU Kids Act includes a list of dos and don'ts that tech companies will have to follow to ensure their digital services provide a safe, age-appropriate experience.

In particular, the bill bans design features such as infinite scrolling, artificial notifications and certain reward mechanisms.

Recommender systems, the algorithms that choose which content to display, should be designed to avoid so-called "rabbit holes" and other recommendations driven purely by engagement-based signals.

Risky settings should be disabled by default, while minors' account content would have to be set to private, with unknown users unable to contact them. Reporting harmful content should be made easy.

The bill also envisages offering parents age-appropriate parental control tools.

"These rules and principles will be complemented by tailored commitments for online games, AI chatbots and companions, offering a co-regulatory approach based on industry-led self-regulation," the document reads.

Enforcement

Brussels has often been criticised for being too soft in enforcing its digital rules, as the online environment tends to move too fast for public authorities to keep up.

As a result, the Commission is proposing to shift the burden onto tech companies to prove they are complying with child-safety rules.

Online services already subject to the Digital Services Act's stricter regime, because they are deemed to pose a systemic risk to society, will have to seek authorisation from the Commission before rolling out any new features that could affect children.

Tech companies would be charged a supervisory fee to finance enforcement.

World.title: France ties EU sanctions renewal to prisoner release
World.content:
But first, a scoop: The European Commission is set to propose restricting children’s access to social media such as Instagram, TikTok and YouTube while introducing safety requirements for online services like video games and AI chatbots, my colleague Luca Bertuzzi reports.

 

Under the proposal, due to be unveiled Thursday, minors under 15 years old would not be able to create their accounts on social media or video sharing platforms without their parents’ approval, while tech companies would have to make their digital services safe by design, according to a confidential document obtained by Luca.

The bill is set to feature in European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament tomorrow, and follows similar moves by several EU member states to tighten restrictions on children’s access to social media.

EU sanctions deadlock: In other news, France is pressing for Russian-Uzbek businessman Alisher Usmanov to be removed from the EU sanctions list in an effort to secure the release of an unspecified number of French nationals detained in Azerbaijan, according to several officials and diplomats familiar with the negotiations who spoke to Euronews last night.

France’s demand – also backed by Slovakia, a rare joint effort that has baffled Brussels – forced EU ambassadors to agree to extend the existing sanctions for just one week until 22 September to give themselves more time to find a solution that has so far proven stubbornly elusive, my colleague Jorge Liboreiro writes in to report.

The renewal of the sanctions relates to as many as 3,000 Russian individuals accused of supporting Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"France isn't for budging, but it would send the absolute wrong message at the wrong time," one official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. "I'm not sure what will change in a week."

Most member states remain opposed to removing names from the sanctions list while Russia continues its war in Ukraine and amid concerns over hybrid attacks in Europe.

‘National security’: However, some officials acknowledge that France has cited national security concerns, a principle applied to critical issues. The French government declined to comment. "Everything has an explanation," one diplomat said.

"Consultations will continue, and further discussions are expected to be held in due course," a spokesperson for Ireland's EU Council presidency said.

"Renewal of the listings is essential to continue undermining Russia's war machine, and keeping the pressure on those individuals and entities supporting, enabling and benefitting from it. This is a priority for the Presidency."

State of the Union countdown: Expectations are running high ahead of tomorrow’s State of the Union speech by Ursula von der Leyen, and my colleagues Vincenzo Genovese and Luca Bertuzzi, currently en route to Strasbourg, have dug into the main topics set to feature.

The annual address is known for its breadth and length, covering issues ranging from defence readiness to natural disasters while setting the agenda for the next legislative cycle through new policies, strategies, initiatives and action plans.

Yet the sheer number of promises means some inevitably go unfulfilled, while others are quietly dropped or simply fall apart. Our team parsed over last year’s speech to assess von der Leyen’s performance. The results are defintely a mixed bag.

VDL’s U-turn: A spokesperson for the European Commission confirmed last night that von der Leyen will attend the plenary on Thursday when Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, the guest of honour at this plenary session, delivers his much-anticipated speech.

That’s despite the Commission initially saying the president would skip Carney’s speech, despite the Canadian premier attending hers tomorrow. Von der Leyen’s agenda was re-arranged to “make it possible”, the spokesperson said.

EU-Canada renewal: Von der Leyen could flesh out in her speech her vision for a deeper relationship with Canada, EU officials say, after Carney publicly made the case for building a “unique alliance” between Brussels and Ottawa. Yet experts tell me that the revamped relationship is likely to be symbolic above all else, with deeper integration on trade and economics likely to require pain-staking negotiations.

In other news this morning: The European Commission Vice-President for social rights, Roxana Mînzatu, has told Europe Today that a new EU platform on labour mobility set to be presented today will avoid “talented” people “wasting their skills” when they move across EU borders.

The Commission will later today unveil a new European platform designed to make it easier for Europeans to request, receive, and verify social security documents online. The aim is to address the difficulties Europeans face when their documents need to be recognised across borders, ensuring that their social security rights are fully upheld. Watch the full interview.

Ukraine’s prosecutor general suspended after leaving country amid corruption scandal

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy suspended Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko on Monday, hours after it emerged that he had left the country after resigning amid a major corruption probe that had reached his own office, Sasha Vakulina reports.

Kravchenko crossed the border overnight, according to Ukrainian media citing law-enforcement sources, and later released a video saying he had signed a notice of suspicion against Semen Kryvonos, director of Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), whom he alleged had forged official documents to obtain an unlawful benefit.

Kryvonos rejected the allegation and told reporters later on Monday that he had neither seen the notice nor been formally served with one.

NABU and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) described Kravchenko’s actions as part of what they called a “systematic attack” on Ukraine’s independent anti-corruption institutions.

Zelenskyy intervened later on Monday, signing a decree suspending Kravchenko and asking parliament to dismiss him. “This prosecutor general has only one path ahead: dismissal from office,” Zelenskyy said, urging lawmakers to act without delay. Lawmakers expected to vote on Kravchenko’s dismissal on Tuesday.

Read the full story.

Parliament pushes tougher energy permit deadlines, setting up clash with EU countries. MEPs are pushing for tougher EU-wide deadlines and automatic approvals to speed up energy infrastructure, setting the stage for a clash with EU countries seeking more flexibility over how their national permitting systems work, according to an internal document seen by Euronews’ Marta Pacheco. More.

EU trade chief to visit Manila to finalise Philippines trade deal. EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič will visit Manila next week to finalise a trade agreement with the Philippines, the European Commission confirmed to Euronews’ Peggy Corlin on Monday.

US Supreme Court rejects Trump mail ballot restrictions ahead of midterm election. US President Donald Trump's attempt to limit mail-in ballots for the midterm elections was denied by the US Supreme Court on Monday, ending a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting already under way, Jeremy Fisayo-Bambi reports.

World.title: Three of the world’s best new hotels are in Europe, according to the Michelin Guide
World.content:
From a 19th-century mini château to a former US embassy turned ultra luxury property, the Michelin Guide has just named the five best new hotels in the world.

 

Of the candidates for the “Opening of the Year” award, which will be revealed on 18 September, three can be found in Europe.

Only in its second edition, the inaugural winner in 2025 was the The Burman Hotel in Tallinn, a 17-key property in the Estonian capital’s UNESCO-listed Old Town.

The Michelin Guide began awarding “keys” – the equivalent of Michelin stars – to hotels in 2024.

The best new hotels around the world

The European hotels that made the cut are located in Venice, Luxembourg and London.

Airelles Palladio Venice offers an escape from the chaos of Venice while still offering remarkable views, with a location on Giudecca Island opposite St. Mark’s Square.

The hotel is made up of four heritage buildings: The Palladio, dating back to 1561; Villa Froll, a former aristocratic academy from 1677; The Conventino, a refuge for noble widows; and the church of Santa Maria della Presentazione.

Michelin’s inspectors highlighted the dining options in particular, with restaurants and bars from Jean-Georges Vongerichten, Nobu Matsuhisa and Norbert Niederkofler.

Villa Pétrusse in Luxembourg also made the shortlist The Chancery Rosewood

Luxembourg City’s entry – Villa Pétrusse – was originally designed by architect Pierre Kemp in 1880, and its interiors have now been restored to be in line with how the house would have looked at the time by interior architect Tristan Auer.

One of the hotel’s restaurants, Le Lys, has already been awarded one Michelin star.

Following the move of the US Embassy in London to its new location in Nine Elms in 2018, 24-31 Grosvenor Square has re-emerged as The Chancery Rosewood.

The Grade II-listed landmark, restored by British architect Sir David Chipperfield, is now an all-suite property.

With more than 700 pieces of art inside, the hotel boasts the largest collection of artwork in a European property.

Another hotel known for its dining options, guests can eat at the first European outpost of Carbone, try Southern Mediterranean cooking at SERRA, discover Masayoshi ‘Masa’ Takayama’s creations at TOBI MASA, or enjoy tea and dessert from executive pastry chef Marius Dufay at JACQUELINE.

World.title: Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is signalling a move to expand nuclear power cooperation with Russia, just as his country’s first Russian-built nuclear station prepares to go live later this year. The deepening partnership is likely to unsettle Turkey’s western allies.

Advertising

On the sidelines of a recent gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan told his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that Russia and Turkey “will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant”.

The Akkuyu nuclear power plant, built by Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due to go online later this year.

Erdogan’s announcement comes amid strained ties with Russia, as the Turkish leader has deepened relations with United States President Donald Trump.

Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, head of the Ankara office of US think tank the German Marshall Fund, describes Erdogan’s move as a “gesture” to Putin.

“Although Turkey is competing with Russia geopolitically, and although Turkey is firmly anchored in NATO and is improving its relationship with the United States, it does not intend to sever all ties with Russia,” Unluhisarcikli explained.

“Indeed, Turkey sees the Turkey-Russia relationship as a long-term strategic one. And this is, by the way, consistent with Turkey's balancing act.”

Trump tests Turkey's energy dependence on Russia with lure of US power

Nuclear lifeline

For Ankara, nuclear energy promises to help it break free from its heavy reliance on imported power. Once operational, the Akkuyu plant in southern Turkey will supply as much as 10 percent of the country’s electricity.

Rosatom owns the Akkuyu power plant and will recoup the estimated €21.5 billion construction costs by selling electricity to Turkey, generating annual income of around €2-3 billion.

Such income could be a vital tool for Moscow to mitigate tightening sanctions by both the European Union and the United States.

“The Akkuyu nuclear power plant allows Russia to build itself various state-to-state payment channels to store liquidity in Turkish banks without necessarily interfering with any sanctions regulations,” according to George Voloshin of Acams, a global organisation dedicated to anti-financial crime, training and education.

Voloshin believes that, given the project's 60- to 80-year lifespan, Turkey’s commitment to Russian nuclear power will shape bilateral ties for the long term, with consequences.

“It will be a source of scrutiny from western partners of Turkey. At the same time, nuclear energy has been so far shielded from any sanctions, so for Russia it is clearly a kind of lifeline,” he said.

The Akkuyu plant, currently under construction, will be Turkey's first nuclear power station. © AFP/Dogan News Agency/Ibrahim Mese

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ankara has maintained that it is not bound by EU or US sanctions on Moscow. Yet behind the scenes, it has quietly followed many restrictions and secured crucial waivers, especially for Russian gas.

By leveraging its pivotal location near Syria and Iran, Ankara has walked a diplomatic tightrope between its western partners and Moscow.

However, deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia threatens to complicate the already difficult balancing act.

“It would reinforce the already existing distrust between Turkey and Europe and Turkey and the United States,” warned Unluhisarcikli.

“But at the same time, Turkey is in talks with other countries, the United States and South Korea. These are the main two competitors for Russia.”

Mutual dependency

Turkey’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels has stirred unease at home, and the idea of doubling down with Russian nuclear energy only heightens the sense of anxiety. “It is a dilemma,” Unluhisarcikli conceded.

Yet with Russia willing to shoulder the hefty construction costs, cash-strapped Ankara has a strong incentive to continue the partnership.

Russia expert Zaur Gasimov of Istanbul’s Turkish-German University points out that more than a decade of joint investment makes it tough for Turkey to turn to alternative suppliers.

"It's quite a profound project,” said Gasimov, “Russia conducts the training of Turkish specialists in the field of nuclear energy, which started 15 years ago. We now have three or four waves of Turkish engineers who stayed for longer periods in Russia; they learn the Russian language for two years, and you have an infrastructure of specialists.”

However, Gasimov stresses that, given the scale of investment by both sides, it has created an important mutual dependency. “Its importance makes the two sides, somehow, at the end, interested in preserving a certain level of the relationship,” he said.

This shared reliance might help keep Turkish-Russian rivalries in check, from North Africa to the Middle East, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

Yet any step toward deeper nuclear cooperation is bound to invite sharper scrutiny and rising suspicion from Ankara’s western allies.

World.title: US confirms it has weapons in space
World.content:
The US Space Force justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China.

The United States has weapons deployed in spatial orbit, the US Space Force said, confirming the existence of such capabilities for the first time.

"The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," a US Space Force spokesperson said in a press release. The statement did not provide specifics on the weapons in question.

"Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain — employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities," it said, adding that "these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes."

US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink also confirmed the existence of US weapons in space, while speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday.

The Space Force, the US military's arm dedicated to space, justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China. It said both countries pose a threat to American interests in space.

China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy," while Russia "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts," the statement read.

AI and satellites: The new nuclear watchdogs? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The final frontier

The militarization of space is an issue as old as the race to space itself.

In 1967, the world's biggest superpowers and other nations signed the Outer Space Treaty addressing the single biggest concern — deployment of nuclear weapons in space.

Since then, Russia, US, India and China have been exploring ways to fight in space outside of that treaty. That includes targeting each other's satellites critical for military communication, navigation and surveillance.

World.title: US scraps greenhouse gas rules for power plants
World.content:
The Environmental Protection Agency said it was repealing Biden-era limits on emissions made by power plants, in the "largest power sector deregulation action ever."

US President Donald Trump's administration has scrapped limits on carbon emissions from coaland gas-fired power plants, in its latest move to dismantle regulations aimed at curbing climate change.

"Today, we are cutting the red tape to deliver the largest power sectorderegulatory action ever," Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin said at a press conference. Zeldin made the announcement during a G20 energy ministers' meeting in Houston.

"We are not going to bend the law to climate alarmism and climate radicalism at all at the Trump EPA," he said, while accusing journalists of trying to "scare" the public.

The EPA's Lee Zeldin said the Biden-era rules were unrealistic Image: Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP

What has changed?

The EPA has repealed Biden-era standards, introduced in 2024 under the Clean Air Act, to control the emission of planet-heating gases from existing and new power plants. The rules had required power plants to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by up to 90% or shut down by 2039.

The latest move not only rolls back the initiatives introduced under former Democrat presidents, but also proposes to stop future greenhouse gas regulations affecting the power sector.

"For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy," Zeldin was quoted as saying in an EPA statement. The Trump administration would change that, he said. "Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices."

Emission as a result of power generation accounts for about a quarter of the country's greenhouse gas emissions.

The EPA said coal production for the power sector was expected to rise more than tenfold after the repeal.

EPA likely to face pushback

Meredith Hankins, a legal expert at the Natural Resources Defense Council, said the agency's actions had contradictory legal justifications.

"We'll have to look at the final text of the rule," Hankins said. "But I think on its face you can see the contradictions. So I'm certainly looking forward to seeing them in court."

"They're propping up fossil fuel industry profits and completely sidelining people's health and well-being," said Rachel Cleetus of the nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists.

"The EPA has deserted its mission entirely, and they're doing it in a way that's cruel. They're gleefully taking credit for it," she said.

World.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Lithuania
World.content:
Lithuania has reported frequent drone incursions since Moscow launched its war against Ukraine. Lithuanian media reports suggest the drone was coming from Russia ally Belarus.

A drone entered Lithuania's airspace before NATO fighter jets shot it down, the Baltic country's president said in the early hours of Tuesday.

Gitanas Nauseda thanked the military alliance for its "swift response."

"With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace," Nauseda wrote on X.

What do we know about the latest drone incident?

Lithuanian national radio LRT cited preliminary data from the National Crisis Management Center (NKVC) as saying the drone came from neighboring Belarus, an ally of Russia. It was heading west as it was shot.

The broadcaster reported that the drone fell in a rural area near Lake Kaunas, in the center of Lithuania.

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said the NATO response sent "a clear message that NATO stands vigilant, committed, and ready."

Lithuania shares a border with Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad as well as Belarus. Since Russia's fullscale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, such drone incursions have been common in Lithuania, as well as NATO members Latviaand Estonia.

World.title: US Supreme Court denies Trump bid to restrict mail-in ballots
World.content:
The court said election officials do not have sufficient time to implement the rule before the November midterms. Trump has argued, without providing evidence, that the system is vulnerable to fraud.

The US Supreme Court has denied President Donald Trump's attempt to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the November midterm elections.

Trump had requested that the top court lift a lower court's order which blocked his bid to restrict the mail-in voting.

In a concurring opinion with the majority, conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh said that while the Republican president's plan might ultimately prove legal, "state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections."

Conservative Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas publicly dissented from the brief order.

The Supreme Court's decision means states are allowed to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years.

The case has major implications because nearly one-third of the country votes by mail.

Where does Trump stand in the GOP ahead of the midterms? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do Trump's mail-in restrictions entail?

Trump's plan would obligate states to adopt a uniform envelope style and provide lists of mail ballot recipients to the Postal Service, which could then refuse to send out ballots that fail to comply with the new standards.

A whistleblower report has alleged that the postal system's requirements could result in millions of mail ballots never getting sent as the portal was not properly built and could therefore experience glitches.

Critics argue that the restrictions could disrupt the delivery of thousands of legitimate ballots ahead of the November 3 vote, for which states including Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin have already begun sending mail ballots to voters over the past week.

Democratic state officials and voting rights groups challenged the restrictions in court, arguing that the president has no constitutional authority to set election rules that would "virtually eliminate mail voting on the eve of a major election."

Lower courts have pulled the brakes on Trump's new system, which is why he had resorted to the Supreme Court.

Why is Trump trying to restrict mail-in ballots?

In March, Trump signed an executive order to restrict mail-in voting, saying it is vulnerable to fraud, without providing evidence.

The US president, who himself often relies on mail-in voting to cast his own ballot, has long opposed the system. He even falsely blamed it for his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden.

Restricting mail-in ballots would benefit Republicans, various surveys have concluded, as Democratic voters disproportionately use the system to cast their ballots.

Polls predict that the Republican Party is in serious danger of losing its narrow hold of Congress in November, particularly the House of Representatives.

Trump offers Americans $5,000 for midterm victory To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What are the reactions to the Supreme Court decision?

Democrat California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose state led one of the lawsuits against the restrictions, welcomed the Supreme Court's decision.

"Today is a good day for democracy, the rule of law and the American people looking to exercise their constitutional right to vote," he said. "Trump's attacks on democracy these last 20 months have been nothing short of un-American."

Also welcoming the ruling was Sophia Lin Lakin, voting rights project director at the American Civil Liberties Union, which helped to represent some of the challengers to the mail-in voting rule.

"This administration keeps testing the limits of its power, as if the rules governing our ​elections are merely suggestions to ignore when they don't suit the president's agenda. But the Constitution gives states and Congress the power to set the rules for federal elections — not the president, and not the Postal Service," she said.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer described the ruling as "one of the most important cases to protect voting rights before the Supreme Court."

"Donald Trump: you lost another one. The President’s attempt to screw around with vote by mail was obscene. Finally, his scheme is dead."

World.title: Germany news: Merz urges CDU discipline as pressure grows
World.content:
Unlike in London, where passengers need to present their tickets at these electronic barriers, in Germany access to trains is barrier-free [FILE: Feb 21, 2018] Image: picture-alliance/NurPhoto/N. Economou

German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger has expressed an openness to introducing ticket barriers at the entrance of big train stations in the country, amid a rise in violent attacks against train conductors while carrying out routine ticket inspections.

In statements to newspapers published by the Funke media group, Bilger said it would make sense to have stricter control of entry to stations by ensuring those coming in have valid tickets.

As it stands, German train stations have no ticket barriers, with Deutsche Bahn staff routinely roaming trains and asking passengers to provide valid tickets.

"In other countries it's sometimes the case that one can only access the platform for long-distance travel with a ticket. This system cannot be directly replicated in Germany, because we have railway stations that have developed over time."

He gave the UK and France as examples of places where ticket barriers were the norm.

Germany has recently seen a rise in violent incidents aboard trains. In February, a train conductor died due to wounds sustained from being physically attacked by a ticketless passenger.

World.title: Kremlin-linked Russian oligarch helped fund Trump Jr.'s wedding celebration
World.content:
Trump's son and his wife confirmed reports that Umar Kremlev paid for parts of the festivities. Kremlev was awarded the "Order of Friendship" by Putin earlier this year.

A Russian businessman with close ties to the Kremlin paid for parts of the wedding celebrations of the US president's son, Donald Trump Jr., and his socialite wife Bettina, the couple confirmed on Monday.

The ProPublica investigative website first reported the news, saying that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the parties which took place after the couple's wedding in May.

Bettina Trump said in a post on her Instagram cosigned by her husband that their "dear friend" Kremlev "very generously hosted two incredible nights" of festivities in the Bahamas.

What do we know about Kremlev's contribution to Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding festivities?

ProPublica said Kremlev footed the bill for the party in the Bahamas, renting a private island for around $100,000 (roughly €86,586) per night, and paying for a fireworks display which reportedly cost some $70,000.

"It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful," said the post by Bettina and Donald Trump Jr.

Bettina Trump went on to add that she married Trump Jr. in a private ceremony "surrounded ONLY by our family." The US president did not attend the wedding or the festivities, saying he had to remain in Washington amid talks on the Iran war.

Bettina (pictured here in white next to her husband) clarified that Kremlev paid for the festivities which followed their wedding Image: Elder Ordonez/Cover-Images/IMAGO

"The weekend that followed had actually been planned well in advance as a fun weekend with friends. It was never intended to be our wedding weekend," the Instagram post added. "When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds."

The couple then defended Kremlev's contribution to their wedding celebration.

"It's unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn't require a political motive. Generosity doesn't automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift."

Who is Umar Kremlev?

Kremlev is the head of the International Boxing Association (IBA). The International Olympic Committee severed links with the Kremlev-led body after repeated warnings over financial governance and ethical concerns.

Russian investigative media outlet Proekt reports that Kremlev is a Tajik native who initially worked as a mid-level boxing promoter.

In April this year, Russian President Vladimir Putin presented Kremlev with the "Order of Friendship" award.

Putin awarded Kremlev the 'Order of Friendship' earlier this year Image: Artyom Geodakyan/ZUMA/IMAGO

Both Trump and his son have been previously scrutinized over Russian ties.

During the 2016 US election campaign, Trump Jr.'s meeting with a Russian attorney was under much federal and congressional scrutiny.

A Senate Intelligence Committee report concluded that the Russian government attempted to influence the 2016 vote in Trump's favor.
