World.title: Copyright complaints as a tool to pressure Azerbaijan’s independent media
World.content:
Blocking media accounts in Azerbaijan

Published by Meydan TV

Following a series of account blocks targeting independent Azerbaijani media outlets at the end of August, the story has taken on an international dimension. In early September, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and the Exiled Media Network (NEMO) publicly condemned attacks on the social media pages of Azerbaijani newsrooms. They urged platforms to examine possible abuses of copyright-protection mechanisms.

The issue concerns a series of copyright complaints that led Meta to block the Instagram accounts of Abzas Media and Toplum TV. Earlier, pages belonging to Azadlıq Qəzeti and Azərbaycan Saatı had been blocked in a similar way. Meydan TV and HamamTimes have also reported receiving comparable complaints.

Independent newsrooms consider the incidents part of a coordinated campaign. They see them as a continuation of the pressure Azerbaijani media have faced following journalists’ arrests, website blocks and the forced relocation of some editorial operations outside the country.

Four complaints in a matter of days

On 25 August, Meta blocked the Instagram pages of Abzas Media and Toplum TV following complaints of copyright infringement.

Abzas Media director Gunel Safarova told Meydan TV that the newsroom received four such complaints between 22 and 25 August.

One concerned a video originally published by the newspaper Azadlıq. Another involved a video based on an interview published on Musavat.com. A third concerned material from HamamTimes. The fourth complaint targeted a short video about flooding in Goychay in 2022, which Abzas Media had taken from social media.

According to Safarova, Abzas Media credited the sources when it published the material. However, she said, the complaints did not come from those sources.

The newsroom was particularly struck by the information provided by the complainants. Safarova said several complaints had been submitted under different names but used the same email address, registered to Farid Guliyev.

In addition, the complainants cited as links to the alleged original material the publications of the same media outlets that Abzas Media had credited as its sources — Azadlıq, Musavat.com and HamamTimes.

HamamTimes separately told Meydan TV that it had not submitted any complaints to Meta against Abzas Media over its use of the outlet’s material.

These circumstances led the newsroom to suspect that the complaints may have come from one person or a group of connected individuals.

Abzas Media sought assistance from the digital rights organisation Access Now and requested a review of Meta’s decision.

Similar complaint against Toplum TV

Toplum TV faced a similar situation.

The outlet’s editor, Parvana Gurbanli, told Meydan TV that someone had filed a copyright complaint against a video about a landslide in Baku’s Khatai district on 3 August. Several cars were buried under the soil.

According to Gurbanli, the video came from the official YouTube channel of the state-funded public broadcaster İctimai TV, and Toplum TV had credited the source in its post.

However, the complainant claimed that the material had come from his personal profile. Following the complaint, Instagram also blocked Toplum TV’s account.

Like Abzas Media, the Toplum TV newsroom suggested that the incident was not an ordinary copyright dispute but a targeted action against an independent media outlet.

Other media outlets also targeted by blocks

Abzas Media and Toplum TV were not the only Azerbaijani media outlets to face such restrictions.

The Facebook and Instagram pages of the newspaper Azadlıq were also blocked following copyright infringement complaints. The outlet’s editor-in-chief, Rahim Hajiyev, told Meydan TV that the platform cited copyright complaints as the reason for the block.

The Instagram account of Azərbaycan Saatı was also blocked in a similar way. Meydan TV and HamamTimes have received comparable complaints about their material at different times.

For newsrooms that continue operating abroad after facing persecution in Azerbaijan, social media are among the main channels for distributing information inside the country.

In recent years, employees of Abzas Media, Toplum TV and Meydan TV have been arrested and prosecuted in Azerbaijan. The journalists and their newsrooms reject the charges and link the criminal cases to their professional activities. Some outlets continued operating from abroad after their staff members were arrested.

Eight newsrooms issue a joint statement

On 28 August, eight independent Azerbaijani media outlets — Abzas Media, Meydan TV, Toplum TV, Azadlıq Qəzeti, HamamTimes, Azərbaycan Saatı, Qəzetçi and Mikroskop Media — published a joint statement.

They described the series of copyright complaints as a possible coordinated campaign against independent media.

According to the newsrooms, the complaints targeted material published at different times, unrelated to one another and obtained from different sources. Media representatives said the complainants had provided no evidence that they held the copyright to the disputed material.

The newsrooms also reported that some complaints came from the same person and identical email addresses. In other cases, the names differed, but the email addresses, information contained in the complaints and the submission process were the same.

The signatories linked the incidents to a broader campaign of pressure against the independent press, which has intensified in Azerbaijan since late 2023.

During this period, authorities arrested and prosecuted journalists from several independent outlets. Some media effectively ceased operating inside the country, while others moved abroad. The websites of several independent media outlets also remain blocked in Azerbaijan.

The newsrooms believe that, following journalists’ arrests, website blocks and the forced relocation of their operations abroad, social media have become the latest target of pressure. They are among the few remaining ways to deliver material directly to audiences in Azerbaijan.

How Meta’s system is being used

According to the joint statement, the problem is partly linked to how platforms handle copyright infringement complaints.

The newsrooms claim that, after receiving such complaints, platforms’ automated systems may remove individual posts. A build-up of complaints can also lead to an entire account being disabled.

As a result, a complaint may concern a specific video or post, but its consequences can affect the media outlet’s entire page and the newsroom’s access to its audience.

The eight media outlets called on Meta and other social platforms not to assess such cases in isolation. Instead, they urged the platforms to examine possible links between complaints, including matching email addresses and complainant details, whether the complainants actually hold the relevant copyrights, and possible systematic abuse of the copyright complaint mechanism.

They also called for the affected accounts to be unblocked.

International organisations respond

On 2 September, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and the Network of Exiled Media Outlets (NEMO) condemned the incidents.

CPJ highlighted the blocking of accounts belonging to Abzas Media, Toplum TV and Azadlıq. It linked the blocks to the broader problem of copyright-protection systems being abused against independent media.

The organisation also pointed to similar cases previously recorded in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Georgia, where copyright complaints had been used against journalistic material.

NEMO, meanwhile, said platforms must prevent their moderation systems from being used to restrict the work of media outlets operating in exile.

The organisation stressed that social platforms are particularly important for newsrooms forced to work outside their countries. They allow journalists to maintain access to audiences at home.

World.title: Another head of Georgia’s State Security Service resigns: what does it mean?
World.content:
Georgia’s State Security Service chief Geladze resigns

Another head of Georgia’s State Security Service has resigned. On 14 September, Gela (Geka) Geladze announced on Facebook that he was stepping down.

Parliament approved his candidacy on 28 April 2026 for a six-year term, but he headed the State Security Service for less than five months.

The media and opposition link these personnel changes to the ongoing developments that began with Mamuka Mdinaradze’s sudden withdrawal from politics, although no one in the government has confirmed such a connection.

Geladze is described as a close friend of former Deputy Prime Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze, whom he replaced in the post. Mdinaradze, who was considered one of the leaders of the ruling Georgian Dream party, also headed the State Security Service for a short time before becoming deputy prime minister. He resigned and left politics altogether at the end of August.

“Following consultations with the political team, I will continue my work in another agency, where I will continue to serve the interests of our country and society with full responsibility,” Geladze wrote, without specifying where he would work next.

In his statement, Geladze thanked the “political team”, singling out Bidzina Ivanishvili, the honorary chairman and founder of the ruling Georgian Dream party, and Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

It remains unknown who will replace him as head of the State Security Service..

Frequent changes in the State Security Service leadership

Parliament approved Gela Geladze as head of the State Security Service on 28 April 2026. Before that, he served as interior minister. His candidacy received the support of 85 MPs, while 12 voted against.

Over the past year and a half, he has become the fourth head of the security service to leave the post ahead of schedule.

Grigol Liluashvili left his position as head of the State Security Service on 2 April 2025. He is currently in custody on bribery charges, which he denies.

left his position as head of the State Security Service on 2 April 2025. He is currently in custody on bribery charges, which he denies. His successor, Anri Okhanashvili , served in the position for less than five months and resigned on 23 August 2025.

, served in the position for less than five months and resigned on 23 August 2025. Mamuka Mdinaradze took over on 3 September 2025, but left less than eight months later, on 21 April 2026.

His successor, Gela Geladze, headed the law enforcement agency until 14 September.

Significantly, two prominent members of the ruling team at the Finance Ministry also left their posts just two days before Geladze’s resignation: Revenue Service head Mikheil Maghlakelidze and Investigative Service head Levan Kharabadze.

According to official information, Maghlakelidze resigned at his own request. No reason has been given for Kharabadze’s resignation.

World.title: Iran envoy: Georgia not the only destination for Iranians
World.content:
Iranian envoy to Georgia makes pointed remarks

Iranian Ambassador to Georgia Seyed Ali Moujani has responded to a statement by Georgia’s Civil Aviation Agency saying the country would fully comply with sanctions against Iranian airlines imposed by the United States. The ambassador said Georgia had been one possible destination for Iranians, but was not the only one.

On 8 September, the United States imposed sanctions on 27 Iranian airlines. Six of them — Sepehran Airlines, Varesh Airlines, Qeshm Air, Fly Kish Airlines, Taban Airlines and AVA Airlines — also operate flights between Georgia and Iran. “As the expanded sanctions list announced by the US State Department includes airlines that currently operate flights between Georgia and Iran, the Georgian side, as in other cases, will act in full compliance with the international sanctions regime,” the Civil Aviation Agency said.

In turn, the Iranian embassy published a map of the Black Sea region showing only half of Georgia. When the Georgian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty asked the Iranian ambassador whether the map was intended to convey a political message, he replied:

“Sometimes a diplomat can say nothing, write nothing and simply share a picture… Water knows no borders; the Caucasus and Iran need a common, interconnected future.”

Map published by Iranian ambassador to Georgia

What Iran’s ambassador said

Seyed Ali Moujani said Iranian tour operators had contacted the embassy’s consular section in recent days with questions about whether tourist trips to Georgia would continue.

“Georgia has undoubtedly been one of the important Black Sea tourist destinations for Iranians,” Moujani wrote, noting that the country had attracted many Iranian tourists in recent years.

He also said Iran respected Georgia, the Georgian people and the country’s independent decisions.

“Georgia’s recent decision to introduce certain restrictions in connection with Western sanctions is one that we must respect as the country’s choice. However, respecting the choices of others does not mean disregarding our own right to choose,” the Iranian ambassador wrote.

Moujani said Iranian tourists, like citizens of other countries, considered a range of factors when choosing a holiday destination, including safety, convenience, cost, mutual respect and dignity.

The ambassador also noted that tourism generated mutual economic benefits.

“The arrival of tourists does not simply mean travellers entering a country. Hotels, restaurants, transport providers, shops, tour guides, craftspeople, public services and dozens of other sectors of the economy all benefit,” Moujani wrote.

He said travellers had also historically played an important role in building links between cultures and peoples, and sometimes in creating new opportunities for cooperation and development.

“If a new situation has emerged today, we should not view it solely as a restriction; every restriction can become an opportunity to find new paths,” the ambassador said.

Seyed Ali Moujani said there were other coastal destinations in the Black Sea region besides Georgia that could serve as alternatives for Iranian tourists.

“There are other destinations — other countries worth visiting, other cultures worth discovering and other peoples worth engaging with,” Moujani wrote.

The ambassador described Iran’s respect and friendship for Georgia and the Georgian people as unwavering, but stressed that Iran and the Iranian people’s right to choose also deserved respect.

World.title: Second chance: South Ossetia revives efforts to promote Ossetian amid leadership change
World.content:
South Ossetian Education and Science Minister Aslan Lolayev has announced plans to open a specialist class offering advanced study of the Ossetian language and literature.

Lolayev said the class would accommodate more than 30 pupils, but did not specify which school it would be based at or which year group it would be for.

“The authorities plan to open another three such classes in the next academic year — two in Tskhinvali and one in one of the districts,” Lolayev added.

He said the authorities hoped the introduction of classes offering advanced Ossetian-language study would “become one of the stages in developing a national Ossetian school system and expanding the use of the native language in education”.

Russian and Ossetian are South Ossetia’s official languages, but administrative work and education are conducted only in Russian. Russian is dominant overall, and is also the language predominantly used by the local population in everyday life.

However, Zarema Ts, a schoolteacher from Tskhinvali, says there is demand among young people for greater promotion of the Ossetian language. She believes the younger generation should therefore be encouraged to study the Ossetian language and literature, as well as Ossetian history and ethnography.

“There should be more opportunities, clubs and classes for studying Ossetian, not only within the education system but also outside educational institutions. For example, why not organise Ossetian-language classes for visitors and Russian specialists working here?”

North Ossetian experience not fully embraced

Zarema says, however, that proficiency in Ossetian is considerably higher in South Ossetia than in North Ossetia. Statistics appear to support her claim: in North Ossetia, which is part of the Russian Federation, the situation surrounding the Ossetian language has been recognised as critical, prompting the local authorities to take serious steps to preserve it.

The Alan Gymnasium, a multilingual Ossetian-Russian boarding school, has been operating in Vladikavkaz for nine years, with most subjects taught primarily in Ossetian. The school was established at the initiative of then North Ossetian leader Vyacheslav Bitarov, who continues to provide it with financial support.

South Ossetian officials, however, have been slow to adopt this model.

In early 2026, Aslan Lolayev was preparing to present a project for a national school in Tskhinvali modelled on the Alan Gymnasium. Reports said the project had already been agreed with the relevant Russian authorities and only needed to be implemented.

Lolayev was subsequently dismissed as education minister, and acting minister Rimma Pliyeva said the North Ossetian gymnasium model was unsuitable for South Ossetia. She argued that South Ossetia’s education system was already “perfectly fulfilling its role in teaching the Ossetian language”.

Second chance

Several months later, however, there was another twist: South Ossetian President Alan Gagloyev resigned early and Prime Minister Marat Kambolov took over as acting president.

Kambolov reinstated former Education Minister Aslan Lolayev, giving him another opportunity to implement at least part of his programme to expand advanced study of the Ossetian language and literature.

How successful the initiative will prove remains unclear, with South Ossetian experts so far reluctant to make predictions.

Three years ago, in September 2023, Aslan Lolayev raised concerns about a shortage of Ossetian-language textbooks.

“These textbooks cannot be purchased commercially because they were published under a state procurement programme. All copies were distributed to educational institutions. Moreover, the textbooks were published in 2019 and, if handled with care, have a lifespan of five years. After that, they need to be replaced,” he said at the time.

Lolayev added that the republication of the textbooks was included in a three-year programme that was due to be submitted to parliament and the government for consideration.

“I hope it will receive support and that we will be able to resolve this issue,” Lolayev said in 2023. There have been no reports of new textbooks since then.

South Ossetia is due to hold a presidential election on 18 September. Whether the change of leadership and the arrival of a new team, which includes Aslan Lolayev, will alter the situation remains to be seen, although there are hopes within society that it will.

Madina Valiyeva, a finalist in the Team of the Future personnel programme, for example, says that if she is appointed to an official post, one of her goals will be to establish a South Ossetian version of the Alan Gymnasium.

“There is a very apt saying: ‘No language, no nation.’ We must preserve our native language and pass it on to future generations. That is the future of our people,” Valiyeva said.

World.title: Abkhaz president voices blacksmith in cartoon
World.content:
Abkhaz President Badra Gunba has voiced a character in the animated film Nart Sasrykva, dedicated to a hero of the Abkhaz epic. Gunba provided the voice of one of the film’s characters, the blacksmith Ainar.

Work on the 36-minute animated film, which has taken five years to complete, is nearing its end, with its official premiere due in a month. Director Astamur Kvitsinia adapted the heroic epic, which has several versions, into a format designed to be engaging and accessible to children.

It is unclear why the president became involved in voicing the film. One possible explanation is the longstanding friendship between Badra Gunba and Astamur Kvitsinia, dating back to Gunba’s time as Abkhazia’s culture minister from 2011 to 2014.

Astamur Kvitsinia is widely regarded as the father of Abkhaz animation and has created more than a dozen animated films based on Abkhaz fairy tales and myths.

Versions of the Nart epic, about warrior brothers who battle giants, are found among many peoples of the Caucasus. Most scholars date the epic to the 8th-7th centuries BC.

Each people’s version has its own distinctive features and reflects its particular worldview. In the Abkhaz version, the Narts are a family of 100 brothers and their only sister. Sasrykva, the youngest of the brothers, is the epic’s main hero.

World.title: We will open new paths of cooperation with Turkmenistan - South Korean President
World.content:
Photo: The press office of the President of the Republic of Korea /Blue House

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. South Korea and Turkmenistan will jointly open new paths of cooperation in business, technology and culture, President Lee Jae Myung said.

The statement was made in a post on the Korean president's official social media account on September 15.

“Just as people and goods once traveled along the ancient Silk Road, our two countries will now jointly open new paths where businesses, youth, technology, and culture can flow back and forth,” Lee said.

The South Korean president said the two countries have steadily expanded cooperation since establishing diplomatic relations in 1992.

According to Lee, bilateral cooperation has been centered on the energy and plant sectors.

Meanwhile, Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov is paying a state visit to South Korea and taking part in the first Central Asia-Republic of Korea Summit in Seoul on September 16-17. The summit brings together the leaders of South Korea and the five Central Asian countries - Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan - marking the first elevation of the Korea-Central Asia dialogue to the leaders’ level. Seoul has said the summit is intended to deepen regional cooperation and produce practical results for the participating countries.

For Turkmenistan, the summit is taking place alongside a state visit and bilateral negotiations with the South Korean leadership. During South Korean President Yoon Suk Yeol's state visit to Turkmenistan in June 2024, the two countries signed a memorandum aimed at strengthening cooperation in areas including the economy and investment, culture, education, communications and human exchanges. Turkmenistan also expressed support for Seoul's K-Silk Road initiative, which South Korea presented as its comprehensive strategy for expanding cooperation with the five Central Asian countries.

The current summit is therefore taking place against the backdrop of an effort by Seoul to elevate its cooperation with Central Asia to the leaders' level.

World.title: Presentation of "Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan business barometer" initiative underway in Baku (PHOTO)

The platform will track monthly business needs, identify existing barriers, and pinpoint new opportunities to expand economic cooperation between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.

The head of the CPR, Mirshokhid Aslanov, is participating in the presentation; he is currently visiting Azerbaijan to foster expert and practical cooperation between the two nations.

The business barometer will be updated monthly based on interviews with companies, surveys of business representatives, and the analysis of relevant data.

The primary focus will be on practical issues companies face when entering the Azerbaijani and Uzbek markets, including export-import procedures, customs clearance, tariff preferences, documentation and certification requirements, as well as technical and sanitary standards.

A specific area of ​​monitoring will focus on the Middle Corridor and its role in expanding trade and economic ties between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. The initiative plans to analyze transport infrastructure, logistics capabilities, new routes, and the prospects for their utilization by the business community.

Based on the monthly monitoring results, CASPIA and CPR intend to develop concrete recommendations for business representatives and government institutions in both countries.

The initiative aims to establish a permanent mechanism for information exchange between the business communities of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan, while fostering the development of new partnerships, investment projects, and trade and logistics opportunities.

World.title: Kazakhstan plans tokenization of Iconic Tower, Birlik projects by end-2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. Kazakhstan plans to launch the tokenization of the Iconic Tower complex worth up to $50 million by the end of 2026, Chairman of the National Bank of Kazakhstan Timur Suleimenov said at a government meeting.

The project will be implemented through the National Bank's regulatory sandbox and the infrastructure of the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE), according to the government's press service.

Tokenization of the Birlik logistics center, worth up to $10 million, is also planned to be launched by the end of 2026, Suleimenov said.

He said the National Bank, together with government agencies, had developed a joint action plan for the development of the digital assets industry.

The plan provides for moving capital from foreign and unregulated platforms into a transparent Kazakh regulatory framework, developing payments and the capital market, financing the real sector, protecting investors and expanding exports of digital financial services.

Suleimenov also outlined measures to implement the President's July 7, 2026 decree aimed at developing the digital assets industry.

The measures include expanding the capabilities of licensed providers, using Kazakhstan-issued stablecoins for payments for goods and services, export-import transactions and cross-border transfers, as well as introducing a special tax regime.

A Committee on Digital Assets and Payment Systems will also be established under the National Bank.

Particular attention is being paid to cooperation between Kazakhstan's nationwide regulatory regime, the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) and Alatau City.

"It is necessary to strengthen practical cooperation between the jurisdictions, jointly develop projects and create seamless mechanisms for market participants. The first such solutions are already being developed - crypto-fiat gateways are expanding, and projects with international participants, including the regional Binance model, are being considered," Suleimenov said.

World.title: Kazakhstan's Bitcoin futures ETF records 34,000 trades worth $45.8M in 1H26
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. A total of 34,000 trades worth 20.5 billion tenge ($45.8 million) were made in the Bitcoin futures exchange-traded fund (ETF) in Kazakhstan in the first half of 2026, Chairman of the National Bank of Kazakhstan Timur Suleimenov said at a government meeting.

This was announced by the government's press service.

Another 650 trades worth 1 billion tenge ($2.2 million) were made in the first half of 2026 through new ETFs covering three crypto assets, Suleimenov said.

According to him, Kazakhstan's digital assets market is moving from pilot projects to licensed operations. The Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE) has received the status of an operator of a digital financial assets platform and a digital assets trading platform.

Three licensed operators of unsecured digital asset exchanges are currently operating in Kazakhstan, with their combined turnover reaching around 2 billion tenge ($4.5 million) in the first two months. Another five companies are undergoing licensing, Suleimenov said.

Infrastructure for the custody of digital assets is also being developed, while opportunities to use digital assets for payments are expanding.

"Crypto-fiat services are expanding. Non-bank payment providers are joining the servicing of transactions. Crypto cards, crypto QR and crypto acquiring are already available. Thus, extensive work has been carried out in a short period and a full-fledged market infrastructure has been formed. Its key elements are already operational," Suleimenov said.

He added that the global digital assets market currently has around 750 million users, with its capitalization reaching $2.3 trillion. Stablecoin turnover amounted to $50 trillion in 2025, while the tokenized assets market has grown 12-fold over the past three years.

Kazakhstan launched a regulatory sandbox for digital assets in 2025, with 34 projects currently being implemented across 14 areas, including stablecoins, tokenization, crypto exchanges, custodial services and crypto-fiat services.

Since May 1, 2026, Kazakhstan has operated the region's first comprehensive nationwide regulatory framework for the digital assets market.

"Kazakhstan's task is to create a competitive regulated market. Operations, liquidity and capital should be concentrated within the country. This will help develop the domestic financial market and attract international participants," Suleimenov said.

The exchange rate used for the conversion is 447.8 tenge per $1.

World.title: Mother's videos of dying toddler may be used to train junior doctors
World.content:
Mobile phone videos of a dying toddler recorded by her mother during her care at two regional NSW hospitals could be used to train junior doctors to avoid other "preventable" deaths, an inquest has found.

Deputy State Coroner Joan Baptie made the recommendation today while delivering her findings from an inquest into the death of two-year-old Pippa Mae White at the Orange hospital in 2022.

Loading...

Judge Baptie said that while the toddler died of "natural causes due to sepsis and bacterial pneumonia", it was due to "delayed diagnosis and treatment" and was "wholly preventable".

Annah White filmed nine short videos of her daughter's deteriorating condition from the time they presented at Cowra hospital on the afternoon of June 12 2022 until Pippa's death 18 hours later at Orange.

Pippa Mae White (right) with mother Annah White in June 2022. (Supplied: Annah White)

Ms White told the ABC she and her husband Brock were "so on board" with the recommendation.

"If it can help prevent the outcome that happened to Pippa [from happening] to other children, we're all for it," she said.

"I think the more junior doctors and nurses that can witness the videos and see that story of Pippa and the outcome, it can help in the future with early detection, earlier implementation of the sepsis pathway and a better outcome.

"That's what we were hoping for."

Pippa White in 2022. (Supplied: Annah White)

The inquest heard Pippa's symptoms should have triggered the "paediatric sepsis pathway" — a protocol that escalates medical oversight and shortens the time between reviews — but this did not happen in a timely manner.

Judge Baptie said the videos "proved to be invaluable" and were described by experts giving evidence as "striking" and showing "a clearly septic child".

"Without that primary source material, it is highly likely this inquest would have come to different conclusions," she said.

The inquest heard that Pippa's family had pushed for a coronial inquest after Orange Hospital determined her death was not reportable because it was not an "unexpected outcome".

Pippa Mae White (left) with uncle John and twin brother Leo in May 2022. (Supplied: Annah White)

Ms White said an experience with Pippa's twin Leo, who suffered a cardiac arrest at a young age, pushed her to write to the coroner asking for an investigation.

"Leo's been in an ICU environment and … I saw how well they worked and how great that outcome was," she said.

"Then I experienced, with Pippa, the opposite … it went so horribly wrong.

"My instincts were saying, 'This is not OK. We need to do something about it.'"

Judge Baptie said the Western NSW Local Health District supported the recommendation.

She said the videos should be provided to the Clinical Excellence Commission to "develop training for junior doctors working in emergency departments or paediatric wards".

Pippa White (front left) with her parents and siblings. (Supplied: Annah White)

For Ms White, the end of the inquest has meant the start of a new chapter advocating for better healthcare.

"We can get into the actual fixing part now and implementing some changes," she said.

"If you ever met Pippa, you would know it was easy to mother her and it's easy to fight for justice and to get some change in her honour.

World.title: Detective had three theories about Queensland mum's 1998 disappearance
World.content:
A former Queensland police detective who led the initial investigation into the 1998 disappearance of Mossman mother Joanne Butterfield has told a coronial inquest he believed it was most likely she had taken her own life.

Ms Butterfield was last seen leaving a home at Mowbray, south of Port Douglas, and hitchhiking late on June 26, 1998.

Joanne Butterfield's daughter recounts final conversation Skye Lemon has told a coronial inquest she felt a detective "committed" to finding out what happened to her mother dramatically changed his line of inquiry after he learnt what she told her mother before she went missing in Far North Queensland 1998.

About two days later, some of her personal belongings were found about 160 kilometres away.

A coronial inquest is investigating whether Ms Butterfield has died and the adequacy of the police investigation into her disappearance.

Graeme Eaton was the lone detective in Mossman when he took carriage of the investigation in July 1998.

His final report in July 2002 concluded three possibilities — that Ms Butterfield had taken her own life, had travelled south and was still alive, or met with foul play while travelling south.

Inquest to hear from male associates

Mr Eaton made a nationwide appeal for information on TV program Australia's Most Wanted in November 1998 but by mid-1999 had formed the view Ms Butterfield "wanted to disappear".

Joanne Butterfield's property was found beside a cane railway at Pin Gin Hill. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

Counsel assisting the coroner Peter Ah Gee asked Mr Eaton about the extent to which he investigated Concetto "Con" Tati, who had been described as an "intimate partner" of Ms Butterfield.

The inquest heard a statement was taken from Mr Tati, then 38, and that Mr Eaton had written a note saying, "Con has a reputation of belting women".

However, Mr Eaton did not recall whether he looked up Mr Tati's Queensland criminal history or what other follow-up enquiries were made.

Graeme Eaton (left) has given evidence about his investigation into Ms Butterfield's disappearance. (ABC News: Holly Richardson)

Mr Eaton said Mr Tati was "certainly a person that needs to be spoken to" but said he did not stand out as a person of "great" interest.

Mr Tati and another associate, Michael O'Donoghue, are due to be examined as witnesses at the inquest this week.

Both men have lawyers representing them during the proceedings. Neither is accused of any wrongdoing.

Mr Eaton told the inquest he was not aware of Mr O'Donoghue during the investigation.

"Specifically with relation to the foul-play hypothesis, did you identify any persons who required elimination as suspects during the course of your investigation?" Mr Ah Gee asked. "I don't recall identifying anyone, no," Mr Eaton replied.

Mr Eaton was asked about a Cairns phone number that was the most frequent to appear on a call charge record from the landline at Ms Butterfield's home, and whether he ever enquired as to whom it belonged.

Mr Eaton said he did not recall looking into it and that if any avenue of inquiry was not undertaken, it was because the investigation was not "swaying that way".

"I can't respond or provide an explanation to it, Your Honour, primarily because I don't recall every enquiry or every avenue of enquiry I made in an investigation 28 years ago," he said.

Items not sent for DNA analysis

Some of Ms Butterfield's personal belongings, including clothing, a resume and identification documents, were found near a lookout along a cane railway at Pin Gin Hill on June 28, 1998.

An extensive ground search of surrounding cane paddocks and rainforest took place the following month.

Mr Eaton said he would have been "surprised" to find any biological material given the time that had passed.

Mr Eaton agreed with Mr O'Donoghue's barrister James Sheridan's proposition that the absence of blood or fluids on Ms Butterfield's items would have contributed to a decision not to send them for DNA testing.

However, he said: "There was a heavy focus on the suicide [theory]."

"In my view, discarding those items at such a prominent location would not be the behaviour of someone who has been involved in foul play of a missing person," he said.

A day after reporting her mother missing, Ms Butterfield's daughter, Skye Lemon, received some of her mother's other personal effects in an envelope addressed to her at school.

Joanne Butterfield's items were found near this lookout beside a cane railway. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

The envelope, postmarked July 29, 1998, bore Ms Butterfield's handwriting.

Mr Ah Gee asked Mr Eaton whether he had considered if someone else could have mailed it.

"I don't recall having that thought process but it wouldn't make sense to me that someone would have posted it on her behalf," he said.

The envelope was checked for fingerprints but none were found.

The inquest continues.

World.title: SA school charged after student hurt in hammer-throw incident
World.content:
Criminal proceedings have been lodged against an Adelaide school after a student was seriously injured during an athletics training incident.

A Christian Brothers College student was struck in the head with a hammer-throw ball at St Albans Reserve at Clearview on September 5, 2024.

In a statement, SafeWork SA said a worker was also allegedly "exposed to the risk of being struck".

It said it had lodged the proceedings against Edmund Rice Education Australia Colleges Ltd, trading as Christian Brothers College (CBC), in South Australia's Employment Court earlier this month.

The safety watchdog said it had charged the school with a category two offence under the Work Health and Safety Act.

"It is alleged that workers and students participating in athletics training at St Albans Reserve, Clearview, were exposed to risks to their health and safety while undertaking javelin and hammer throw activities, in close proximity to each other, on 5 September 2024," SafeWork SA said in the statement.

"SafeWork SA alleges the school failed to provide adequate instruction or training to workers responsible for organising and supervising the athletics training and failed to ensure its safety policies and procedures were followed."

SafeWork SA says it lodged the proceedings against Christian Brothers College earlier this month. (YouTube: SafeWork SA)

The safety watchdog said it would be further alleged that the school "failed to perform an adequate hazard identification and risk assessment for the athletics training".

According to the statement, the school allegedly "failed to maintain a safe work environment" by failing to ensure the hammer throwing was not carried out in close proximity to students participating in javelin and by not using a safety cage that complied with the relevant industry safety standards.

"SafeWork SA alleges these failures exposed workers and students to a risk of death or serious injury from being struck by a hammer throw ball," SafeWork SA said.

The matter is expected to appear in the SA Employment Court at a later date.

World.title: Irreversible surgery as a baby left Stephanie with lifelong questions that are only now being answered
World.content:
Stephanie Saal has lived with a series of what-ifs since doctors carried out irreversible surgery on her as a baby that she believes reduced her chances of having children.

Born in 1995 with an intersex variation, a term that includes genital, hormonal and chromosomal variations that do not reflect a typical male or female body, and affect 1.7 per cent of births.

Stephanie was born without ovaries or a uterus but with male gonads.

Within days of her birth, doctors removed them because they were worried about the risk of cancer.

A doctor recommended that Stephanie have surgery within days of her birth. (Supplied)

That decision haunts Stephanie to this day. She believes she would have had a better chance of having children if her gonads had been kept, or removed then frozen for potential future use.

"I think that has created a big void and a lot of unanswered questions, a lot of what-if questions," she told 7.30.

"I feel like there is a second version of me in another universe that got to explore [having children].

'Joyous moment' turns to rushed confusion

Stephanie Saal and Linda Brodie with Stephanie's medical records. (ABC News: Eddy Gill)

Stephanie's mother, Linda, said her daughter burst into the world a little bruised and "blue" but overall healthy after a fast trip through the birth canal.

In the hospital, Linda sat in bed surrounded by pink balloons and flowers.

"My husband bathed her in the room and it was a joyous moment. It was beautiful," she said.

But the next day a doctor came to her with some news.

The hospital room was decorated with pink balloons and gifts after Linda gave birth to Stephanie. (Supplied)

"He indicated that he wasn't sure what gender we had," Linda told 7.30.

"We were told, when she was born last night, that she's a girl and she looked like a little girl, and he said, 'All babies can look a bit puffy and a bit different. Now that we've had a proper look, we're not sure what we've got to deal with here.'

"We were confused. We were like, 'How can this happen? We've never heard of this before.'

"Everything was set, ready to go, and now we've got to pause button on this and we've got to reconsider our baby's gender?

" We were even told to hold off naming her. "

Linda said she felt pressured to make a quick decision about her newborn's future.

Stephanie says she felt different to other girls as a child. (Supplied)

"He's then said, 'You will need to have them [the gonads] removed very quickly.' And we said, 'How quick, are we are looking at months, a year?'

"He said, 'No, we're looking at probably next week to have surgery."

That was because of fears the gonads could be cancerous or become cancerous.

"My husband and I, we both went, 'the last thing we want now is a child with cancer.' We decided that we would raise her as a girl."

Medical records uncovered

Driven by the desire to understand what happened to her as a baby, Stephanie set off on a search early last year for her 1995 medical records.

It led her to a batch of documents released under right to information laws but they proved to be a dead end, shedding no light on the events of 30 years ago.

After 7.30 inquired about Stephanie's case a second batch of documents was found, fully detailing the medical procedures.

One of the reports says the gonads removed from Stephanie as a baby had no evidence of malignancy at that time.

The Queensland hospital where Stephanie was born released documents to her under right to information laws. (ABC News: Christopher Gillette)

"It has given me answers," Stephanie told 7.30.

"It hasn't given me every single answer, but what it has done is it's provided a timeline of what has happened to me.

"I'm very, very glad that I have these papers because this has just provided so much more information, and I think it's a very rare thing for a lot of people to have this much information about their life as a baby and as a child.

" It's a real fight to have to go through the system to be able to get anything like this. "

No easy answers in intersex healthcare

Healthcare for intersex people is complex and has evolved over the past 30 years, paediatric endocrinologist and Monash University lecturer, Dr Jacky Hewitt, who was not involved in this case, told 7.30.

"With time there's been increasing understanding that young people should be involved in decisions regarding their own healthcare," Dr Hewitt, who has advised governments and international organisations on intersex health, said.

Dr Jacky Hewitt is a paediatric endocrinologist and lecturer at Monash University. (ABC News)

"[They] should be provided with as much information as possible in order to participate in shared decision-making around treatments.

" This is what has been happening internationally and also in Australia. "

Medical understanding around cancer risk in intersex people has also changed.

"We know that some children will develop cancer in childhood if we don't mitigate that risk for that child," Dr Hewitt said.

"These cancers can have serious outcomes. But with time now we've discovered that we can counsel more individually around that risk.

"For some individuals we're able to accept the risk and monitor for it and leave the gonads in the individual and consider removing them only later on."

Dr Hewitt said the while the chances of preserving fertility in intersex cases was low, scientific advances are raising hopes that might change.

"For an individual with variations of sex characteristics, even having progressed through puberty, often the sperm are not able to be used for fertility treatments, even if cryo-preserved as they are.

"However, there is likely to be future technologies that scientists are working on where we would maybe able to use that tissue if it had been stored."

A changing legal landscape

Stephanie is now campaigning for nationwide legal changes to prevent irreversible medical procedures on children born with sex characteristic variations.

Some jurisdictions have already shifted to delayed treatments and provide greater safeguards for intersex rights.

Victoria introduced such laws in February this year while the ACT did so in 2023.

Andrew Barr is the Chief Minister of the ACT. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

In developing its laws the ACT government heard harrowing accounts from intersex people.

"Everything from physical harm to psychological harm, extreme distress from individuals who felt they had their bodies mutilated without their consent," Chief Minister Andrew Barr told 7.30 in 2023.

In Queensland, where Stephanie was born, there are no specific laws but Children's Health Queensland told 7.30 in a statement that under current processes: "Critical management decisions are typically deferred to give the child an opportunity to participate in decisions about their care as they grow."

" Surgical intervention in infants and young children is only undertaken when it is medically necessary and cannot safely be delayed. "

Campaigners want more protections for intersex children against irreversible medical treatments around Australia. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Children's Health Queensland stood by the original surgery on Stephanie as best practice at that time, given that removal of gonads does not necessarily mean there is malignancy at the time but it may occur later in life.

"A clinical decision to remove gonads in individuals identified as having an unacceptably high-risk of developing a future malignancy only occurs after extensive consultation between specialist clinicians and families," it said.

The Australian Medical Association (AMA) is reviewing its position on intersex interventions, however federal president Dr Danielle McMullen said "the AMA supports an inclusive health system for intersex people".

"Our position statement on LGBTQIASB+ calls out the harms which can be associated with medical interventions carried out for 'normalising' purposes where there is no significant health risk."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Minister 'very confident' private maternity care will return to Darwin
World.content:
Private maternity services could soon make a long-awaited return to the Northern Territory, with a new operator set to take over Darwin Private Hospital — but a critical shortage of health staff is casting doubt over how long it might take.

Calvary Health Care announced yesterday it was acquiring 14 Healthscope hospitals across the country, including the troubled Darwin facility, which has faced scrutiny since its maternity ward abruptly shut last year.

The closure forced the public Royal Darwin Hospital to absorb hundreds of extra births, straining staff and resources, and all private obstetricians left the Territory.

Since then, some families have reported choosing to have their babies interstate.

On Monday, NT Health Minister Steve Edgington told the ABC he welcomed Calvary's takeover and reiterated the Country Liberal Party (CLP) government's commitment to taking "any legal, legislative or economic action" required to reinstate private maternity services.

Steve Edgington says he is "very confident" the NT government will be able to reach an agreement with Calvary to reinstate private maternity services in Darwin. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

But Mr Edgington would not be drawn on a plan, how long it would take to achieve, or whether the Territory would need to pitch in and subsidise costs associated with running the service.

"During our preliminary discussions with Calvary, they've indicated they will be working with us to reinstate maternity services at the private hospital in Darwin," he said.

"We're very confident that we'll be able to reach an agreement.

"If that involves bed buys and a whole range of agreements with Calvary, we're going to certainly look at all options.

"And once those options are on the table, we'll weigh them up like any good government does."

Calvary's acquisition is still subject to regulatory approvals and while the NT government is calling it a win, Shadow Health Minister Chansey Paech said the celebration had come too soon.

Shadow Health Minister Chansey Paech has questioned whether the private maternity service "is actually coming back". (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"The CLP government have carried on for some time that any future agreement would absolutely, front and centre, feature maternity services for the private hospital," he said.

"But [the] announcement falls short of making it clear that there is that service on offer.

"Territory mums have already lost this service once, they should not be left reading between the lines to work out whether it is actually coming back."

Staffing constraints in Top End

Last month, the head of NT Health issued an urgent plea for more staff, warning Darwin's hospitals had been grappling with critical shortages for months.

Australian Medical Association NT (AMANT) vice-president Dayna Duncan said those staffing challenges remained a concern and could slow Calvary's progress.

Dayna Duncan has welcomed the announcement of a new operator for Darwin Private Hospital. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"Maternity services don't just pop up overnight," she said.

"Our workforce at all times at Royal Darwin Hospital is stretched to capacity, across almost every department, and we've normalised a state of crisis.

"We don't just need private obstetricians, we also need midwives, paediatricians, anaesthetists, and we'd much rather see a long-term implementation that's sustainable rather than a snap implementation that's not sustainable."

Advocacy group Our Birth, Our Voice's Danielle Mulhall said Calvary stepping in had given local families hope of once again having access to private maternity services, but she said she wanted to see it enshrined in the hospital's operating licence.

Danielle Muhall says she hopes the NT government makes good on its commitment. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Calvary, a Catholic provider, has previously featured in media reporting for prohibiting elective abortions and voluntary assisted dying within its existing facilities interstate.

However, Dr Duncan said the AMANT was not overly concerned at this point as referral rules remained in place, meaning access to care could not be blocked.

Hospital sale sparks concern over private abortion access The operator of the Hobart Private Hospital has agreed to sell the facility to Catholic healthcare provider Calvary, leading to concerns about access to certain procedures.

"If you have a patient who comes to you and says 'I would like a termination of pregnancy', and that's not something that you personally do due to conscientious objection, then you have an obligation to effectively refer," she said.

"We as a territory will just need to make sure that we keep an eye on it.

"As the AMA, we're talking to our doctors, we're talking to our members to make sure that the system is set up in a way that doesn't impact patients."

Mr Edgington said he expected the hospital transition to be complete by November 30 this year.

Calvary Health Care has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Analysts warn 'uncontrolled demand destruction' may be needed to tame oil price
World.content:
The Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and inland Saudi Arabia are now active war zones.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis fired dozens of missiles and drones at a military air base in Khamis Mushait in southern Saudi Arabia overnight.

This latest escalation follows an attack on Thursday, which knocked out the Saudis' East-West pipeline.

The pipeline played a crucial role in easing the world's concerns about an impending global oil shortage.

For months, it had allowed oil tankers to bypass the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, a critical supply route for roughly 20 per cent of the world's oil supply.

Loading...

That was a major reason why oil prices were lower than they otherwise would be in the past few months.

The Houthis have also advanced rapidly in Yemen, capturing territory including Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea — a development which pushed oil prices above $US100 per barrel late last week.

And the British maritime security agency, UKMTO, reported on Sunday that another vessel had been struck by a projectile in the strait, forcing the crew to be evacuated as the ship caught on fire.

US in Middle East quagmire

The fighting between the Saudis and Houthis creates another problem for US President Donald Trump and other authorities trying to minimise the disruption to global oil supply.

Why our trillion-dollar debt pales against the rest As the US crosses the $40 trillion mark it's easy to look at dollar signs but ratio to GDP is more relevant, writes Ian Verrender.

Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015, but the conflict had largely quietened under a ceasefire in the past few years.

The fragile truce collapsed in July as Houthi strikes hit Abha Airport and the Houthis declared a naval blockade targeting Saudi-linked shipping.

Reuters reported that Washington has so far resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention beyond intelligence support.

More pain at the pump

All those worrying developments have pushed the global benchmark, Brent crude, above $US107 per barrel today.

US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude also jumped to $US103 per barrel.

Tapis, which is Australia's regional benchmark crude price, is now trading at $US110 per barrel, up 46 per cent since July.

The price of Tapis effects the wholesale petrol price, or what service stations pay for fuel.

But the motoring group NRMA has told the ABC that the difference between the wholesale and retail price is currently non-existent.

This means the price of fuel at the bowser is likely to increase in coming weeks.

The average price of unleaded petrol, according to NRMA, has risen to $2.19 per litre, while the national average for diesel has lifted to $2.68.

Houthis seize key Yemen port and island Iran-aligned Houthis reach a key island along the Yemeni coast as Iranian strikes damage multiple US military aircraft in an escalation on two fronts of the war.

"Unfortunately, the trajectory [for motorists] for the petrol price is up," NRMA spokesperson Peter Khoury said.

Mr Khoury, however, expects the price at the bowser to fall quickly if the Middle East conflict were to de-escalate.

But the message today from oil analysts is not encouraging on that front.

"The closure of the East‑West pipeline in Saudi Arabia following multiple attacks has materially altered the state of the oil market," Commonwealth Bank's lead mining and energy commodities strategist, Vivek Dhar wrote in a note.

"[It] means that instead of 40‑45 per cent of prewar flows through the Strait of Hormuz needed to keep global oil and refined product inventories unchanged, 65‑70 per cent of prewar flows are now required.

"The sizable shift almost single-handedly reflects the closure of the East‑West pipeline."

World running out of oil

Analysts now say the world is weeks away from returning to critically low levels of oil supply.

"Our low estimate that global markets had five to 11 weeks of global oil and refined product stockpiles is growing in likelihood," Mr Dhar said.

"This compares with our base case of 15‑20 weeks — where flows through the Strait of Hormuz were 30 per cent of prewar levels and global oil markets had the benefit of pipeline bypasses, subdued Chinese imports and rising non‑OPEC+ supply outside the Middle East."

He wrote that: "If inventory depletion is reached, we estimate that Brent oil futures may need to rise to [around] $US150 per barrel to force uncontrolled demand destruction (i.e. where high prices force lower demand) for emerging Asian economies."

Renewed fighting between Houthis and Yemeni forces Renewed fighting has erupted between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemeni government forces, supported by Saudi Arabia.

That oil price would be even higher than what it was at the height of the global financial crisis.

In July 2008, Brent crude surged as high as $US147 per barrel.

"This price level is derived from the last time that emerging Asian economies saw uncontrolled demand destruction in 2008.

"With nonlinear rises in both oil and refined products now a real possibility, Iran has maximised its leverage against the US."

This will likely make it harder for Mr Trump to extract the United States out of its war with Iran, in a way that does not sound like defeat or capitulation.

Until then, the rest of the world is bearing the brunt of more expensive oil prices and higher cost of living.

World.title: Three-year-old girl dies after being hit by car in Western Sydney
World.content:
A three-year-old girl has died after being run over in a driveway in Western Sydney.

Emergency services were called to a home in Auburn about 2:05pm on Tuesday.

Police said the child was playing in a communal driveway when she was struck by a car entering the property.

A crime scene has been established and an investigation is underway. (ABC News)

She was taken to Westmead Hospital in a critical condition, but has since died.

A 27-year-old man was taken to Auburn Hospital for mandatory testing.

It is understood the driver was not known to the child and her family, and did not live at the address.

'It's very sad'

Neighbour Yuyi Hao was on her balcony when she heard a loud noise, followed by shouting.

"I heard big noises, [it] looked like some kids were maybe playing," she said.

"I saw her mother very worried and crying."

Ms Hao said the girl and her older brother often played on the street near their home.

"Sometimes I'm walking and I saw them, they're very happy," she said.

"It's very sad because I'm a mother, so I hear the girl dying is very sad."

A crime scene has been established and an investigation is underway.

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: Teacher who sexually touched students claims she was ‘depressed, hypersexual’
World.content:
NationalNSWPolice Teacher who sexually touched students claims she was ‘depressed, hypersexual’ Perry Duffin September 15, 2026 — 5:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Sydney high school teacher who had sex with one student and touched a second wants to be spared prison because she was suffering hypersexuality and bipolar depression, a sentencing hearing has been told. Tayla Brailey, 32, was arrested in August 2024 and pleaded guilty to sexual intercourse and sexual touching of the boys, and two child abuse material charges related to photographs exchanged online. Tayla Brailey (right) departs surrounded by family at Campbelltown Local Court, Wednesday, December 3, 2025. Sam Mooy She had sex with a 17-year-old boy in his car in July that year after the pair left the western Sydney high school where she taught and drove to a secluded location nearby. She had been chatting with the boy on social media. That same month Brailey was chatting with another 16-year-old student on Snapchat and asked him, “do you like what you see?” a court heard on Tuesday.



Brailey sent him a photograph in the shower and he sent back a video that constituted child abuse material. She sexually touched the boy in her classroom after the end of class later that month. The crown prosecutor told the Parramatta District Court on Tuesday that Brailey “was aware that what she was doing was wrong but persisted in her conduct”. Tayla Brailey leaving Amber Laurel Correctional Centre. She said the media coverage amounted to additional punishment. Louise Kennerley A forensic psychiatrist, in a report discussed in court, said Brailey had likely touched the boys out of “disinhibition and poor judgment”. She has since been diagnosed with bipolar depression. “Her sex drive had increased substantially that she couldn’t control what she was doing, that she felt hypersexual that some of those urges were not being met in her home environment,” the prosecutor said, quoting from the report.



But Brailey had noticed the mental changes in herself and done nothing to get help, and had asked her victims to delete their conversations with her, the prosecutor told the court. “In the Crown submission, the offending was motivated by a want for sexual gratification,” he said. Brailey tied the knot in September 2023. Facebook “She took steps to avoid the detection of the inappropriate relationships she was cultivating with the two victims.” Brailey was initially hit with more serious charges but they were later dropped under negotiation with her lawyers.



In a letter to the court she complained about the media reporting, which included her former charges. Her lawyers argue it amounted to additional punishment that could impact her rehabilitation. “My entire life is laid bare on criminal social media and television. It has been very confronting accepting this as a reality,” Brailey said in her letter. Brailey’s barrister April Francis said it was clear her client was “not in control”. She said it was not a case about the “abuse of children” but sexual contact, which was deemed unlawful because Brailey was in a position of care. The age of consent in NSW is 16 years old but there are laws prohibiting sexual contact with people aged under 18 if they are under the adult’s care. Brailey hopes to be given a conviction that allows her to serve her time in the community, rather than prison.



She will return to court on October 16 for sentencing. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Anyone affected by sexual, domestic or family violence can also access 24/7, free and confidential trauma-specialist counselling through Full Stop Australia (1800 385 578). World.title: Former athlete grilled over police statements about alleged Jones kiss
World.content:
A former athlete who has accused Alan Jones of kissing him non-consensually at an event in Sydney has denied suggestions by the former 2GB host’s barrister that the alleged incident never happened. “M”, one of six complainants giving evidence in the trial, was taken to his police statements about Jones during his cross-examination in the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Alan Jones leaves court on Tuesday afternoon. Wolter Peeters The complainant has alleged the then-broadcaster kissed him at the function on the corner of the mouth after he departed the stage and was returning to his table. He said he believed he froze during the alleged incident. Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, put to him on Tuesday: “Alan Jones never kissed you at that [function], did he?”



The complainant replied: “Alan Jones kissed me.” “M” agreed that he did not tell police in his statements that Jones kissed him on the lips or lip at the function about a decade ago. Bashir took him to his evidence on Monday in which he said Jones “kissed me close to my lips, not on my cheek … on the side part of the outer part of my lip, towards the cheek”. “And [you said] that ‘his mouth touched my lips’. Do you remember giving that evidence?” Bashir asked. “Something similar to that, yes,” the man answered.



Bashir asked if he remembered telling police in his statement that Jones kissed him on his “face, close to the corner of my mouth”. He said he did. Related Article Live

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones trial as it happened: Photos from function where 2GB host allegedly kissed ‘M’ shown in court as indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues “You did not say to the police that it was on your lip, did you?” Bashir asked. “I don’t think I did, but in having a discussion, I believe I pointed to where it was,” “M” said. He agreed he had also not told police that he froze during the alleged kiss.



Bashir spent hours of her cross-examination on Tuesday questioning “M” on his movements throughout the function, including when he was on stage, who he sat with for dinner, and what guests ate.



She showed him pages of photos of him and Jones with various people to challenge him on his timeline of events, including where he was standing and when he left the dinner. Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent relating to six male complainants over a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. Alan Jones leaves court on Tuesday afternoon. Wolter Peeters The former 2GB broadcaster denies any of the physical acts alleged by the complainants occurred. Of the 22 charges in the trial, one count each of indecent assault and sexual touching relate to “M”. The court has heard that “M” was in his early 20s when he started meeting Jones socially, after being interviewed by him as a young athlete. He has alleged that Jones kissed him non-consensually twice when he was in his 30s.



Earlier on Tuesday, “M” agreed that he had “a close relationship with Jones over a period of time”, and that “in certain areas” he could go to the broadcaster if he needed help. Related Article Alan Jones trial ‘I want to kiss you for hours’: Jones’ texts to ex-athlete revealed “I think there was both [a] professional and personal side to that relationship,” he said. He said it was fair to say their closeness was demonstrated through “M” sending Jones texts on occasion with love and kisses. The court heard on Monday that Jones sent the complainant a series of effusive messages referring to kisses and love, as well as sending him gifts and arranging for a helicopter to take “M” to his rural property.



“M” was asked on Tuesday about a Christmas message he sent Jones after the broadcaster allegedly kissed him non-consensually for the second time, years after the function in Sydney. “I was being polite. I made reference [in court yesterday] to the challenges of the relationship between myself and the defendant,” he said. Asked what sort of challenges he was referring to, he said: “Someone who has a presence in media, someone who has a reputation around what they do, someone also who’s been generous to me at times in my life. “That’s why I believe I am wishing them the best for Christmas, even though an incident occurred prior to this at their house.” The trial continues on Thursday.



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny as it happened: Jean Nassif attacks enemies, defends daughter Ashlyn in angry tirade
World.content:
Jean Nassif’s questioning has wrapped and the corruption inquiry has adjourned for the day.

World.title: Nassif tells ICAC it can’t handle the truth
World.content:
NationalNSWOperation Rosny Editorial Nassif tells ICAC it can’t handle the truth The Herald's View Editorial September 15, 2026 — 5:08pm

September 15, 2026 — 5:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jean Nassif’s comic turn before the Independent Commission Against Corruption inquiry into allegations that a group of conservative Liberal Party powerbrokers accepted illegal political donations from the fugitive developer cannot disguise the personal and public damage he has inflicted on NSW. ICAC had endeavoured to have Nassif provide evidence over claims that he gave $2 million to be split between three Liberal apparatchiks – Jeremy Greenwood, Christian Ellis and Charles Perrottet – in exchange for political favours including moves to oust former NSW building commissioner David Chandler. Jean Nassif gave his evidence from his bedroom in Beirut. Outside ICAC’s jurisdiction, Nassif led the corruption watchdog on a merry chase, initially declining to appear, changing his mind, then providing a medical certificate excusing him from providing evidence. All this before he dialled in on Monday from his bedroom in Beirut. Swearing to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, Nassif set about settling the score with those who thwarted his dodgy empire, including Chandler, former police minister David Elliott and retired radio broadcaster Ray Hadley. He also asserted there was nothing wrong with offering millions of dollars to Liberal backroom boys in exchange for them using contacts to get stalled projects approved.



Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny Sweat, swears and smears: Deconstructing Jean Nassif’s explosive ICAC appearance The scandal of building defects in new developments erupted in 2018 with the evacuation of residents at the Opal and Mascot towers. Nassif became ensnared after Chandler imposed a prohibition on one of his Toplace Group projects, and he fled Australia for Lebanon in December 2022. Several months later, in his absence, the company collapsed. It left about 20,000 homeowners in 20 buildings across the state seeking remedy for more than 40 “serious and potentially serious” defects, and he was nowhere to be seen. The ICAC inquiry has evolved into a major indictment of backroom wheeler-dealing in NSW politics and business. It was important that Nassif put his side of the story to clarify allegations, but it is no surprise his evidence turned into a circus. Nassif fronted again on Tuesday and played the victim, even pointing a finger at the camera to declare ignorance of corrupt conduct and frequently resorting to ranting wildly. While he hides out in Beirut, his daughter, Ashlyn, narrowly missed jail for doing her father’s bidding. The 32-year-old Toplace executive was sentenced to a six-month intensive correction order last week after pleading guilty to her part in her father’s fraud in falsifying pre-sale contracts for the Skyview Apartments in Castle Hill to help him obtain a $150 million bank loan.



Regrettably, Nassif’s idiosyncratic and self-serving ICAC performance holds little solace for the thousands of homeowners and small business operators left out of pocket by Toplace’s collapse. Administrators say the company and various offshoots have about $2 billion in debts. Most won’t get their cash back. They are the real victims of Nassif’s schemes and antics. In a sense, the people of NSW are his victims, too. Nassif tried to interfere with the way our democracy works and almost got rid of the building commissioner. World.title: One Nation’s first WA lower-house MP sworn in to parliament
World.content:
NationalWAOne Nation One Nation’s first WA lower-house MP sworn in to parliament Hamish Hastie September 15, 2026 — 5:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New Secret Harbour MP Luke Herdegen’s swearing in was met with cheers and half a standing ovation from a crowd of about 40 supporters, who filled the public gallery at Harvest Terrace to watch WA’s first-ever lower-house One Nation MP take his chair in parliament. Herdegen replaced former Labor minister Paul Papalia, and his election to parliament grows the crossbench and reduces Labor’s presence in the chamber – but the party still has a commanding presence of 45 seats. One Nation MP Luke Herdegen at WA Parliament House. Ross Swanborough However, the first day of the new MP’s job was slightly overshadowed by the furore surrounding the party’s national leader Pauline Hanson over past comments she made about Indigenous Australians and for a One Nation cartoon describing federal WA Liberal MP Andrew Hastie as a “traitor”. Herdegen was asked whether he supported the comments Hanson made a year ago describing Indigenous Australians as “the most primitive race on Earth”, which have been widely condemned by all sides of politics including Northern Territory Coalition senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price.



Premier Roger Cook welcomed Herdegen to parliament, but said he needed to respond to Hanson’s comments. “It’s his leader; he’s the one that should respond to what she’s saying, and saying deeply offensive things, [that are] quite frankly, racist,” Cook said. But Herdegen would not be drawn on whether Hanson’s comments were appropriate. “I don’t want to comment on anything that Pauline Hanson said. I haven’t heard the podcast, so I’m not going to comment,” he said. On Hastie, he said: “I don’t think about Andrew Hastie at all.”



When pressed on his party’s involvement in the cartoon, Herdegen replied: “If you want to comment on those comments, ask the people that made the comments.” One Nation WA leader Rod Caddies lashed the scrutiny of Hanson’s comment on Indigenous Australians, before deflecting to reporting in The Australian around complaints from child protection workers that their concerns about Indigenous girls being raped were not being followed up by the government. “People are outraged by something [Hanson] said, pretty much out of context because what she was talking about was sort of history,” he said. “What I’m outraged about is that a child protection worker in the north has come out saying four children were allegedly raped and reported, and nothing supposedly nothing done about 23 child notifications.” Herdegen, who was late to his first question time by 15 minutes, said the first issue on his to-do list was the fortnightly collection of rubbish bins in his electorate.



He said he would start a petition to push for red-top rubbish bins to be collected by the City of Rockingham weekly again. Herdegen was sat next to Liberal-turned-independent Nedlands MP Jonathan Huston, who is the brother of Herdegen’s newly employed adviser Michael Huston. New One Nation MP Luke Herdegen with former Liberal-turned independent Jonathan Huston. Keane Bourke After his byelection win, Herdegen visited parliament during question time sessions last week, and at the time said he had a newfound respect for Cook. “I was really impressed. You know, there’s certainly some good performers in there. A lot of respect for Roger. I thought he’s a really good performer on the floor, and I was impressed,” he said.



“A lot of respect there, and hopefully, I can earn some respect.” Hunter returns after four-day suspension Meanwhile, Nationals MP and resident troublemaker, Lachlan Hunter, has also returned to WA parliament after finishing his four-day suspension for repeatedly interjecting during question time last month. “It’s good to be back,” he told reporters outside parliament on Tuesday. Asked if he would be curtailing his behaviour in light of the suspension, he replied: “Absolutely not. We need a strong opposition in the state parliament.”



“When I was kicked out of the state parliament just a little while ago, that was prior to the Secret Harbor by-election, and we just saw ... the Labor Party got their arse handed to them around that electoral result,” he said. “If the Labor Party want to use their majority numbers to silence what the majority of Western Australians are thinking, then good luck to them.” WA Nationals MP Lachlan Hunter at WA Parliament. Ross Swanborough Asked if he could have competition as parliament’s biggest troublemaker from Herdegen, Hunter said he was looking forward to having another voice on the opposition benches. “Hopefully we can give him a few tips and tricks about how to stir up the government,” he said.



But Hunter criticised One Nation for its push to slash 750,000 temporary visa holders over three years to push the country into net-negative migration, warning it could impact WA farmers. “This is the first piece of detail that we’ve ever seen from a grievance political party from the ’90s. So, good luck to them,” he said.
