World.title: Teacher who sexually touched students claims she was ‘depressed, hypersexual’
World.content:
NationalNSWPolice Teacher who sexually touched students claims she was ‘depressed, hypersexual’ Perry Duffin September 15, 2026 — 5:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Sydney high school teacher who had sex with one student and touched a second wants to be spared prison because she was suffering hypersexuality and bipolar depression, a sentencing hearing has been told. Tayla Brailey, 32, was arrested in August 2024 and pleaded guilty to sexual intercourse and sexual touching of the boys, and two child abuse material charges related to photographs exchanged online. Tayla Brailey (right) departs surrounded by family at Campbelltown Local Court, Wednesday, December 3, 2025. Sam Mooy She had sex with a 17-year-old boy in his car in July that year after the pair left the western Sydney high school where she taught and drove to a secluded location nearby. She had been chatting with the boy on social media. That same month Brailey was chatting with another 16-year-old student on Snapchat and asked him, “do you like what you see?” a court heard on Tuesday.



Brailey sent him a photograph in the shower and he sent back a video that constituted child abuse material. She sexually touched the boy in her classroom after the end of class later that month. The crown prosecutor told the Parramatta District Court on Tuesday that Brailey “was aware that what she was doing was wrong but persisted in her conduct”. Tayla Brailey leaving Amber Laurel Correctional Centre. She said the media coverage amounted to additional punishment. Louise Kennerley A forensic psychiatrist, in a report discussed in court, said Brailey had likely touched the boys out of “disinhibition and poor judgment”. She has since been diagnosed with bipolar depression. “Her sex drive had increased substantially that she couldn’t control what she was doing, that she felt hypersexual that some of those urges were not being met in her home environment,” the prosecutor said, quoting from the report.



But Brailey had noticed the mental changes in herself and done nothing to get help, and had asked her victims to delete their conversations with her, the prosecutor told the court. “In the Crown submission, the offending was motivated by a want for sexual gratification,” he said. Brailey tied the knot in September 2023. Facebook “She took steps to avoid the detection of the inappropriate relationships she was cultivating with the two victims.” Brailey was initially hit with more serious charges but they were later dropped under negotiation with her lawyers.



In a letter to the court she complained about the media reporting, which included her former charges. Her lawyers argue it amounted to additional punishment that could impact her rehabilitation. “My entire life is laid bare on criminal social media and television. It has been very confronting accepting this as a reality,” Brailey said in her letter. Brailey’s barrister April Francis said it was clear her client was “not in control”. She said it was not a case about the “abuse of children” but sexual contact, which was deemed unlawful because Brailey was in a position of care. The age of consent in NSW is 16 years old but there are laws prohibiting sexual contact with people aged under 18 if they are under the adult’s care. Brailey hopes to be given a conviction that allows her to serve her time in the community, rather than prison.



She will return to court on October 16 for sentencing. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Anyone affected by sexual, domestic or family violence can also access 24/7, free and confidential trauma-specialist counselling through Full Stop Australia (1800 385 578). World.title: Former athlete grilled over police statements about alleged Jones kiss
World.content:
A former athlete who has accused Alan Jones of kissing him non-consensually at an event in Sydney has denied suggestions by the former 2GB host’s barrister that the alleged incident never happened. “M”, one of six complainants giving evidence in the trial, was taken to his police statements about Jones during his cross-examination in the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Alan Jones leaves court on Tuesday afternoon. Wolter Peeters The complainant has alleged the then-broadcaster kissed him at the function on the corner of the mouth after he departed the stage and was returning to his table. He said he believed he froze during the alleged incident. Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, put to him on Tuesday: “Alan Jones never kissed you at that [function], did he?”



The complainant replied: “Alan Jones kissed me.” “M” agreed that he did not tell police in his statements that Jones kissed him on the lips or lip at the function about a decade ago. Bashir took him to his evidence on Monday in which he said Jones “kissed me close to my lips, not on my cheek … on the side part of the outer part of my lip, towards the cheek”. “And [you said] that ‘his mouth touched my lips’. Do you remember giving that evidence?” Bashir asked. “Something similar to that, yes,” the man answered.



Bashir asked if he remembered telling police in his statement that Jones kissed him on his “face, close to the corner of my mouth”. He said he did. Related Article Live

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones trial as it happened: Photos from function where 2GB host allegedly kissed ‘M’ shown in court as indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues “You did not say to the police that it was on your lip, did you?” Bashir asked. “I don’t think I did, but in having a discussion, I believe I pointed to where it was,” “M” said. He agreed he had also not told police that he froze during the alleged kiss.



Bashir spent hours of her cross-examination on Tuesday questioning “M” on his movements throughout the function, including when he was on stage, who he sat with for dinner, and what guests ate.



She showed him pages of photos of him and Jones with various people to challenge him on his timeline of events, including where he was standing and when he left the dinner. Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent relating to six male complainants over a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. Alan Jones leaves court on Tuesday afternoon. Wolter Peeters The former 2GB broadcaster denies any of the physical acts alleged by the complainants occurred. Of the 22 charges in the trial, one count each of indecent assault and sexual touching relate to “M”. The court has heard that “M” was in his early 20s when he started meeting Jones socially, after being interviewed by him as a young athlete. He has alleged that Jones kissed him non-consensually twice when he was in his 30s.



Earlier on Tuesday, “M” agreed that he had “a close relationship with Jones over a period of time”, and that “in certain areas” he could go to the broadcaster if he needed help. Related Article Alan Jones trial ‘I want to kiss you for hours’: Jones’ texts to ex-athlete revealed “I think there was both [a] professional and personal side to that relationship,” he said. He said it was fair to say their closeness was demonstrated through “M” sending Jones texts on occasion with love and kisses. The court heard on Monday that Jones sent the complainant a series of effusive messages referring to kisses and love, as well as sending him gifts and arranging for a helicopter to take “M” to his rural property.



“M” was asked on Tuesday about a Christmas message he sent Jones after the broadcaster allegedly kissed him non-consensually for the second time, years after the function in Sydney. “I was being polite. I made reference [in court yesterday] to the challenges of the relationship between myself and the defendant,” he said. Asked what sort of challenges he was referring to, he said: “Someone who has a presence in media, someone who has a reputation around what they do, someone also who’s been generous to me at times in my life. “That’s why I believe I am wishing them the best for Christmas, even though an incident occurred prior to this at their house.” The trial continues on Thursday.



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Former NZ First MP and brother of party leader Jim Peters dies
World.content:
Former MP Jim Peters has died, with Parliament holding a moment of silence to honour him on Tuesday.

James Leonard Peters, the brother of New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, was himself a NZ First MP between 2002 and 2005.

He was also appointed a Member of the New Zealand Order of Merit in 2008 for services to local body affairs, education and the community

Speaker Gerry Brownlee informed the House of his passing on Tuesday, and requested MPs stand to observe a period of silence to mark his memory in respect.

NZ First paid tribute to Jim Peters in a post on Facebook on Tuesday evening.

"It is with deep sadness that we mark the passing of New Zealand First life member and former Member of Parliament, Jim Peters MNZM," the post said.

"Jim dedicated his life to public service, education, and regional development. A widely respected educator, he shaped countless young minds throughout his career - serving as head of department at Mount Albert Grammar School in Auckland, as principal of Northland College in Kaikohe, and later leading tertiary education as pro vice-chancellor Māori at the University of Auckland.

"His commitment to service in politics saw him elected as chairperson of the Northland Regional Council and in 2002, Jim entered Parliament as a list MP for New Zealand First.

"Within New Zealand First, Jim was a foundational figure. A stalwart life member and long-serving electorate chairperson, he was revered across the party for his quiet wisdom, integrity, and principled guidance.

World.title: Police appeal after woman assaulted while putting rubbish out in Wellington
World.content:
Police are appealing for witnesses and footage after a woman was assaulted by two men in Wellington's Mount Victoria.

Police were called to Austin Street about 11.40pm last Wednesday after the woman was randomly approached while putting rubbish out for collection.

Detective Senior Sergeant Tim Leitch said the two men were standing on the footpath a short distance south of Derby Street before speaking briefly to the woman and producing weapons.

The offenders fled after neighbours heard the struggle and came to her assistance.

The woman suffered wounds to her arm.

The two men then ran south along Austin Street. A police dog handler tracked them to Porritt Avenue, where the trail was lost near the intersection with Ellice Street.

"We suspect they had a vehicle parked there and fled in it," Leitch said.

Both men were described as muscular and wearing dark hoodies. One was about six feet tall, with the other slightly taller.

One was wearing a face covering, while the other had dark hair and a dark complexion.

World.title: Conservationists call on bird-watchers to help save one of NZ's most endangered birds
World.content:
Amateur bird-watchers are being called on to help with the great bittern bird count.

The bittern Matuku-hūrepo lives in wetlands around the motu and is one of New Zealand's most endangered birds.

There are concerns that some of its wetland habitat is being destroyed and poor water quality is affecting the birds' food supplies, with fewer than a thousand of the species left.

Every year there is a head count to see how the bittern population is tracking.

The Love Bittern project co-ordinates the great Matuku-hūrepo muster to avoid the birds being double-counted.

Project founder Wendy Ambury told Checkpoint the bittern's reclusive nature made them hard to count.

However, spring time means breeding time for the normally shy birds, and the "mighty boom" of the male makes them much easier to track.

"Their mighty boom at this time of the year, especially going into spring, their breeding season, is heard across those wetlands up to 5 kilometres away."

Ambury said the booming was a similar sound to that made by blowing over the top of a glass bottle.

"We can hear that from quite a distance away, which puts us in the unique spot where we can have listeners listening at wetlands around the country to record the boom of the male bittern as an indication of their presence."

She said humans were currently their only resource for tracking the bittern.

Bird-watchers called on to help with Bittern bird count Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

"We can actually record the direction that boom is coming from and estimate the distance to the boom as well, which means that we can triangulate the position of each booming and determine how many individuals we've got."

That helped create a population estimate.

Ambury said typically around 400 to 500 people volunteer to help with the count each year, but she is hoping to boost that number to at least 1200.

The task involves finding your nearest wetland and sitting at the edge of it, keeping an ear out for any booming bird calls.

"Record the time and try and estimate the distance and the direction to that boom [and] how many booms he's boomed before he's stopped for another break."

DOC researchers also work to put GPS trackers on the birds, which Ambury said gave them vital information about how the birds are travelling from region to region.

With over 90 percent of Aotearoa's wetlands already lost, the bittern are also being lost at great rates.

"As long as we continue to lose wetlands, we're losing that vital habitat that they need to thrive."

World.title: NZ fuel supplies face increased risk, and no price relief

NZ fuel supplies adequate and unaffected by latest Middle East conflict developments

Global stocks and supplies to remain pressured for foreseeable future

The safety margin for fuel supplies is getting thinner

Challenge to NZ is not fuel supply but price, which will stay high until market rebalances

The head of the country's biggest fuel importer says supplies are flowing as normal and expected but the risks have increased, while there is no prospect of significantly lower prices.

Supply lines from the Middle East through the Strait of Hormuz and the Saudi Arabian pipelines have been further pressured in the past week by the US-Iran conflict and the broader involvement of the Iranian aligned Houthi in Yemen.

Z Energy's chief executive Lindis Jones said New Zealand's fuel supplies have been flowing normally and meeting local demand.

"Supply remains secure, fuel is still moving, it's just taking longer and is more expensive to move, so it's just a story of price not supply security."

However, Jones said the risk margins for supplies have narrowed.

"While system is coping the safety margins are thinner, so inventories are being drawn down, some refineries are deferring maintenance to keep operating and that reduces the market's ability to absorb another disruption."

Z Energy chief executive Lindis Jones. Supplied

No price relief in sight

Jones was loath to predict prices other than to say a continuation of current conditions would underpin higher prices.

He said prices were being driven by headlines and while that continued they would remain elevated.

Jones said even after the end of the conflict prices would remain high until the global fuel market rebalanced.

"It will take quite some time for the system to recover. Ships need to get into the right place, refineries need to do maintenance, products need to start flowing, and we're still unclear about the level of damage to facilities in the Middle East.

"This is a tough time for business and households in terms of elevated fuel prices and I believe it will be some time before prices return to normal."

Jones said he accepted the view of a top official at MBIE handling fuel supplies, who recently told RNZ he was reasonably confident that New Zealand would avoid fuel supply shocks.

World.title: Bigger venue, same scramble: Tickets for Warriors' must-win semifinal at Eden Park snapped up
World.content:
Warriors tickets snapped up for Eden Park game Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

The Warriors' shift to Eden Park has done little to ease the scramble for tickets, with Sunday's must-win semifinal against the Newcastle Knights appearing to sell out soon after going on sale to the general public.

The move to Eden Park was intended to accommodate the huge demand after last weekend's NRL qualifying final against the Dolphins at Mount Smart Stadium sold out within minutes.

With a capacity of 50,000, Eden Park holds roughly twice as many spectators as the Warriors' spiritual home in Penrose, but the extra capacity has been quickly swallowed up.

Tickets for the match went on sale to the general public at midday on Tuesday. By 1pm punters were flocking to Warriors fan pages on social media to express their disappointment at missing out.

Officials are yet to confirm the sell-out. The NRL has been contacted for comment, while Ticketmaster referred enquiries to the event organisers.

Warriors centre Ali Leiataua said given the huge demand he was relieved his friends and family were able to get in early to secure tickets for the do-or-die clash.

"My family managed to get some luckily, got maybe 15 tickets, that's on the smaller side compared to some of the others, Dallin [Watene-Zalezniak] requested like 60 tickets, like holy hecka! They are running out fast so good the boys were able to get in for their families," he said.

Second-rower Jacob Laban also managed to help his family out in landing tickets - although he joked his assistance had its limits.

"The total was like two grand in tickets, I'm happy they're paying, I'm not paying for that!"

The rush for tickets has also raised concerns that some will try to cash in by buying them up and reselling them at inflated prices.

By Tuesday afternoon there were already eight listings on online marketplace Trade Me for tickets for this weekend's semifinal.

It comes after Warriors boss Cameron George urged ticket scalpers to stay away and let genuine fans enjoy what will be the club's final home game of the season.

Tickets for last week's NRL qualifying clash against the Dolphins at Mount Smart Stadium sold out within minutes of going on sale to the general public, leaving many die-hard fans out in the cold.

Not long afterwards, listings began appearing on Trade Me and other online marketplaces for up to five times the original purchase price.

One listing offered four tickets in the Eastern Stand for a buy-now price of $1200, while another listing for two tickets in the uncovered South Stand had a buy-now price of $500.

Warriors chief executive Cameron George has warned ticket scalpers to "get out of our road". Andrew Cornaga / www.photosport.nz / Photosport Ltd 2025

In an interview with Morning Report on Monday, George said he was "disappointed" to see genuine fans miss out because of people seeking to cash in.

"They've just got to pull their heads in, those people, let the genuine people buy the tickets and come to the game and enjoy it with their family," George said.

"I was really disappointed to see it last week and I just hope they pull their heads in this week and get out of our road and let the families and the genuine people pay for the tickets at the right price.

"If I was to ever catch anyone doing it, I'd be barring them from every Warriors game for the rest of their life."

Ahead of last weekend's game, Ticketmaster, the official ticketing agent for the NRL finals, warned fans that tickets purchased through unofficial resale sites could be cancelled.

In a statement to RNZ, a spokesperson for the organisation recommended fans only purchase tickets through authorised ticket sellers.

"Ticketmaster does not guarantee the authenticity of tickets purchased from unauthorised third-party resellers or resale sites.

"While only a relatively small number of tickets appear to have been listed for resale, the NRL's ticket terms restrict unauthorised resale for the Warriors game.

"Tickets identified as sold or transferred in breach of those terms may be cancelled."

World.title: Highway closure costing West Coast pub owner thousands
World.content:
West coast businesses owners suffering from highway closures Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

The small South Island township of Haast would usually be steadily humming with whitebaiters ahead of a busy summer.

Instead, Hard Antler Bar and Restaurant owner Nick Kummer estimated he had lost about $30,000 since State Highway 6 was closed on 28 August during a significant winter storm.

A few days later it partially opened for three daily escorted convoys as work continued to repair the damage from slips, rockfalls and inundation.

Haast locals have been questioning why it was taking so long to restore the route, while the Transport Agency said the scale of the clean up was unprecedented and there was no quick fix.

Rockfall on State Highway 6 that happened earlier this month just north of the Isthmus Peak Track. NZTA

The agency hoped to restore full road access in six to eight weeks, but it did not rule out boosting convoy numbers or gradually increasing access before then.

Nick Kummer said bus loads of tourists have cancelled and drivers have been steering clear.

"Tourists think we're cut off and businesses are bleeding money," he said.

He was frustrated by the lack of communication from the Transport Agency, saying he was often getting information that was three to four days old.

The convoys run through on week days, and the road opened to traffic over the weekend during the day.

"Fulton Hogan is saying that the road's dangerous and this and that. Well, they're leaving it open on a Saturday and Sunday. It's a joke," he said.

"They're milking the system ... it's taxpayers' money."

The West Coast was no stranger to slips and Kummer did not understand why the latest disruption was dragging on.

"I want to see some urgency. This is a state highway. It affects people's lives. The only one that's making money is Fulton Hogan," Kummer said.

Aspiring Court Motel and Haast Lodge owner Vivienne Beagle said business would usually be steady at this time of the year.

Instead, she was dealing with plenty of cancellations.

One of the slips on SH6 Makarora-Hāwea. NZTA / SUPPLIED

"I've had guests contact me and say, 'we're booked for three days time and we've heard the roads closed, so we're not coming'. And I'll say to them, 'do you realise that there are convoys?' And they say, 'no, we didn't'."

She was not happy with the signage.

"So if you're leaving Haast, there's an electronic sign that says 'slips road closed', and that's all it says. And then you have to get three quarters of an hour down the road to find out that there actually are convoys going through three times a day and the same at Hāwea," she said.

Vivienne Beagle has been relying on the Transport Agency website for updates.

Road closures were a fact of living on the coast, she said.

"Every time, they talk about, yes, there needs to be closer communication with the businesses, and every time, nothing happens. It just stays the same.

"You don't hear from anybody. So it's frustrating."

One of the slips on SH6. NZTA / SUPPLIED

Fulton Hogan declined an interview request and deferred to the Transport Agency for comment.

Its lower South Island area manager Chris Harris defended the crews on fix-up duty.

"I'll just start by absolutely rejecting the idea that the roading crews are dragging out this recovery," he said.

"The crews on site are working extremely long hours since 28 August to clear the road and inspect any damage left behind, relocate material.

"There's significant damage there. This is not a small event."

The storm and heavy rain had caused multiple slips, bridge inundations and drains compromised, causing damage that made the inundation of Muddy Creek a few years ago seem very easy in comparison, he said.

"This is on a scale unprecedented in recent history."

It had left them with a mammoth clean up.

"There's 80.000 cubic metres of material there or thereabouts which has come down onto the highway and needs to be shifted to permanent disposal sites," Harris said.

"So the average truck and trailer may carry about 15 cubic metres. So there is a huge amount of traffic movements that need to occur to safely get that material from its initial holding site or stockpiling site to a permanent disposal site."

That debris was spread over 105 separate locations, and there were also abseilers clearing the rock fall risks.

It was safer and more productive for crews to close the road while that happened, he said.

The decision to open over the weekend was made at 1:30pm on Friday, 11 September, so they could check all the risks and give crews a break, he said.

The agency needed to reconsider how it used signage, so it was clear there were convoys going through, Harris said.

The agency had used all its usual ways of communicating, including website updates, social media and emailed updates to businesses.

"But it would appear in this case we're not quite hitting our target audience. So we need to double down on those efforts. It may be that we need to use more of the news agencies to try and get the information out to those local communities," he said.

"The decisions are being made at short notice around the openings and closures. However, we should be able to equally communicate that information out at short notice and it might be that we need to establish a regular cadence of updates with the local community."

World.title: Tairāwhiti floods: 'That paddock's usually just underwater now'
World.content:
Te Araroa storm clean up continues seven months on Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Seven months after communities on Tairāwhiti's East Cape were hammered by a destructive summer storm, locals are facing new problems related to its aftermath. Checkpoint's Teuila Fuatai has been in the coastal settlement of Te Araroa, where regular flooding is now adding to the damage.

Something isn't right with Carl Mullany's land.

When he greets us, it's a typical spring day. There are clouds overhead and enough of a breeze that we've all got a warm layer on. But it's the water around our feet, pooling on the gravel driveway and heading down Tokata road that's a bit puzzling.

Since my cameraman Baz and I arrived in Te Araroa the previous night, there's been no rain. In fact, it's been dry skies for at least a couple of days, according to Carl.

The water at our gumboots, he says, is the Wairenga stream - only it's no longer flowing down the stream bed that goes through his 57 hectare land block. Instead, it is spreading across the property and grazing paddocks and onto the neighbours' places.

It started after the January storm, he says.

Te Araroa resident Carl Mullany says the Wairenga stream no longer flows down the stream bed that goes through his 57 hectare land block and is instead spreading across the property. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"The water here is the Wairenga, and the Wairenga comes out of Pukeamaru, and it's supposed to head down in a straight line to Karakatūwhero river. But after the January flood, it's all changed."

Pukeamaru is the maunga that borders Carl's land. It's covered in native bush, and like many of the hillsides, slopes and maunga in the area, it bears scars from January storm. According to research organisation Dragonfly, the sheer amount of rain that came down triggered more than 11,000 slips across the East Cape area.

Carl shows us videos of what that looked like on his property. The deluge coated his land in mud, silt, bush and trees washed from the surface of Pukeamaru and the range behind his property.

"It was crazy," he says.

The immediate emergency response was about cleaning up the obvious damage, he says.

Diggers were brought in to help clear the land. Uprooted trees and logs were stacked into piles and burned.

"I've got to be thankful to the [Gisborne District] Council because they spent two-and-a-half to three months in here with diggers… and tidied it all up. They did a lot of work and burnt some of the stacks."

However, it wasn't until after the initial clean-up the full effects of the storm on the land and waterways became clear, Carl says.

Standing on the edge of a bridge on his property - which has been closed by the Gisborne District Council due to damage from January's storm - Carl shows us the stream bed where the Wairenga used to flow. The day we visit, it's dry and almost level with the rest of the land.

"You can see all the shingle there - it's just all built up and that's come out after the flood and it's just filled our Wairenga stream," he says.

"I could ride a horse under this bridge before, and now you can hardly walk under there."

A dry creekbed after in Te Araroa after its water was diverted by January's storm. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

When we put the drone up, we can see why the stream bed is dry.

The Wairenga is forming a new path to the sea, across Carl's land and the surrounding properties. It's a network of waterways winding through different sections, even pooling in some. Significantly, it's separate from the route the stream previously took which didn't interfere with people's use of the land and their homes.

'I can't drive down my drive anymore'

Sarah Jamieson's property is a few blocks over from Carl's.

We meet at her aunt's house, and she walks us through a paddock to get to her place.

"I lost access in January after the [storm]," she tells us. "I can't drive down my drive anymore."

When we get to her property, its two dwellings look out onto a pond filled with noisy ducks basking in the afternoon sun as it peaks between clouds.

Sarah Jamieson can't drive down her driveway anymore. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

It's only when Sarah gets us to look closer that we see the tracks which used to be her driveway. The pond, which has been there since the January storm, has made it unusable.

"That paddock's usually just under water now, doesn't go anywhere - it's got nowhere to go."

Sarah has been parking at her aunt's house since then, traversing the neighbouring paddock on foot to get to her place. The wheelbarrow has been critical for trucking groceries in and rubbish out, she says.

"It's a bit inconvenient, but it is what it is."

Rainfall, she says, changes things dramatically.

After a few hours, the water begins to pool on three sides of her property. The pond creeps up at the eastern side of her land, where one of the two homes is located.

That house was flooded in the January storm, and while it's managed to stay dry since, Sarah says she has abandoned plans to move into it. Instead, she has chosen to stay in the property's second dwelling, which is about 10 metres away but located on slightly higher ground.

"It gets pretty bad," Sarah says.

"[It's] scary because it's getting worse so I don't know if I'm going to be able to stay here for my lifetime, which sucks."

Around the back of Sarah's property, the landscape has also changed since the January storm.

Sarah Jamieson's driveway has been cut off by stormwater following January's storm. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

A new wetland is forming between paddocks, with one steer even taking a dip to get to the grazing spot he wants. The area is filled with logs and debris which has added to the water accumulating around the back of Sarah's land. It also means the water level rises steadily when there is enough rainfall.

"It's a wetland so I'm not sure if we can touch it. We have to talk to the Council on that. But as far as I know, we're not allowed to touch it to clean it," she says.

"So I'm not sure what we can do….It's a bit uneasy, not knowing."

'Within hours of the rain, it's just all up'

Our next stop is Lynda Akuhata-Brown's place. Like Carl, she is on Tokata road, just further away from Pukeamaru maunga and closer to the sea.

I spoke to Lynda and her brother Marcus before travelling to Te Araroa. Both sent me videos of their family land soaked in ankle-deep muddy water due to rainfall.

The afternoon we meet Lynda, she is mowing the lawns and the property looks to be in pretty good nick.

Lynda Akuhata-Brown's property has been flooded at least five times since January. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

She smiles and shows us around, starting with where the water has started to pour in when it rains.

It comes from the western side of the property, downhill from Carl's place, Sarah says. She takes us to the fenceline, and points to the water which now sits on the surface amongst tall grass permanently - even on dry days and weeks.

"So within hours of the rain, it's just all up and then it just continues. It just fills up really fast so it floods really quick," Lynda says.

Since January, the property has been flooded at least five times. Lynda, like many residents, is a keen gardener growing her own vegetables and herbs for kai. The day we're there, the rows of lettuce and silver beet look pretty good, but the potato patch is a whole in the ground.

Lynda says it simply didn't make it through the ongoing floods and she dug it out. Her planter boxes also loose soil every time it rains.

"The last time it rained our toilet system went out so I had to leave the property.

"That's the first time since I've been here it's done that. So obviously the water table's really high. So even though it might be dry here, it's pretty wet under land."

Like Sarah, Lynda says the pattern of flooding has raised questions about her future on her family land.

"[It's] definitely getting worse.

"My concern is that I want to live here and I want to grow my kai on here and my rongoā, and my business is on here as well.

"So that means sometimes I have to shut my business on days where it's toilets out or it's too wet."

She also reckons she is lucky both homes on the property are slightly raised, meaning they haven't been flooded during a rainfall yet.

"I mean, I spend a lot of time on this land too, taking care of it and looking after it. So it's really, really disheartening when it floods."

'The Wairenga stream's got to be cleaned out'

It's a kind of stress and uncertainty that Carl and Sarah are also grappling with.

Carl says he's now spending up to $300 a day on hay bales for his stock because the grass in his paddocks isn't growing.

"Because all our [land], it's all covered in shingle and water, the grass won't grow anymore. So you actually have to feed your animals with hay bales and stock feed.

"It's probably taken like 80 percent of my grazing [land]."

Slash collected on Carl Mullany's farm following January's storm. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He says he and some of his affected neighbours met with the Gisborne District Council last month to see what could be done. He is mindful that while the flooding starts on his land, it's affecting at least half a dozen other properties and big land blocks.

"We had a meeting with the Council right here, and we've all came to the same conclusion that the Wairenga stream's got to be cleaned out from Karakatūwhero river to Pukeamaru."

Carl says a stop bank has also formed near the top of the stream on Pukeamaru, which also has to cleaned out.

"And once they get the creek done, we can fix everything else. I can do everything else and get it back to how it was."

Despite that, Carl says he has heard nothing from the council since the meeting.

Checkpoint asked the Gisborne District Council about the ongoing flooding and the Wairenga stream bed.

It says in a statement that a "technical assessment of the stream and surrounding catchment" has been completed.

"The assessment considers the changes that have occurred in the stream and potential options for addressing the resulting flooding issues."

It says that while the council has undertaken work in the area following weather events, like removing woody debris and restoring access across the stream ford, the Wairenga stream does not fall under its responsibility.

Specifically, it says "Wairenga stream is not part of a council-managed river control or land drainage scheme, so council does not have the same maintenance responsibilities it has for waterways within those schemes".

The council also points out it's the regulatory body for waterways, therefore any work on the stream bed must be approved by them.

"We can provide technical advice to landowners about what work may be appropriate for them to carry out and what consenting requirements apply," it says.

When I ask Carl about what's happening, he shakes his head.

Rivers diverted across properties in Te Araroa following January's storm. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

As far as he understands, he is not allowed to remove anything from the stream bed. He also says he and the other landowners simply can't come up with the cash for the kind of machinery and clean-up job needed on their own.

Meanwhile, Sarah reckons it's not hard to know what people need. In addition to dealing with the new pond and wetland around her property, she's also among a group of residents who still haven't had their water supply restored since the January storm. They're either collecting it in big plastic barrels off their roofs, or carting in external containers as they wait for tanks.

World.title: Cowan warns BBL privatisation could 'spiral out of control'
World.content:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan believes that the Big Bash League doesn't need to rush privatisation to compete with other T20 leagues around the world.

A Cricket NSW board member, Cowan told the ABC Cricket Podcast fears of a player exodus to rival leagues was premature, and a move toward privatisation could "spiral out of control".

Cricket Australia (CA) confirmed earlier this month that they would go ahead with an opt-in model that allows states to take their BBL teams to market with the option of selling stakes or entire franchises to private investors.

"[In previous seasons] they've been able to reshape scheduling, to reshape international stars and the salary cap around that. We've seen already there's no friction to attracting some of the world's best players," Cowan said.

Former England captain Ben Stokes will join the Adelaide Strikers for BBL16. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde-ICC)

"Ben Stokes is going to Adelaide, Finn Allen has just signed a mega deal. So the argument that is put forward is we're gonna lose players to the South African League. We haven't lost one yet.

"There's a view that the business could be run more effectively, which would enable some time to work out whether you actually do need to sell your star assets or not.

"Because when you start burning the furniture to warm the house, it can spiral quickly out of control from there."

The BBL has, in recent seasons, reshaped the fixture of the competition to make it shorter and in turn has increased viewership and attracted some of the games biggest names.

In the 2025/26 BBL season fans were treated to the likes of Colin Munro, Chris Jordan, Muhammed Rizwan and Sam Billings tearing up the competition. Coupled with Australian Test stars like Steve Smith, Alex Carey and Mitchell Starc who joined the tournament after their international duties finished.

Steve Smith has played 40 matches for the Sydney Sixers, including 6 in BBL15. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Compare that with recent seasons of The Hundred where Mitchell Marsh, Adam Zampa, Jos Buttler and Trent Boult were some of the biggest name players in that competition, all of whom have played in the tournament or are set to play in the upcoming BBL16 season.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

Cricket Australia believes that privatisation would allow the BBL to keep up with other T20 leagues around the world, like The Hundred in the UK and the SA20 in South Africa.

"There are opportunities now for our best Australian players to play in other leagues at the same time potentially with bigger salary caps. So when we talk about should we wait for two years or four years? No, we can't wait," CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said.

"Those challenges are on our doorstep today. So we've got to make some decisions about how we compete.

"We're a relatively small country in a big global sport. So it's incumbent on us to make decisions that we can compete with elsewhere and that's exactly what we're doing."

Cricket NSW has been the most vocally opposed to the current model, while Queensland Cricket has also said it will likely have further questions but intends to hold on to its BBL franchise for the time being.

Mitch March playing for the Leeds Sunrisers in The Hundred in the UK. (Getty Images: Annabel Lee-Ellis)

"We will closely monitor the sales process and at this stage, intend to retain 100 percent ownership of the Brisbane Heat, but of course remain open to private investment at the appropriate time," Qld Cricket Chair Kirsten Pike and CEO Terry Svenson said in a statement.

Meanwhile, Cricket Victoria is in support of the move, and will be the first to sell a license with the Melbourne Renegades set to be put to market to be sold in full.

"Private investment will unlock value for reinvestment across Victorian cricket, from the grassroots through to the elite game," Cricket Victoria Director Shaun Richardson said in a statement.

CA and the state's cricketing associations will continue negotiations ahead of the BBL16 and WBBL12 seasons starting, which are likely to be the last seasons involving the original eight franchises.

World.title: Longmuir, Dockers vow they won't be 'ambushed' by undermanned Swans
World.content:
Many see it as a golden opportunity for Fremantle to reach just their second AFL grand final, but Justin Longmuir insists there is no chance the Dockers will underestimate a Sydney side missing a host of star players in Friday night's preliminary final at the SCG.

Fremantle is set to enter the game as warm favourite, despite being away from home against a team which thrashed reigning premier Brisbane by 53 points in their qualifying final, with the Swans hard hit by suspension and injury.

When Sydney stood down Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice in the wake of the off-field scandal at a Melbourne hotel, Swans chairman Andrew Pridham said they had "effectively torpedoed" their season.

Remarkably since then, they have defied expectations, beating North Melbourne just days later before the stunning upset of the Lions.

Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

That was despite losing Callum Mills during the game, with the captain joining the long list of absentees, ruled out for the season with a knee injury.

Longmuir has urged his side to put its full focus on the Sydney players who are taking the field, rather than those ruled out.

"Already done that. They dropped 141 points on Brisbane who were the flag favourites, it's a wake-up call," he said.

Errol Gulden and the Swans are undermanned but coming off a dominant qualifying final win. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"They didn't seem to miss those guys, so we just play what's in front of us.

"Clearly they haven't lost any of their scoring power, and all I can go on is what I see from the last two games, and playing like a really galvanised team, playing with great spirit, great physicality.

"It looks like whatever has happened has galvanised them, and they're playing a really tough brand of footy.

"We're definitely not going up there and getting ambushed by what they're trying to do. We've seen [it] in the last couple of weeks and we've seen it work really well.

"We've got to make sure that we don't just think it's going to happen for us, we've got to make sure we impose our footy."

Longmuir calls for no fear

The Dockers rebounded from their qualifying final loss to Hawthorn with a 14-point semifinal victory over Geelong, with Longmuir pleased with how his players took the contest on against the Cats.

Luke Jackson was instrumental in Fremantle's semifinal win and shapes as a big factor against Sydney. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

He urged his side to not to be afraid of making mistakes on the big stage, and to always be prepared to move on to the next contest.

"If we're going to make mistakes, let's make sure we make mistakes playing our way and playing with the right mindset, because usually those mistakes you can move on from a little bit quicker," he said.

Dockers show they have the steel to be AFL's best Fremantle booked a spot in the AFL preliminary finals with a stirring win over Geelong, breathing life into the club's premiership dream.

"At times we didn't make those mistakes the right way against Hawthorn and we stood still after, because we didn't move on from them.

"It's been a message for a long time because we play such an imperfect game, players who have played their best games would've been full of mistakes. It's just the nature and the scrappiness of our game, so let's make them with the right mindset."

The Dockers are set to fly to Sydney on Wednesday, with the two clubs naming their teams on Thursday ahead of the clash.

World.title: The moment this Knights finals rookie will hold on to forever
World.content:
Last Friday's semifinal win over South Sydney was one of the great nights in Newcastle's recent history, and nobody enjoyed it more than Jermaine McEwen.

In his first finals match, the 21-year-old had the game of his young life, inspiring the 20-10 upset victory that has the whole Hunter dreaming big ahead of Sunday's sudden-death clash with the Warriors.

McEwen scored the first double of his NRL career and ran for 187 metres, the best mark of his 37 first-grade matches, and set the tone for the Knights' right-edge defence with a physical brutality that would make a mafia kingpin proud.

Knights win is proof the future has come Stars were born under the finals lights as Newcastle knockout finals win over South Sydney announced the dawn of a new tomorrow.

On a night of many highlights, McEwen's personal favourite was his second try that helped Newcastle kick clear in the second half, as he backed up winger Dom Young to score right in front of the Knights faithful.

McEwen crawled the last few metres before slamming the ball down so hard it's a wonder they could dig it out of the turf.

"The only reason I slammed it was because my parents and my family were right in front of me. I just looked at them, and I was like, 'hell yeah,'" said McEwen.

"That was the best moment I have ever had in my footy career. That moment right there, that's something I will hold forever. So I am just super grateful and so happy."

McEwen's first try of the evening helped get things started as he again trailed Young after the Englishman claimed a bomb inside the first five minutes.

It brought Newcastle into the match and gave the team the start they needed en route to their first away finals win since 2013 and just their third since their last premiership 25 years ago.

Repeating the dose in Auckland is a tall order, but even before the win over Souths, McEwen and his teammates did not lack for belief.

"The Knights have given me everything, and I believe in the coach, Justin (Holbrook). He's allowed me to be the greatest version of myself on that field," said McEwen.

"But when I put the ball down and looked up and saw all the fans, I was (thinking) how happy I am to be a Knight. I'm just so grateful.

"We just wanted to go out there and play with energy and lift each other up."

Newcastle's right edge did a fine job shutting down South Sydney's attack. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

McEwen spent much of the week thinking about how the Knights would shut down South Sydney's left edge, which is just about the most dangerous attacking weapon in the NRL.

Between them, Alex Johnston, Latrell Mitchell, Tallis Duncan and Cody Walker scored 63 tries in 2026, two more than Newcastle managed as an entire club last season.

But McEwen, Sandon Smith and Dane Gagai rose to the occasion magnificently, locking onto the superstars and refusing to let go, moving and defending as one.

Souths did end up scoring down the left through Jye Grey, but only after McEwen had left the field late on.

"When you have challenges, you get more prepared for it. You think about it more. When you're at home or training, you get flashbacks of what you have to do," said McEwen.

"When I have Cody Walker and their left edge — they do it the best in the whole comp. Cody Walker, he is just so good at that stuff.

"Us in D, we had a big job to do, and we just went out there and did it."

Jermaine McEwen and the Knights will look to pull off another finals ambush this Sunday against the Warriors. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The journey through this year to Sunday's knockout final has not always been smooth for McEwen.

He was suspended for one match in June after being charged with low-range drink driving, an incident for which he apologised unreservedly and left him "deeply ashamed".

At the time, McEwen said he let his community down, and he's been trying to make amends ever since.

"Bro, at the end of the day we're all human and just because I play footy doesn't mean I'm special," said McEwen.

"In those circumstances, with the rollercoaster (of this year), that has taught me a lot in life.

"I feel like people can either shy away from it or own up to it. I wanted to show up for the fans and show them what I could do, and repay them in that way."

"Because I know how much the town speaks to this club and the hold this club has on the town. I wanted to repay them with good footy."

A sellout crowd is expected at Eden Park on Sunday, and a win would send Newcastle to just its second preliminary final in the last 25 years.

They'll again be underdogs against a Warriors side that beat them just three weeks ago, and the match marks the biggest game of McEwen's career, as it is for several of his teammates.

But the same was true last Friday, and by leaning on the experience of men like Gagai and prop Tyson Frizell, McEwen was inspired to make a difference, and all he wants is to do it all over again.

"These are experienced boys who have been in the game for a lot of years, and when you have them talk to you, it makes you more comfortable," said McEwen.

"You're not nervous. You're going out there to do a good job."

World.title: HYROX apologises after Aussie athlete soils herself mid-race
World.content:
A founder of HYROX has apologised after an athlete who suffered sudden faecal incontinence mid-competition was allowed to continue, with the incident sparking rule changes after backlash online.

Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk experienced the medical episode during the competition that she went on to win in Beijing at the weekend.

The incident went viral on Chinese social media, with videos of her competing while visibly soiled shared widely.

HYROX sees competitors combine running with multiple workout station challenges, including sandbag lunges, burpees, sled pushes and rowing using shared equipment.

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) holds the HYROX Women's Solo Pro world record. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

Following the incident, many online criticised HYROX's health and safety standards, while some also questioned athlete responsibility.

"Blast HYROX. Blast the race director," Chris Hersh posted on a HYROX community Facebook page.

"But please leave the athlete alone or have a tiny bit of empathy for someone that really just was in a horrible situation and got zero assistance from anyone in a high pressure, make a decision on the fly scenario."

HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste took to Instagram to apologise "to all who were directly or indirectly involved".

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race," Fürste said in a statement on Instagram.

"In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not."

He said that new event procedures and rules were being drawn up to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

The rules now state that if a "racer's blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers, a Race Director may withdraw the racer from the race on medical grounds".

Before the rule change, competitors were penalised for littering, spitting, or clearing their nostrils onto the race course, which some online described as a double standard.

Following the event in Beijing, HYROX World issued a statement saying that "protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".

HYROX China said the competition area was cleaned after the competition finished and relevant equipment was removed.

It also said it would replace the floor at the venue to protect future athletes.

The incident went viral in China, with many taking aim at HYROX organisers and rules. (Weibo, RedNote and Douyin)

Wietrzyk, an elite HYROX athlete, was invited to compete at the Beijing event.

She has been contacted for comment.

The ABC has also contacted HYROX for comment.

Event's growing popularity

HYROX is held in indoor venues, with a consistent race format that lets athletes compete against each other worldwide.

Organisers say it suits both elite athletes and people trying to improve their general fitness.

Chinese netizens have described HYROX as "paying to do farm work", with an individual entry fee of 799 yuan (about $170), on top of the cost of training and equipment.

The sport has attracted Chinese celebrities, including elite athletes, singers, and actors, helping it reach beyond the traditional fitness crowd.

Hybrid training is a healthy social media trend Thousands of social media followers are trying out the hybrid training model, but it's not something to dive straight into.

Some Chinese media have even dubbed HYROX "the new identity card of the middle class".

HYROX held its first event in mainland China in November 2024, attracting fewer than 1,700 contestants.

By 2025, average registrations had surged to 5,079 per event — more than three times the previous year's figure, according to Grace Yu, research director at Daxue Consulting.

"China's HYROX scene is heavily community-oriented, with doubles and relay formats accounting for roughly 66-72 per cent of Beijing participants across 2024-2026," Ms Yu said.

By April 2026, the #hyrox hashtag on Xiaohongshu, known as RedNote outside China, had surpassed 130 million views and generated more than 780,000 discussions.

World.title: Young Brisbane Lions star Logan Morris re-signs with reigning premiers
World.content:
Young Brisbane Lions star Logan Morris has signed a two-year contract extension, tying him to the club until the end of 2029.

The 21-year-old, who earned his first All-Australian blazer this year, was set to be one of the biggest names on the market at the end of next season.

The signing comes as the Lions prepare to take on the Hawks in a preliminary final on Saturday at the MCG.

"There’s no point dragging [contract negotiations] out if I know what I want to do, and I wanted to stay at Brisbane," Morris said.

"I wanted to just get it done and now I can focus on this week, and hopefully the next few years will be exciting."

Morris kicked 67 goals in the 2026 home-and-away season, finishing second in the Coleman Medal behind Sydney's Charlie Curnow.

It marks the third huge signing coup for the Lions in a week, after Zac Bailey and Dayne Zorko also extended their careers with the club.

When asked about interest from other clubs that may have made higher offers, Morris said he had not given much thought to the money.

"I just thought … more about what I'm happy with and the team that I'm at; I don't want to leave a team where I'm happy where I am mentally and I've got a good group of mates," he said.

"I think playing within a good team that’s got good values and playing with all my mates is more valuable to me than a bit more money, so that's what it ultimately came down to."

World.title: Ella Heads cops big ban for bump that broke star Demon's jaw
World.content:
Port Adelaide defender Ella Heads has been handed a three-match AFLW ban for her bump that fractured the jaw of Melbourne's Eliza McNamara.

McNamara had just fired off a handball in Sunday's 51-point win when Heads ran in and collected the midfielder front-on with her shoulder.

A dazed McNamara had blood coming out from her face as she was assisted from the ground.

The 24-year-old was taken to hospital, with the Demons confirming on Monday she had undergone surgery, with no timeline set for her return.

The incident was classified as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact, drawing a three-match ban.

"That was a really poor challenge," former AFLW star Kate McCarthy said.

"It was probably one of the worst bumps I’ve seen on the AFLW field in regards to being late, being high and just being really careless and not eliciting that duty of care that we now know is placed on you as an AFLW player when you elect to bump."

That equates to a quarter of the 12-round home-and-away season, and Heads will miss games against Sydney, the Western Bulldogs and Adelaide unless Port can downgrade the charge.

In other tribunal news, West Coast's Abbygail Bushby was handed a one-match ban for her clumsy collision with the Brisbane Lions' Sophie Peters.

Peters had her head over the ball when Bushby ran in and tumbled over her opponent.

Richmond's Montana McKinnon was handed a one-match rough conduct ban for her run-in with St Kilda's Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw.

World.title: India refuses to accept Asia Cup cricket trophy from Pakistani minister
World.content:
Political tensions between India and Pakistan have spilled onto the cricket field again, with India's women refusing to accept the Asia Cup trophy from Asian Cricket Council (ACC) chairman Mohsin Naqvi.

India dominated from the start to win the tournament for a record eighth time, beating Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final in Dubai.

After winning the toss, India scored 5-183 before dismissing Sri Lanka for 111 in 20 overs.

The presentation ceremony was delayed nearly an hour, during which the Indian team conducted its own medal presentation, with Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia presenting the best fielder medal to Nandani Sharma.

Naqvi — chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board and the ACC, as well as Pakistan's interior minister — stood on the dais with several ACC officials, but the Indian team did not appear to receive medals or the trophy, with social media footage showing them leaving the field as the officials waited on stage.

The ceremony ended abruptly after medals were presented to the Sri Lankan team and match officials, and Naqvi presented the runners-up cheque to Sri Lanka captain Chamari Athapaththu.

"This is BCCI's stand [to not take trophy from Naqvi]. We can't say anything on this," India coach Amol Muzumdar said.

"India are officially the champions. Trophy or no trophy doesn't matter to us.

"For us, this tournament is over, we are the champions. That's good enough. It was on the big board that India are the champions of Asia Cup 2026."

Cross-border tensions between India and Pakistan brought the two countries to the brink of war last year, with the acrimony also spilling onto the cricket field. Indian cricketers have avoided handshakes with Pakistan players and refused to accept the trophy and medals from a Pakistani official at several tournaments.

The Indian men's team beat Pakistan three times in the Asia Cup, including the final, but Suryakumar Yadav's team refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi and did not shake hands with Pakistan players in any of the three games.

The Indian women's team did not shake hands with the Pakistan team in its match earlier in the tournament, after which Muzumdar also said: "That stand has been taken by BCCI and we stand by it."

World.title: The Stinear effect: The stat changing Geelong in 2026
World.content:
The biggest coup of the off-season wasn't Anne Hatchard to Gold Coast, Taylor Smith to Sydney, or Eden Zanker to Fremantle.

It was premiership coach Mick Stinear's shift away from Melbourne to take the reins at Geelong.

He became the first coach to be poached by another club, leaving his position to take up another, and just the third coach to ply their trade at a second club.

The reasons behind Geelong's desperation to appoint Stinear have been immediately evident. Outside of a big round one loss to two-time reigning premier North Melbourne, the Cats have found their feet in a new style.

And although there have been early challenges on the injury front — the club has been forced to name top up players in its extended squad already this year — the system itself has proved sound.

Stinear's signature stat

Aishling Moloney has been a vital goal kicker for the Cats. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Josh Chadwick)

Teams coached by Stinear have one thing in common: Goal Assists are a priority. Sharing the ball neatly around the attacking arc to generate the highest percentage opportunity to score has always been fundamental to how his teams work, and that has already become a feature of Geelong in 2026.

Leading Melbourne for the first 10 seasons of its life in the AFLW, the Demons sat in the top two for goal assists in four of the five seasons from 2022 S6 onward. The one outlier was 2024, where the club was desperately stretched due to an onslaught of injury.

Melbourne's Goal Assists Avg. goal assists AFLW rank AFLW average 2025 5.3 2 3.6 2024 3.1 8 3.0 2023 6.3 1 3.4 2022 (S7) 4.2 1 2.6 2022 (S6) 3.9 2 2.5

This year the Cats average 7.8 goal assists — sitting second in the league behind only North Melbourne — and as a result, a host of other key scoring statistics have improved dramatically.

Aishling Moloney leads the way for the stat, with 1.6 per game, while having also kicked seven goals in the opening five games, but there are a total of seven Cats averaging 0.6 goal assists or more in that time.

Only two Geelong players averaged 0.6 or more goal assists across the 2025 AFLW season; Julia Crockett-Grills with 1.0, and Moloney with 0.6.

Julia Crockett-Grills averaged one goal assist per game in the 2025 AFLW season. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Elsby)

Because of this increased willingness to bring teammates in and create those deeper forward entries by way of looking for goal assist opportunities, Geelong is kicking more than four more goals per game in 2026, and goaling more regularly from the inside 50s it creates than in years gone past.

In five games the Cats have already kicked 50 goals. They kicked 69 across the whole of 2025.

They have made a marginal improvement on average inside 50s, but it is what they are doing once in the arc that has been the real difference.

Geelong's growing attack Avg. Points For Avg. Inside 50s Avg. Goal Efficiency (%) Avg. Goal Assists Avg. Goal Accuracy (%) Avg. Goal Kickers 2026 66.2 36.2 27.6 7.8 55.0 6.4 2025 41.7 32.6 17.7 3.4 36.3 4.1 2024 43.6 32.6 19.0 4.2 44.7 4.3 2023* 44.9 33.8 18.9 4.5 41.3 4.6

*Geelong reached the preliminary final

Getting it there

Obviously, to create these opportunities ahead of the ball, movement up the field needs to be more effective.

The Cats currently sit number one in the AFLW for disposal efficiency at an average of 69.8 per cent — this is something that the club has prided itself on in recent years.

The Cats move the ball via the hand a lot more under Mick Stinear. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Elsby)

The shift in disposal, however, has come via the method. A greater reliance on moving the ball by hand has been clear, with a league-low kick rate of 54.5 per cent, and a significant increase in uncontested possession indicates greater control outside the contest.

Issues of recent years are still present — ruck availability and strength is still a concern, clearance numbers have only marginally grown compared to 2025 — but the capacity to adapt on the outside has been the difference.

Outside ball Avg. uncontested possession Avg. contested possession rate (%) 2026 166.0 41.8 2025 136.4 45.8 2024 124.3 45.8 2023 131.5 46.0

Generating and scoring from turnover is a clear point of improvement, with the Cats averaging 24.0 points per game from the source in 2025 compared to its 42.6 points this year.

From turnover, they are effectively getting on the move, handballing to runners, and going quickly.

Becky Webster's work across the half back line, to intercept and drive the ball forward has been crucial in this respect, as has Mikayla Bowen's hard two-way running efforts while also carrying a heavy load through the midfield.

Not yet the complete package

Mick Stinear has moved to the Cats from Melbourne. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

While there are plenty of positive signs when it comes to Geelong's attacking game, there is still room for improvement in its defensive phase.

Conceding higher scores, more inside 50s, and more marks in the opposition's attacking zone, there is a vulnerability when sides can get the ball moving quickly against them.

There is an element of high risk, high reward in the game style the Cats have employed this year, and they are only five matches into the system, but protecting that defence more effectively is surely high on Stinear's priority list as they continue through the season.

Opposition attack Avg. Points Against Avg. Inside 50s Conceded Avg. Marks Inside 50s Conceded Avg. Shot Efficiency Conceded (%) 2026 53.8 38.4 9.6 50.0 2025 44.9 33.4 7.5 40.9 2024 39.7 30.7 6.3 44.4 2023 33.4 27.5 5.5 43.9

It is worth mentioning that after the Cats' round one loss to powerhouse North Melbourne, their average score conceded is in fact 42.3 points, indicating an improvement in that area.

But as the old adage goes; to be the best, you have to beat the best.

Come finals, this system needs to be able to stand up to what North Melbourne — or Stinear's old side Melbourne — has to offer.

There is every indication to suggest it can, but without a match against the Demons fixtured in the home and away season, and the Roos already in the rear view mirror, finals will be the chance to really test the system once more.

Tech.title: Volvo’s plug-in hybrid XC60 and XC90 can really go the distance
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Most plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEV) today get an average of around 30-50 miles of battery-only range: decent, but not mind-blowing. With hybrid sales dominating the market today, Volvo is out to prove that its PHEVs can push the limits of what’s possible.

Today, the Swedish automaker revealed the updated PHEV versions of its popular XC60 and XC90 SUVs are its first “long range plug-in hybrids,” delivering class-leading ranges of 78 miles and 73 miles, respectively. That’s more than double the electric range of previous PHEV variant. The numbers are still preliminary and based on EPA testing standards. But if confirmed, they would make Volvo’s PHEVs “the longest electric range of any plug-in hybrids available in the American market,” the automaker claims.

Volvo took a page from its all-electric vehicle design by integrating the battery directly in the floor of both vehicles for improved efficiency. The batteries are also higher capacity — 41.2 kWh (37.9 kWh usable) for both — and able to send more energy to the motors, which are also more powerful.

Previous Next



1 / 3

Of course, those batteries are just dead weight if owners forget to charge them — which tends to happen with a lot of plug-in hybrids. Hybrid owners often neglect to charge, thanks to the gas tank that continues to power their vehicle even with a dead battery. Still, the higher capacity batteries in the XC60 and XC90 are sure to appeal to a lot of car shoppers who may still like the sound of increased range even if they don’t exactly plan on taking full advantage of it.

The XC60 is getting new styling to bring it inline with Volvo’s new design language. That includes an upgraded grille, redesigned front bumper, hood, front wings, rear bumper, tailgate, new wheel designs, and a refined “Thor’s Hammer” LED headlight light signature. Like the redesigned XC40, the XC60 also has a more expansive driver assist that includes Automatic Emergency Steering and Braking, collision prevention, and a door-opening cyclist alert.

The addition of Google’s Gemini chatbot as the new voice assistant rounds everything out. Volvo was one of the first automakers to adopt Google’s software for its infotainment systems, so naturally that now includes Gemini.

Production on the the XC60 and XC90 begins late Fall 2026, with customer deliveries scheduled to begin in early 2027. Volvo is hoping that a boost in hybrid sales can help fund its future pure EV models, like the EX50, EX60, and new affordable model that will replace the EX30.

Tech.title: Valve is still figuring out ‘how and when’ to do Steam Deck 2
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Now that Valve has finally launched its entire 2026 hardware lineup — the Steam Controller, the Steam Machine, and today’s Steam Frame — are we any closer to a next-gen Steam Deck handheld? Valve isn’t saying so yet. The company is figuring out “how and when we can deliver something like that,” Valve designer Pierre-Loup Griffais now tells IGN.

Valve has been clear for years that 1) a Steam Deck 2 will indeed happen, and 2) it’s not coming until Valve finds the right chip. The original Steam Deck worked because it delivered the right combination of price, performance, and battery life, and Valve has repeatedly said it won’t sacrifice efficiency in the sequel.

“We also don’t want more performance to come at a significant cost to power efficiency and battery life,” Griffais told me in 2023, saying he wanted to see a “leap” instead — but suggesting that leap might not be physically possible for another couple of years.

Earlier this year, Valve got my hopes up that the wait for a chip was over — when Griffais revealed the team was “hard at work” on the next Steam Deck gaming handheld in an interview with IGN. He wouldn’t say when it might happen. I assumed that was caution, because RAMageddon had already pushed the company to delay and reprice the Steam Machine and Steam Frame headset by then.

Today, IGN’s new question was: “Has the current hardware shortage impacted the way Valve is thinking about actually putting a Steam Deck 2 into development?” Griffais’ immediate answer was “Not really.”

That could be good news for impatient gamers — or it could mean that the company will wait out RAMageddon before it dares intercept the silicon supply chain again. Valve originally wanted to build a “far more affordable” headset, for instance, but instead it faced brutal RAM negotiations to eventually arrive at a $1,059 pricetag.

The real question is: has Valve yet identified the future chip that will appear in the Steam Deck 2? Because the company will work backwards from that chip’s availability to create the hardware it lives within.

Intel’s Panther Lake handheld chip in the MSI Claw 8 EX AI Plus is the first I’ve tried that comes close to the kind of “generational leap” that Griffais has been talking about, but Panther Lake handhelds are incredibly expensive, and the Intel chip wasn’t a silver bullet in my tests. But I bet Valve has seen the future of Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm chips, and maybe a future one will do the trick.

I hope a Steam Deck 2 will kickstart a new golden age of handheld gaming; I fear it may cost too much for that.

Tech.title: Is Big Tech’s AI slowdown a safety pact or a cartel?
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX head Elon Musk loosely agreed over the weekend to slow down AI development, skeptics spotted an ulterior motive immediately. The AI titans had declared that their aim was to “pace the frontier,” signing on at least partially to a proposal for embedding third-party auditors, regulating domestic labs, and reaching a global slowdown agreement. Their critics, however, argued they simply wanted to stop would-be competitors, kneecap the open-source movement, and avoid real legal safeguards — some dubbed it an outright “cartel.”

The truth is more complicated, according to sources across the industry. The three-step proposal, laid out in an essay by Amodei, is calling for changes long espoused by AI safety advocates. While it could become a substitute for regulation, under Trump, substantial regulation is unlikely anyway. But experts say that on an issue that’s only likely to grow in importance, AI leaders aren’t the best people to lead the charge.

“The industry as a whole needs new champions,” said Nick Reese, an adjunct professor at New York University and the Department of Homeland Security’s former director of emerging tech policy. “We’ve looked at people like Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk as these people who are closest to the problem and working on it every day, and they’re the ones who know best. But the truth is there’s never been a realistic vision for what we’re building toward.”

“The industry as a whole needs new champions.”

Concerns about AI advancement have been escalating for months, sparked largely by revelations that swarms of agents were behind rogue hacks going on right under the noses of leading frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI. Reports from both companies fueled the fire, as did the resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who posted a public letter explaining his choice. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he wrote, adding that neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is “acting responsibly” and rather “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Dire warnings about AI aren’t anything new inside the industry, but Coxon’s letter seemed to break containment. It’s been viewed more than 170 million times on X alone, while Coxon and his story have made the rounds in newspapers and on TV.

To a significant chunk of AI safety researchers and AI nonprofit workers, however, this is simply drawing more attention to an already widely discussed issue. “A lot of people are thinking of this as Dario’s idea, or it’s coming from the CEOs, but that’s false,” said Daniel Kokotajlo, an ex-OpenAI employee who now leads the AI Futures Project, an AI research nonprofit. “People outside the companies have been calling for this for years … There’s been this growing chorus of voices saying, ‘Please don’t build superintelligence soon. We are not ready. You need to slow down.’”

Kokotajlo said that after years of people “yelling at them to do this” — including more than 1,000 AI lab employees signing a public letter from July, which called for a slowdown in AI development after the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident — the CEOs are now “now bowing to that pressure and also claiming credit for it, [although] not rightfully.”

Overall, a handful of sources told The Verge they believe that the verbal agreement made by the AI leaders is a step in the right direction. NYU’s Reese said he “do[es] not think it’s all hot air.” Apollo Research CEO Marius Hobbhahn called it “a good idea,” saying “it’s one of the best things for safety in a long time if it actually happens.” The Midas Project’s Tyler Johnston said it was a “good sign.” Redwood Research CEO Buck Shlegeris said it was “some great news — obviously it’s hard to know whether this is going to convert into anything real, but I’m feeling cautiously optimistic.” All agreed, though, that there was still a lot of work to do to make this verbal commitment a reality, particularly when it comes to making it an ironclad agreement.

“It’s one of the best things for safety in a long time if it actually happens.”

Many still question the motivations of AI’s leaders. The larger tech industry has spent years getting ahead of regulation by lobbying for its own preferred rules or promising self-regulation. Big platforms have proposed policies that could hit smaller competitors harder, using altruistic language to justify self-serving goals. They’ve been accused of safety-washing, or making meaningless changes that give the false impression of actual safeguards. It’s no surprise people are concerned this will happen in the AI industry as well, particularly since AI labs’ voluntary safety frameworks have been criticized for years.

Several sources believe that concerns of safety-washing are valid. “There’s a serious concern that they’re not actually going to slow down,” Kokotajlo says, adding that the fear is that “they’ll just bring in some external auditors, do a bunch of safety paperwork — some of which will be genuinely good — but at the end of the day, it actually won’t slow them down very much at all.”

NYU’s Reese compared this gambit to the social media platforms’ playbook a decade ago, when companies began calling for regulatory action to get ahead of impending, less favorable laws. For the AI industry, Reese said, “the hammer may not come in this administration, but I think if there were a Democratic administration after the next election, there would be a really good possibility.”

That kind of regulation would be vital, said Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project. She said any voluntary framework is essentially regulatory capture and that “we should not be letting the foxes run the henhouse. This is not an opportunity for Congress to once again outsource responsibility to industry.” Daniel Lobo-Lewis, co-founder of the Political Integrity Project, said that voluntary regulation will likely go the way of Meta’s largely toothless Oversight Board.

Most people also, however, believe companies are in no imminent danger of regulation, besides the model pre-release review periods AI labs have agreed to under the Trump administration. President Trump posted on Monday that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” He also called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while Huang was onstage at a conference — Trump told the crowd on speakerphone that recent concerns about AI were a “hoax” and that “the robots will not be taking over.”
